metadata.title: Mass Tort Litigation: How Companies Defend Claims Involving Multiple Plaintiffs
metadata.author: Logan Mayer LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
Episode Summary: 
In this episode of Risk, Liability and Litigation with Kevin C. Mayer, host Lisa Mosbey engages with Kevin Mayer, a seasoned trial attorney, to explore the intricacies of mass tort litigation. Kevin begins by defining mass torts and contrasts them with single lawsuits, emphasizing the scale and complexity involved. He delves into the coordination of cases through judicial council coordinated proceedings (JCCP) and multi-district litigation (MDL), highlighting how these structures manage numerous related claims. The discussion covers the strategic considerations companies must evaluate as isolated claims evolve into broader litigation, including exposure assessment, reputational risks, and the role of bellwether trials. Kevin also explains the defense strategies for varied claims and the potential impact of mass torts on a company's operations and reputation. Listeners will gain valuable insights into the legal and business challenges of mass tort litigation and how to navigate them effectively.

Key Timestamps:
00:01 – Introduction
0:46 – Definition of Mass Tort Litigation
1:49 – Differences Between Mass Tort and Single Lawsuits
2:59 – Coordination of Related Cases
4:30 – Evaluating Exposure and Risks
6:15 – Variability in Plaintiff Claims
7:34 – Bellwether Trials Explained
9:44 – Global Resolution Strategies
10:28 – Defense Against Varied Claims
12:31 – Factors in Resolving Claims
14:52 – Impact Beyond Lawsuits
15:34 – Government Scrutiny and Reputational Damage

About the Show: 
Risk, Liability and Litigation with Kevin C. Mayer is a podcast dedicated to unraveling the complexities of legal challenges faced by businesses. Hosted by seasoned trial attorney Kevin Mayer, the show provides in-depth discussions on mass torts, liability, and litigation strategies. Designed for business owners, legal professionals, and anyone interested in understanding the legal landscape, the podcast offers expert insights and practical advice. Each episode aims to equip listeners with the knowledge needed to navigate high-stakes legal situations effectively and make informed decisions.

#MassTort #LitigationStrategy #KevinMayer #LegalChallenges

segments.text: Welcome to Risk, Liability, and
Litigation with Kevin Mayer.
Welcome back to Risk, Liability, and
Litigation with Kevin C. Mayor, partner
at Logan Mayor LLP in California. Kevin
is a seasoned trial attorney with
decades of experience handling mass tort
and other complex litigation for
businesses facing large numbers of
related claims. I'm Lisa Mosby and today
we're looking at how mass tor litigation
develops and what companies face when
similar claims begin multiplying.
Welcome Kevin. It's good to be back with
you again.
>> Thanks so much Lisa. Great to see you
again.
>> You know we're talking about mass tort
litigation. But before we get into the
details of that, could you share with us
a definition of mass tort litigation?
>> Right. So we start with what is a tort?
It is a civil wrong and that can take
many forms. Obviously, it could be a
product liability claim. It could be a
negligence claim. It could be a breach
of warranty claim. And when we talk
about mass tort, we're literally talking
about in essence the number of
claimants, the number of plaintiffs who
are involved. So instead of having what
I would call a one-off situation where
you have one individual who has been
affected in some way by either the
conduct or the product of another and
they file a lawsuit. Here we have many
people who are alleged to have been
affected in largely the same way. That
could be countywide, statewide or
nationwide. And indeed sometimes it
becomes international in its scope. So
when we talk about mass tort, we're
talking about a substantial number of
similar claims.
>> And how does defending a mass tort
differ from defending a single lawsuit
involving the same product or alleged
harm?
>> Well, at bottom, it's really about the
cost and the resources and the time and
the personnel that have to be devoted to
addressing this litigation. And the
plaintiff's bar has become
extraordinarily sophisticated over many
decades of dealing with various types of
mass tor claims in terms of bringing
appropriate organization and resources
and most of all money to the table in
order to litigate these claims against
the defendant or in some cases multiple
defendants who are involved. So when a
company gets involved in a mass tor

metadata.title: Inside the Making of A Mass Tort  | Coral M. Odiot-Rivera & Silvino John Diaz
metadata.author: On The Docket with Napoli Shkolnik
metadata.shortDescription:
How does one person’s experience become part of a major national litigation?

In “Inside the Making of a Mass Tort,” attorneys Silvino John Díaz and Coral M. Odiot-Rivera explain how legal teams identify patterns, investigate potential claims, and manage thousands of cases while keeping each person’s circumstances in focus.

In this episode of On the Docket, we explore:

• The differences between mass torts, class actions, and multidistrict litigation
• How medical records, research, and expert analysis help attorneys evaluate claims
• Why people affected by the same product or exposure may have different cases
• The work happening behind the scenes during lengthy litigation

A conversation about the investigation, coordination, and individual stories behind large scale litigation.

Subscribe to On the Docket for more conversations with the attorneys behind the cases.

Learn more: https://www.napolilaw.com

This episode is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice.

metadata.title: Ep 70 - Private Equity, MSOs, and the Ethics of Law Firm Ownership
metadata.author: Confido Legal
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of Financially Legal, Confido Legal co-founder Emery Wager sits down with Trisha Rich and Josh Porte of Holland & Knight to explore the legal ethics behind the rise of Management Service Organizations (MSOs) and private equity investment in law firms.

With over 100 law firm MSO transactions closed or in progress at Holland & Knight, Trisha and Josh bring a firsthand perspective on how these deals are structured and where the ethical boundaries lie.

The conversation covers ABA Model Rule 5.4, what MSOs can and cannot control, how management fees are structured without violating fee-sharing rules, and the growing regulatory activity in states like Illinois and Colorado. They also discuss why private equity is entering the legal industry now, what law firms should watch out for when considering an MSO partnership, and how these arrangements could ultimately impact the client experience.

As the legal industry attracts more outside capital and technology, this episode explores how law firms can pursue growth while protecting lawyer independence and the attorney-client relationship.

Law firms that use call centers are very, very common. >> Quickly add that while 5.4 is the rule that gets a lot of attention in these conversations, these structures are really built around rule 5.3, which allows law firms to outsource non-legal business services to third-party vendors, so long as the lawyers are supervising the provision of those services on behalf of their clients, and so long as the service providers uh comply with the lawyers' underlying ethical obligations to the underlying clients. So, that really is at the heart of of what this MSO relationship is. And while 5.4 certainly tells you, you know, where to draw the line and what and what the MSO cannot do, we view 5.3 is more of an affirmative, you know, these are the conditions under which this type of a structure is is permissible and in which which can work. >> What What can an MSO do to manage uh trust account? What access can they have? What access can they not have? >> So, a trust account for a lawyer law firm is an account that we have to have to hold other people's money in trust. Those need to remain in the law firms and with the lawyers. Um that is in our view um a pretty, you know, a pretty important principle. Um and so, the lawyers maintain ownership of those trust accounts. That's a different than a law firm's operating account, which is like its business account on like, you know, how it pays its light bills and its salary and things like that. >> Yeah, and I would add that, you know, like all kinds of law firms, almost every law firm has internal accounting folks who are not lawyers. I mean, you know, Holland & Knight, our CFO is not a lawyer. And whenever Trish or I needs to make a disbursement from our trust account from for one reason or another, we send a request to the accounting department, and they do their thing, and then magically the money moves from point A to point B. An MSO is not really different from that, right? The these are service providers who are working under the direction and purview of the lawyers to help the business function in a seamless fashion. So, um the fact that those um accounting personnel are now employed by the MSO as opposed to by the law firm doesn't really change the underlying fundamental nature of the relationship. >> Is there anything that um a law firm would need to guard against in terms of any of the revenue the firm's revenue flowing through the MSO? >> Yes. So, under rule 5.4, attorneys are prohibited from splitting fees with non-attorneys. What that rule means in practice is that the MSO cannot charge a fee to the law firm that's based on a percentage of the law firm's profits or revenues. Uh instead, the MSO needs to charge a fee that is either a fixed monthly fee or a cost-plus fee, and we've seen a million different variants of each of those. Uh so, typically for one of these transactions, there is a an underwriting process to determine what a fair market value fee for services rendered would be. On almost every single one of these deals, uh we involve uh a third-party valuation firm to provide um you know, to to analyze the set of facts and to provide a essentially a fairness opinion that the fees that are proposed to be charged are in fact fair and reasonable. Um and uh you know, anytime there is a change that needs to be made to the fees, they're not, you know, set in stone forever and ever. Vendors reprice uh periodically with their customers, and that's no different here. Um but our general, you know, feedback here is that you know, the the parties should not be constantly tinkering with the fee, right? Less is more when it comes to to fee adjustments. If you're doing it annually, um that, you know, seems more or less sensible from our standpoint, but there's no hard and fast rules there. Anytime a change is made, it should only be made on a forward-looking basis, never on a backwards-looking basis, because that looks more like just pure gamesmanship or like you're kind of you know, playing tricks. Um and then finally, if you're going to make a change to the fee, you know, we want to make sure that we are refreshing that fairness analysis at that time to ensure that we're coloring within the lines of a kind of validated third-party opinion that the increase in the fee is is you know, in the aggregate fair and reasonable. So, from a structural standpoint, that is how we think about and execute on these transactions. >> Can you maybe quickly go through the menu of different options in terms of fee structures? >> So, at the highest level, again, there's kind of two choices. There's either a fixed monthly fee or a cost plus fee. A fixed monthly fee is exactly what it sounds like. You're just charging kind of the same number month over month over month. Um and again, there's an underwriting process to determine what that number should be. For a cost plus fee, you are looking at the expenses of that the MSO is incurring to provide services. Non-lawyer payroll is the biggest of those, but there can be other expenses as well. And then you're assigning a markup to that. So, that's your cost plus X percent. Be that 10 or 15%. It'll kind of vary in terms of what's fair and reasonable depending on the service line. >> Are those common numbers? 10, 15%? Is that a pretty typical >> Yeah, I mean, yeah, that those are kind of reasonable numbers. It really does depend again on the service line. If you know, the the the markup for accounting and bookkeeping services is probably not the same as for M&A strategic advisory services, where you're looking more at like Bain or McKinsey type, you know, consulting uh markups as opposed to uh you know, ordinary course bookkeeping. But even in the course of underwriting the fixed fee, if you look below the hood, there's still a lot of cost plus work that goes into establishing what would be a fair and reasonable fixed fee to charge. And so it all comes back to what is a market rate, you know, markup on the cost of analogous administrative services. And that's a kind of the most, you know, one of the most important components of establishing the fee structure. >> That's great. Shifting gears a little bit, maybe back to to Trish. Can you talk a little bit about some of the activity in Colorado and Illinois recently? What's going on? And um what's the intent? And then what is it actually doing in practice? >> So, lawyers, I'll start by saying lawyers have a monopoly on the practice of law. Um and what you're seeing in these legislative efforts, what's it's what it's really about is lawyers maintaining that monopoly. Um what they will tell you it is about is the independence of the profession. However, um the legislation that's been passed in those two places doesn't really do much more than what the independence rules already require. So, like it really didn't move the ball. We're still doing deals in Illinois. We're still doing deals in Colorado. Um it hasn't slowed activity even a little. Um and it's um it's it's kind of I don't know, it's kind of a nothing burger at the end of the day. You have to comply with the statutes in both states. Um you know, that makes the process a little bit clunkier, but not a lot clunkier. We like I said, it really hasn't slowed activity at all. Um I will say importantly in both states, those statutes are in our view unconstitutional. We're planning on bringing challenges to both of them. Um the uh unlike in California, um both Colorado and Illinois have uh vested in their judiciary uh the exclusive uh right to regulate the profession of law. And so, the legislature in both states stepping in here is a fundamental rule of law separation of powers issue, um, that actually is the bigger threat to the independence of lawyers. I mean, the judiciary has that exclusive power for a few reasons, but chief among them is like number one, they are specialists, they're thought to be specialists in regulating lawyers and judges and the practice. Um, and number two, um, it's supposed to, uh, allow there to be greater independence from special interests that would influence the legislature, which is, by the way, exactly what you saw here in Illinois. Um, and so, the, uh, idea that we're going to save the independence of the profession of law by bringing in the legislature, which is the thing that threatened the independence of the practice of law, um, to pass a bill that does not do those things anyway, is really, um, you know, a breathtaking moment of certain types of lawyers cutting off their nose to spite their face, um, in a really ineffective way, um, in my view. Uh, you know, California sits a little bit differently in this respect because their inherent powers doctrine isn't as strong as it is in other states because the California Supreme Court a number of decades ago, um, actually, uh, specifically, uh, delegated some of these regulatory powers to the legislature. So, it's just different in California than it is in states like Illinois. Um, what that means is, for example, right? So, that the lawyers that have supported this in a place like Illinois, um, you know, one of the things they would not like to see the legislature do, for example, is pass a bill like the one that was passed in California that became effective at the beginning of the year on lawyer advertising, which has allowed, um, private citizens to bring, uh, a private right of action against lawyers for statutory damages for even technical violations of lawyer ads without a showing of harm, right? That is a bananas law that hurts lawyers and law firms. And that is the sort of thing that happens when you allow your legislature in this arena. So it's pretty in my view short-sighted for any lawyer to be uh you know, uh trying to erode that very important wall that sits around the profession. And in fact, um there is no difference here between the way judges are regulated and the way lawyers are regulated. So if the legislature thinks that it can regulate lawyers, there's nothing stopping it from regulating judges. And that is that should be a breathtaking moment for like professionals in in the legal practice to think about the power that a legislature could have to regulate, for example, the judiciary. I mean, it is just a fundamental rule of law and separation of powers issue. And it's unfortunate that so many lawyers have lined up to push legislation like this for their own financial benefit without thinking about those long-term consequences. >> That's really interesting. From the layperson's perspective, what are the chances that a a law or series of laws goes into effect that does shut down MSO deal activity? >> It's not zero, but it's very close to zero in my view. It's again because of the legislature's limited power to regulate lawyers and law firms. And because these are not new, the old I mean, we keep a regulatory heat map on our website to track MSO related regulations and laws and opinions. The oldest one on there goes back to 1997. And Emery, do you want to guess where that's from, by the way? >> I'm going to go with Washington. >> Illinois. It's from Illinois. The a opinion from Illinois saying you set these up properly, they're ethical, right? These have existed in the practice of law for literally decades. Um, they obviously have a lot more attention around them right now, but they're not new. Um, and there are opinions go there's an opinion from 2001 out of North Carolina. Like there's These are not um particularly new ideas for those of us who work in the field of legal regulation. >> Along those lines of what you're saying, um I was reading up on the the Texas uh 706 ethics opinion, and can you talk a little bit about the significance of that? Um, not necessarily in the the opinion itself, but what it sort of implicitly agreed to in its response. >> Sure. I mean, again, it's just it's more of the same from my legal ethics perspective because we have I don't know, not quite a hundred, but decades of um years of opinions that um tell us as lawyers and law firms how we have to interact with third-party vendors um in other realms, whether that's litigation, financing, or legal staffing, or court reporters, or landlords, or whatever, right? We have tons of opinions that we're building off when we say like this is what an MSO relationship should look like. Well, it's not just Trish and Josh sitting in our little laboratory and like constructing our little MSO law firm puppets, right? We're not making this up out of whole cloth. We're relying on a hundred years of, you know, law around the way that lawyers and law firms can use and fold in different kinds of vendors to help the profession while also maintaining the independence of the profession. And so, the Texas opinion is just another data point in that long line of cases that says, "Yeah, can you have an MSO? Oh, sure you can have an MSO, but it's got to look like this." Um, and so, it's I I I know people I I think people felt like it was like a seismic moment in this world, but I don't view it that way. I don't know if it's a helpful distillation of some of the issues. Um, it to me it's it has to turn out that way. I mean, for it to be consistent with all of the other things we know about how lawyers and law firms work with their service providers, it has to look like that. Same thing >> example, the common ownership issue and that 706 flags about like whether or not a lawyer can own both an MSO and a law firm, right? >> Um, can lawyers do that? Of course they can. We know they can. We have the conflicts rules. Rules 1.7 and 1.8 talk about this issue specifically and have for a very long time. And it's extremely common in the law for a lawyers to own effectively side hustles that are collateral service providers to their law firms. The quintessential example being plaintiffs lawyers owning medical record retrieval businesses. We know that's allowed. It's been allowed for a long time. So again, these are not just new issues. For you to figure out for a regulator figure out a way to say like a lawyer can't be an owner of an MSO, but can own a medical service, you know, a medical record service company would be a little odd. >> I was kind of baffled by this. In In Illinois, there was an exemption uh for for bigger law firms, but it is also um split down the contingency non-contingency line. What's the deal there? Like what What was the intent there and and >> I mean, you want people to tag me and Josh on LinkedIn and call us horrible people, don't you? A few minutes ago I talked about one of the reasons that we uh the judiciary has the exclusive power to regulate the profession is that it is um thought to be less influenced by special interests. And when you look at this legislation, you can see the places where interest groups left their fingerprints on it, um just like you can in all legislation, right? So, um when you see massive carve-outs of, you know, in bills of certain in any bill uh of certain, you know, um groups or individuals, um you know, I you know, you can think about who benefits from a carve-out like that, right? There's a reason in Colorado, for example, um you know, you you hear the trial lawyers talking about, you know, protecting the public, and it's really important for us to protect the public, but the the bill only applies to litigation cases, right? Um do we not care about protecting the public in transactional context? Do we not care about uh protecting the public when it's pro bono cases? I mean, like, why do we only care in California? Why do we only care about protecting the public on contingency fee litigation cases? Huh, who does that benefit, you know? And so, I I would urge your listeners to look at these bills a little bit critically and think about not only who's included, but who's excluded, and why they're excluded. Um and you know, we saw that happen in Illinois. Um you know, one of the sponsoring legislators talked about this issue on the record, and the way they discussed it on the record was that they thought because of their sophistication and intelligence, and I'm paraphrasing here a little bit, I don't remember the exact quote, but like I I do remember finding it offensive to the, you know, uh tens of thousands of solo and small firm practitioners here in Illinois that make up the bulk of our legal community here in Illinois, but because of their relative sophistication and intelligence, big firm lawyers were less susceptible to the wiles of of PE. Um I don't think about that at all. I've represented a million small firms, very, very good, sophisticated small firms. And uh you know, I found the legislators comments about that unacceptable. >> Again, as a layperson, that that seemed very strange to me that that was in there. >> Yeah. >> Um >> Well, follow the money, my friend. Um whenever you see a big carve-out in any bill, you have to think about who's benefiting from this carve-out. >> Zooming in, brass tacks, there's a lawyer who's considering one of these these transactions. What should they be uh what should they have their guard up against? Um you know, what are what are you seeing maybe in first drafts of some of these agreements that um you uh advise your clients not not to accept? >> This is not an answer to your question. I'm going to do the classic lawyer/politician like, here's an answer to a different question. One thing you see people I think attribute to me and Josh and is that we're proponents of MSOs, we're proponents of MSO relationships. I don't think about us that way at all. Like, we we don't care. If somebody if a law firm wants to do this if they want to access capital this way instead of getting a bank loan or a line of credit or doing a capital call or whatever, like that's fine. If you don't, that's fine, too. I have no feelings about how other law firms access capital to fund their you know, their business plans. Um you know, we're in place to say if you want to do it, this is how you have to do it correctly so that it is consistent with the rules of professional conduct and that the structure is a structure that makes sense. Um you know, this won't make sense for every lawyer in every law firm. Um but for some it might. Uh for some it might make more sense for them that rather than accessing capital in a different way. When we are representing a law firm in an MSO transaction and we see the deal terms for the first time, the thing I'm looking for is does the MSO, your purported MSO partner, understand that the lawyers in the law firm have to remain independent as to the functioning of, you know, their the practice of law. If the first pass of documents we see looks like there's a disconnect there, I'm I'm going to be sort of on high alert because these are long-term partnerships and it's really important that lawyers and law firms are in partner in partner in those partnerships with people that understand that that has to remain independent and that independence has to be respected. >> Yeah, I I cosign all of that and I can give you just a little bit of a flavor, Emarie, for kind of some of the the issues that that were on guard about when we kind of our our representing a law firm and get a set of deal documents from a buyer. Broadly speaking, you got a few categories of risks that were, you know, issue spotting. Number one, ethics risk, as Trish indicated, if we get a set of documents that gives the MSO too much power over the law firm or proposes to to transfer economics from the law firm in a way that would constitute an improper fee split under the it's prohibited by the rules. Of course, we're going to highlight that to our clients, we're going to engage with the buyer and their counsel, and we're going to have to talk to them about that and explain our position as to why that deal constructs does not work. Um two, when it comes to uh personal liability of our clients relating to the MSO structure, we are on high alert for that. So, you know, I think as we've established for our listeners, the way that the structure works is that every month the service fee pays, excuse me, the law firm pays a service fee to the MSO. What happens if the law firm lacks sufficient cash on hand to satisfy the service fee in a given calendar month? The answer to that should be that just put it on the tab, right? It becomes an internal amount that's owed by the law firm to the MSO is a deferred management fees and it's paid in a subsequent period when the law firm has cash available to do so. The answer should not be, oh, if the law firm doesn't have enough money to pay the service fee, then the lawyers themselves take on that obligation personally. Like that's not the deal. And so any, you know, aspect of the MSO documents that cracks the door open to personal liability for our clients, we are very much looking at that with a critical eye and and with a skeptical eye. Um three uh restrictive covenants, as we've already discussed as well, lawyers cannot be bound by non-compete covenants. And this presents itself in interesting and potentially unexpected ways. Uh you actually, you know, our view is that you cannot get a non-solicitation uh covenant as applied to lawyers. So you couldn't, for example, have a covenant that says, for the 5-year period following the closing, uh I seller I'm agreeing not to solicit lawyers at this law firm uh to to leave the law firm. Um or the same thing as applied to clients. And so these kinds of carve-outs from restrictive covenants, we view as important to honor and respect Rule 5.6. Uh so th- those are a handful of places. Of course, there's going to be many more traps for the unwary uh in there. Um but uh you know, personal liability and ethics risk or or, you know, it does in some sense boil down to those two categories to a great extent. >> One final question to you both. How do you see this impacting the client? >> If it's done correctly, it shouldn't impact the client's experience with the law firm. Um in fact, if done correctly, the client wouldn't even know in many instances that their law firm was supported the back offices of the law firm was supported by an MSO. The way that I think this could impact clients is a more global thing, right? Um which is that we're seeing more capital and more technology come into the law at the same time, which I think will um allow for different, hopefully better models for um people to use uh to consume legal services, right? And so that though that's kind of how I see it impacting the way that people access legal services. But for the like an individual client who's working with his or her lawyer and his or her lawyers law firm is in an MSO relationship, that client shouldn't have a different client experience. >> I agree. I think this transaction should basically be neutral as experienced by clients. They you know, think about it from the client's perspective. They prior to this MSO transaction, they have a an engagement letter with a law firm to receive professional services from a group of lawyers. After this MSO restructuring where we strip out the back office assets and move them into a separate company, well, they still have the same engagement letter from the same law firm to receive the same services from the same lawyers. So, this really should not impact you know, that one way or another. In our best version like our our our you know, high case on this, there's a partnership that's you know, allows for more efficient and effective implementation of technology resources which should hopefully redound to the benefit of the clients in the terms of pricing or client experience. But yeah, we do not think that at least it is not the intent or the thesis of the transaction that this is going to fundamentally change anything about the attorney-client relationship. Our objective is to really hold that constant and treat that with the degree of care and sanctity that is you know, merited and and required under the rules. >> Josh, Trish, thank you so much for being here today. For our lawyer listeners who might be curious or considering a transaction, what's the best way to get a hold of you? >> Oh man, I think we're ubiquitous. I think you can find us at >> You are. >> I think we're actually kind of hard to avoid. Like we might be at your house right now if you're a lawyer looking at your No, you're going to email us. Our contact information is on the Holland & Knight website. You can email us at our email addresses. That's the best way to get a hold of us. >> Perfect. Well, thank you thank you so much. This has been really interesting for me and I know our listeners as well. I'm sure we'll we'll see a lot more from you both here in the coming months and years. >> Sounds great. Thank you for having us. >> We appreciate it. Take care.

metadata.title: Top 3 Reasons to Establish a Management Services Organization (MSO) | Jackson LLP Healthcare Lawyers
metadata.author: Jackson LLP Healthcare Lawyers
metadata.shortDescription:
MSOs can play an important role in running a compliant, efficient independent healthcare practice. Learn the most common reasons that clients set up MSOs.
Free Healthcare Attorney Consultation - Book Now : https://jacksonllp.com/book

For information about Jackson LLP Healthcare Lawyers' MSO/MSA services, visit https://jacksonllp.com/management-services-organizations-mso/

segments.text: So you want to start an MSO, or a management services organization.
Why would you want to do that? I'm Erin Jackson with Jackson LLP
Healthcare Lawyers. I'll discuss some of the top three reasons that
clients come to us to establish an MSO. First, one of the biggest
reasons is that you are unlicensed or you're a non-physician, and you
live in a state or want to operate in a state that has corporate
practice of medicine, or CPOM, or fee-splitting prohibitions. This
means that a person who is not a physician cannot practice medicine.
And that includes owning and running a medical practice. By
establishing an MSO, that allows you to participate in the
management of a practice, while steering clear of the actual
practice of medicine. This requires additional contracts to implement
and will require a medical director, but it's a great way to
get your foot in the door and participate in the industry you
want to work in without running afoul of the laws.
Two: the second reason you may want to establish an MSO is because you
want to scale or you want to expand your practice. Now, sometimes if
you have established a practice or business and you are hoping to
eventually sell to private equity, an MSO model could be more
appealing to them. I say could because it really depends on the
specifics of where you're operating, and what you're doing.
There's of course, no guarantees on what PE may be interested in. But
sometimes this is more attractive to investors.
Three: efficiencies. Let's say you're a physician, and you want to
focus on the practice of medicine. You aren't interested in the
day-to-day, mundane tasks of management. Billing, HR stuff --
all of that can be left to a management organization. If this is
you, you may be looking to establish an MSO relationship, but
actually fill the shoes of the physician and look for someone else
to be doing your management.
These are just a few of the long list of reasons why someone may
establish an MSO, which is usually wrapped up and described by the
MSA, or the management service agreement between the medical
practice and the management organization. But if you are
operating in any of the states in which our attorneys are licensed,
we're able to help you navigate this process and get your business
or practice either expanded or up and running. So feel free to reach
out.

metadata.title: MSO (Management Services Organization) Basics | Jackson LLP Healthcare Attorneys
metadata.author: Jackson LLP Healthcare Lawyers
metadata.shortDescription:
In most states, only licensed medical professionals are allowed to own medical practices. 
Free Healthcare Attorney Consultation - Book Now : https://jacksonllp.com/book

However, if you're not appropriately licensed to provide the services you want, you can still offer management services through a Management Service Organization (MSO). 

Erin Jackson, Managing Partner of Jackson LLP Healthcare Lawyers, explains how MSOs work.
MSO Arrangements : https://jacksonllp.com/management-services-organizations-mso/
MSO Resources : https://jacksonllp.com/mso-learning-resources/

you allowed to do that? Or maybe you're a social worker who
wants to expand across state lines into areas where you're not licensed but you

which is a management service organization. I'm Erin Jackson with
Jackson LLP Healthcare Lawyers. I'm going to break down some of the basics
behind the concept of an MSO. In most states, only medical professionals are
allowed to own medical practices. However, if you're not appropriately licensed to
offer the services you want to offer, whether because you don't have a high
enough license, or a state-specific license, you can still offer management
services. Under this MSO model, you have two companies. The first company offers
the actual medical services. Let's say you're a medical spa. That is the entity
that employs the doctors. Then you have a second company. This is your management
service organization. This is your company. Your company offers janitorial,
receptionist, billing, non-medical hiring and firing, everything related to running
a practice that is not medical services. The relationship between these two
parties is then set forth in what's called a management service agreement, an
MSA. This is a really complicated contract that outlines the duties and
obligations of both parties, as well as what your relationship is going to look
like. One of the biggest ones is as a management company, how am I going to get
paid? And the answer is: you're going to receive a flat fee payment each month, or
each week, from the medical practice, but you will not be paid based on revenues
from patient care. The management service agreement will be mindful of all the
laws that apply to you, including things like Stark Law, Anti-Kickback
Statute, False Claims Act, state fee-splitting provisions, and state Corporate
Practice of Medicine doctrine. This sounds really complicated, but it's
doable, and it's a great way for you to
participate in the type of medical discipline that you want to and for you

Your company offers janitorial, receptionist, billing, non-medical hiring and firing, everything related to running a practice that is not medical services. The relationship between these two parties is then set forth in what's called a management service agreement, an MSA. This is a really complicated contract that outlines the duties and obligations of both parties, as well as what your relationship is going to look like. One of the biggest ones is as a management company, how am I going to get paid? And the answer is: you're going to receive a flat fee payment each month, or each week, from the medical practice, but you will not be paid based on revenues from patient care. The management service agreement will be mindful of all the laws that apply to you, including things like Stark Law, Anti-Kickback Statute, False Claims Act, state fee-splitting provisions, and state Corporate Practice of Medicine doctrine. This sounds really complicated, but it's doable, and it's a great way for you to participate in the type of medical discipline that you want to and for you to assist in the management of a medical practice while still complying with the law. To learn more about how this might help you build the practice you envision, you can learn more at our website at or you can schedule a complimentary consultation with one of our attorneys. To learn more about how to keep your practice compliant and running smoothly you can subscribe to our YoutTube channel.

metadata.title: Law Firm MSOs 101: How Private Equity and Managed Services Drive Legal Growth
metadata.author: Mattern LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Is private equity poised to transform the business of law through Managed Services Organizations (MSOs)? Discover how forward-thinking law firms are unlocking growth capital and back-office efficiency without violating legal ethics rules.

In this Coffee Break session, Rob Mattern, President of Mattern, sits down with Holland & Knight partners Josh Porte and Trisha Rich, co-leaders of the firm's law firms legal transactions team. Together, they break down the two-company MSO structure, explaining how firms separate non-professional back-office assets from attorney workforces to attract outside capital and scale operations.

Trisha and Josh address critical regulatory considerations surrounding Rule 5.4 fee-splitting prohibitions, Rule 5.6 non-compete restrictions, and Rule 5.3 supervision obligations. The panel explores how private equity firms value MSO service fees through fair-market accounting, why rising capital demands for legal AI are accelerating deal volume, and how law firm leaders can evaluate whether an MSO structure fits their long-term strategic goals.

Ready to gain complete visibility into your firm's support workloads and optimize your administrative efficiency? Let’s talk.
info@matternassoc.com
matternassoc.com

metadata.title: Law Firm Growth: Avoiding Management Services Organization ("MSO") Model Fee Traps
metadata.author: Holt Law: For Healthcare Businesses
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you an entrepreneurial lawyer struggling to find access to capital to scale, invest in tech, or hire top-tier talent? Traditional ethical rules, some dating back a century, flat-out prohibit non-lawyers from having any ownership stake in your firm, locking you out of traditional investment. This is where the Management Services Organization (MSO) model comes in. This powerful and compliant workaround is fundamentally changing how the business of law gets done.

The MSO model is not new; it has a long, proven track record in the highly regulated field of healthcare, where it was developed to navigate similar rules against the corporate practice of medicine. The core idea is simple: separate the practice of law (handled by a 100% lawyer-owned firm) from the business of law (handled by the MSO). The MSO acts as a vendor, handling finance, HR, marketing, and IT, allowing outside investors to inject capital into the business operations without ever violating non-lawyer ownership rules.

However, this dual entity structure only works if you strictly adhere to absolutely critical ethical guard rails. The entire MSO framework is built to navigate three core ethical rules: no non-lawyer ownership, no sharing of legal fees with non-lawyers, and the MSO cannot influence a lawyer's independent professional judgment (Unauthorized Practice of Law or UPL).

The rule against fee sharing receives the most scrutiny and is the biggest challenge. Compensation must be handled meticulously, as getting this wrong puts the whole structure in jeopardy. A recent opinion from the Texas State Bar established a "bright line rule" that makes it crystal clear: any compensation model that is a percentage of a law firm's revenue is strictly prohibited. This is viewed as an illegal split of legal fees. The MSO must be compensated either via a fixed flat monthly fee or a cost-plus model (actual costs plus a fair margin). The compensation must reflect the fair market value of the services, not a slice of the legal pie.

It’s crucial not to confuse the MSO model with Alternative Business Structures (ABS), which actually require changes in state law (like in Arizona and Utah) to allow non-lawyer ownership. The MSO is a scalable, compliant workaround viable in most US jurisdictions right now. Real-world law firms like Remon PC have successfully used the MSO deal to bring in capital from private equity funds (Alpine Investors) to fund upgrades to their back office and legal tech infrastructure. Even litigation finance firms (like Burford Capital) are strategically using the MSO structure to invest in the operational engine of the firm, funding AI integration and scaling business development.

While the advantages are compelling—access to capital, professionalized operations, and investing in game-changing technology—there are legal and business risks. Your primary defense against risks like fee splitting, UPL, and potential investor pressure is a meticulously drafted, ironclad management services agreement (MSA), which governs the entire relationship. Inaction is no longer a sustainable option as the legal landscape shifts.

segments.text: Today we're diving into a really
powerful and importantly compliant way
for entrepreneurial law firms to get
access to capital and seriously
modernize their operations. It's called
the MSO model and believe me it is
changing how the business of law gets
done. Okay, so let's set the stage here.
To compete today, you need capital.
That's for tech, for top tier talent,
for scale, the whole shebang. But for
most law firms in the US, there's this
massive roadblock. ethical rules, some a
century old, that flatout prohibit non-
lawyers from having any ownership stick.
This has basically locked law firms out
of traditional investment. Well, until
now. So, what's the solution? It's
actually a pretty elegant workaround
that solves this whole capital problem
by making one single critical
distinction. It separates the business
of law from the practice of law. And
that strategic decoupling, that's the
key to this entire model.
And this is where the management
services organization or MSO comes into
play. Now look, this isn't some crazy
new idea. MSOs have a long proven track
record in another highly regulated
field, healthcare. They were actually
developed to navigate very similar rules
against the corporate practice of
medicine. The core idea is just simple
common sense. Let the professionals
practice their profession and let a
dedicated business entity run the
business. This dual entity structure is
really the heart of the whole thing. So
on one side you've got the law firm.
It's 100% owned by lawyers and it
handles all the legal work for clients.
Period. On the other side you've got the
mso and this is where outside investors
can come in. The mso handles everything
else. The finance, the HR, marketing,
IT, it just acts as a vendor to the law
firm which lets capital flow into the
business operations without ever
breaking those core ownership rules. Now
this all sounds pretty brilliant, right?
But and this is a big butt, it only
works if you play by the rules. There
are some absolutely critical ethical
guard rails that you have to respect to
make this model compliant and successful
and every lawyer thinking about this
needs to understand them inside and out.
The entire MSO framework is basically
built to navigate these three core
ethical rules. So, we've already covered
the first one, no non-awyer ownership of
the firm itself. The other two are just
as important. You can't share legal fees
with non- lawyers, and the MSO
absolutely cannot engage in what's
called the unauthorized practice of law,
which really just means it can't
influence a lawyer's independent
professional judgment on legal matters.
But out of all these, there's one that
gets the most scrutiny, the one that's
the biggest challenge, and that is the
rule against fee sharing. How the MSO
gets paid is without a doubt the most
important and sensitive detail in this
entire arrangement. Seriously, if you
get this part wrong, the whole structure
could be in jeopardy. And don't think
for a second that this is some kind of
gray area. It's not. A recent opinion
from the Texas State Bar established
what it calls a bright line rule. And
this quote makes it crystal clear. Any
compensation model that's a percentage
of a law firm's revenue is a no-go. It's
seen as an illegal split of legal fees.
It's as simple as that. So, this table
really lays out the safe path forward. A
fixed flat monthly fee for the services
the MSO provides. Yep, that's
permissible. It's just a standard vendor
relationship. A cost plus model where
the MSO bills for its actual costs plus
a fair margin, that's also fine. But a
percentage-based fee that's tied to the
firm's revenue, that is strictly
prohibited. The MSO's compensation has
to be for the fair market value of its
services, not a slice of the legal pie.
All right, so with those rules in mind,
let's zoom out. How does this MSO model
stack up against other innovations in
the legal space? And maybe more
importantly, how are real firms actually
using it today out in the wild? First
off, it's really important not to get
MSOs mixed up with something called
alternative business structures or ABS.
An ABS, which you'll find in places like
Arizona and Utah, is a formally licensed
entity that actually does allow
non-awyer ownership. The MSO, on the
other hand, is a compliant workaround
that operates within the existing rules.
Here's the key difference. An ABS
requires changing the law state by state
and MSO is a scalable solution that's
viable in most US jurisdictions right
now. Let's look at a real world example
because this is where it gets
interesting. Remon PC, a global
cloud-based law firm, is one of the big
pioneers here. They successfully used an
MSO deal to bring in capital from a
private equity fund called Alpine
Investors. And you've got to hear the
why behind it. Reman's CEO, Michael
Morizad, said the whole point was to
drag law firms out of the stone age. So,
this wasn't just a money grab. It was
about funding a fundamental upgrade to
their entire back office operation and
their legal tech infrastructure, all
while the lawyer partners kept all of
their equity in the law firm. And it's
not just private equity. We're also
seeing this fascinating evolution with
litigation finance firms like Burford
Capital. Now, these guys are
traditionally known for funding
individual lawsuits, but now they're
using the MSO structure to invest in the
law firm itself.
This is a huge strategic shift. Think
about it. Instead of just betting on a
single case to win, investors are now
funding the core operational engine of
the firm. They're injecting capital for
things like AI integration, building
datadriven pricing models, and seriously
scaling up business development. They
are investing in the business of law,
not just the practice of it. So all of
this brings us to a strategic
crossroads. For any entrepreneurial
lawyer watching right now, the MSO model
isn't just theory. It presents direct,
actionable choices about the future of
your firm and really your practice. The
advantages are pretty compelling. Of
course, access to capital is the biggest
driver, but it's closely followed by the
ability to finally professionalize
operations, invest in game-changing
technology, and truly compete for top
talent. It creates a culture of
continuous investment in the business
instead of just paying out all the
profits every year. But, you know, it's
not without risk. You have to be smart
about this. We've talked about the legal
landmines like fee splitting and UPL.
You also have the business risks like
potential investor pressure and the
tricky fact that lawyers often can't be
subject to non-competes. Your primary
tool, your shield to mitigate all of
these risks is a meticulously drafted
ironclad management services agreement,
the MSA, which is the contract that
governs that whole relationship. So, at
the end of the day, this leaves you with
two really clear paths forward. One, you
could implement an MSO for your own
firm, unlocking that capital, but taking
on the legal risk of getting the
structure exactly right. Or path two,
you could build an advisory practice
capitalizing on what is essentially a
green field market opportunity to guide
other firms through this complex
process. Look, inaction is just not a
sustainable option anymore. The legal
landscape is shifting and the firms that
embrace these new models are going to
gain a huge competitive advantage. So
that really brings us to our final
question for you to think about. The
business of law is evolving. What will
your role be?

metadata.title: Law Firms, PE, and MSOs: A Legal Ethics Conversation with Lucian Pera
metadata.author: The Future Is Bright Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Private equity is circling the legal industry, and Lucian Pera is helping make sense of what that means for MSO law firms and beyond. 

Joining Chris Batz and Howard Rosenberg, Lucian breaks down how management services organizations (MSOs) and alternative business structures (ABSs) are giving outside investors new ways to participate in the economics of law - without running afoul of ethics rules like ABA Rule 5.4.

Lucian makes it clear that these models are tools, not shortcuts. For some firms, an MSO structure may unlock the capital needed for technology, acquisitions, or ambitious growth plans. For others, a traditional loan or internal funding might make more sense. The critical step, he argues, is matching structure to strategy, rather than chasing the latest buzz.

As interest from PE firms and family offices surges, the profession faces a choice: see outside money as a threat, or recognize the opportunities it brings to modernize how law firms operate. Lucian leans toward the latter. Just as medicine and accounting were reshaped by investment, he believes law is in the midst of its own slow-motion revolution where the business side of the profession is finally catching up with reality. For lawyers and investors alike, understanding MSOs, ABSs, and the ethics that govern them is a glimpse into where the legal market is headed next.

metadata.title: Legal MSOs: Managed Service Organizations & the Future of Law Firms | MSO Advisor Frederick Shelton
metadata.author: Ten Golden Rules Internet Marketing for Law Firms
metadata.shortDescription:
Law firm MSOs could become one of the biggest structural shifts in the legal industry, but the opportunity comes with significant decisions about growth, control, culture, and ownership. Jay Berkowitz talks with Frederick Shelton, CEO of Shelton & Steele and a legal MSO advisor, about how Management Services Organizations allow outside capital to support the business side of a law firm while attorneys retain responsibility for practicing law. Frederick explains how MSO deals are structured, why growing firms are attracting investor attention, and how capital can fund technology, acquisitions, recruiting, and succession. They also explore the risks of choosing the wrong partner, including governance and loss of autonomy. The primary takeaway is that MSOs can create substantial growth opportunities, but law firm founders need to understand the partner, economics, governance, and long-term implications before making a deal.

Key Topics
04:38 – A Management Services Organization is broken down in practical terms, including what it handles and why the model is gaining traction in legal.
07:27 – See how separating the law firm from its back-office services creates a different ownership and investment structure.
10:05 – Discover how outside capital and shared resources can give smaller and midsize firms access to technology and infrastructure usually associated with much larger firms.
12:07 – Learn what investors may look for in a law firm and why growth trajectory can matter as much as current size.
14:31 – MSO deals may create new options for succession, retirement, recruiting, and transitioning leadership to the next generation.
16:32 – Explore what can happen to marketing, technology, intake, and other back-office functions after an MSO becomes involved.
21:26 – See which types of law firms may have the strongest reason to consider an MSO while the market is still developing.
22:34 – Learn why deal structure can matter just as much as the headline valuation offered to the law firm owner.
26:46 – Discover what separates stronger MSO partners from those that could threaten a firm’s culture, autonomy, or control.
33:52 - Tune into The Golden Rapid Fire Questions 

Resources Mentioned
Technology

Books
📚 Unlimited Power – Tony Robbins – https://a.co/d/08i1m9zM

Podcasts
🎙️ Lunch Hour Legal Marketing – Gyi Tsakalakis and Conrad Saam – https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/lunch-hour-legal-marketing/id973563135

Other
 🌐 Federate Legal – https://federatelegal.com/
 🌐 Attorney at Work – https://www.attorneyatwork.com/

About our Guest:
Frederick Shelton is the Founder and CEO of Shelton & Steele LLC, a national legal consulting and advisory firm with more than three decades of experience working with attorneys and law firms. His work has evolved from legal recruiting and mergers and acquisitions into advising entrepreneurial law firms on strategic growth, emerging business models, and particularly Legal Management Services Organization (MSO) transactions. Today, he helps law firm founders evaluate outside investment opportunities, potential partners, deal structures, governance, autonomy, culture, and long-term financial implications.
Frederick and his team report having evaluated more than 70 Legal MSOs, giving him a broad perspective on the rapidly developing market. He has also been an early commentator on major shifts affecting the legal profession, including remote work and artificial intelligence, with his insights appearing in publications such as Forbes, Bloomberg Law, Attorney at Law Magazine, and The American Lawyer. His current focus is helping law firm owners understand MSO opportunities while protecting what they have built and preparing their firms for the changing business of law.

metadata.title: Alternative Business Structures: Updates from Arizona’s Legal Frontier
metadata.author: The Heart of Law Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of The Heart of Law Podcast, host Mirena Umizaj Dumas welcomes back returning guest Lynda Shely, one of the nation’s leading voices on legal ethics and innovation. A former Chair of the ABA’s Ethics Committee and a current member of Arizona’s Alternative Business Structures (ABS) and AI Steering Committees, Lynda offers rare insight from the front lines of Arizona’s trailblazing regulatory reform.

Back by popular demand, Lynda returns to share the latest developments in Arizona’s ABS model—a topic that continues to spark conversation across the legal industry. She and Mirena revisit Arizona’s groundbreaking elimination of Rule 5.4, which paved the way for non-lawyer ownership of law firms. Together, they explore how the ABS framework has evolved, its current status, and what it signals for the future of legal services nationwide.

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• What ABS actually is and why Arizona replaced the ban on non-lawyer ownership
• Why lawyers and non-lawyers pursue ABS (succession, capital, tech)
• Lessons from 144+ licensed firms and Arizona’s strict oversight
• Ethics guardrails and mandatory compliance protocols
• How Arizona prohibits referral mills under ABS
• Risks and opportunities of private equity in law
• How Arizona compares to other states like California and Utah
• Where AI fits in—and what Arizona doesn’t allow

CHAPTERS:
00:00 – Intro & Guest Welcome  
02:30 – What Is ABS?  
08:10 – Concerns & Safeguards  
15:40 – Mass Torts, PE & Compliance  
25:45 – Renewals & Firm Growth  
34:35 – ABS: What’s Next?  
48:30 – Final Thoughts

ABOUT OUR GUEST:
Lynda C. Shely is an Ethics and ABS attorney with Rosing, Pott & Strohbehn, in partnership with Zelms Erlich Lenkov. Based in Arizona, Lynda provides legal ethics and Alternative Business Structure (ABS) regulatory advice to lawyers and law firms nationwide.

She is the former Chair of the ABA Standing Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility (2020–2023) and currently serves on multiple legal ethics bodies, including the Arizona Supreme Court’s ABS Committee and AI Steering Committee. A respected voice in the profession, Lynda has also taught professional responsibility as an adjunct professor at every law school in Arizona.

Her contributions to the legal field have earned her numerous accolades, including the 2022 Maricopa County Bar Member of the Year, 2023 Hall of Fame Inductee, and the 2024 AWLA Sarah Herring Sorin Award.

🔗 LINKS FROM THE SHOW:

https://rosinglaw.com/services/alternative-business-structure/
• Connect with the host and explore strategic legal consulting services at Mirena & Company: https://mirenaandco.com

Podcast production by Bebo Hajec of EMH Group
Agency-Level Marketing, Without the Overhead | https://www.emhgroup.co

Yeah. They can go wrong if the lawyers allow non-awyery investors or owners to try to dictate how the firm operates. That would be number one. They really go wrong if they think that the ABS law firm in Arizona is just going to be a referral service. So, and a lot of people also who aren't familiar with the program think, "Oh, you've allowed KPMG and other accounting firms to come in and now they're practicing law." No, >> they're not practicing law. Arizona lawyers are practicing law in the law firm. We did not change the rules and permit non-laws to just start practicing law. >> Right? >> So it's I would say those are the biggest ways that ABS law firms could stub their toe and end up in discipline. >> So obviously you have seen and sat in a lot of hearings right in the committee. What do you typically hear? Who are the non- lawyers? What kind of value are they trying to add? everything. We we still see private equity. And so the co again to just understand some of the fundamentals the idea is to help you know you you are establishing an ABS so that you can help people residents of Arizona not necessarily be a bridge to intake clients from all over the country and refer them out without ever doing any work in the Arizona firm. We we being the ABS committee do not want to see something that's simply a referral service or a front >> law firm in another state. >> But you're aware that a lot of people that came out of the mass tort wood would work had that intention and obviously I have experience in that world. I work in that world. I think they've if anything they've re-calibrated understanding that >> we were serious when we said we expected to see the Arizona lawyer practicing law and that the firm has to hire Arizona lawyers. But the only lawyers who can practice law in an Arizona ABS law firm are Arizona admitted lawyers. Not really because we care in Arizona, but because no other state bar will permit their lawyers, >> right, >> to be employed by an ABS. >> And so, can a licensed um Arizona attorney practice out of Arizona? >> Absolutely. On a temporary basis, just like I can in a traditional law firm, right? I have clients that might be in other states and I can even practice the state law of another state on a temporary basis under ethics rule 5.5 as that rule of professional conduct is adopted in most US jurisdictions except Texas and Hawaii. So even for the compliance lawyer, which is a a specific individual who again I'm going to say is the managing attorney of the ABS Arizona ABS law firm, >> they aren't required to live in Arizona, but they have to have the bandwidth to actually do the job. What does it take for an existing ABS to renew? Put your information together. And then as a reminder to leses, unlike in a traditional firm where you can open and close as you want, there are no requirements other than the lawyers comply with the ethics rules. We're hearing at the renewal >> because I know people are concerned about proprietary information being disclosed in these meetings. Um, I would say we don't ask you what your revenue is. Right? You've heard this before. And back to my first point, you should be thanking Arizona because guess what? And so one of the things that I'm engaging with capital is they see the long-term. They're getting the calls. Is that what you're seeing? >> Yes. >> Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, that makes sense. So, all in all, it sounds like the ABS's that were formed are still the majority of them are still active. Hm. Also, Linda can tell you, I can see the the older generation of attorneys and law firms begin to panic because they understand that that hump may be very difficult to overcome. But the interest is there because if they can't compete, they're gonna need to figure out how to partner or how to exit and make some profit off of a business they've worked in for 30, 40 years. So, it's it's going to be super interesting to see. I love that you're such a visionary and not afraid to have taken and tackled this. There's some fear still there, but I'm excited to see the development and again change. I mean, who could have guessed generative AI was going to be taking over our world 10 years ago? Um, that just wasn't even on the horizon. So, who knows what the next five years brings? But I would just ask your viewers to keep an open mind, watch some of the committee meetings that are online and see how it's working. >> Yeah, great advice. very appreciative for you being back on the podcast and maybe we'll do a series where every year we're giving some updates because I know there's a lot of interest on this topic. In this video, Law Leader's Dustin Ruge speaks with Lynda Shely about what we have learned after on the three year anniversary of Arizona's passage of the Alternative Business Structure (ABS) allowing for non-attorney ownership of law firms and allowing attorneys to pay non-attorneys for referrals. Topics Include:

- How many ABS Law Firms have been created to date in Arizona?
- What are the requirements to becoming an ABS law firm in Arizona?
- What are the advantages of an Alternative Business Structure? 
- What is the current process and timelines to get approved? 
- What other states are considering an ABS structure for law firms?
- How can an Arizona ABS handle referrals and co-counseling with attorneys in other states? 
And mush more! 

Previous Overview & Details about Arizona's New ABS Model: https://youtu.be/o4jTdas84Cw?si=k6reJ5qBI09y4ep4

TO LEARN MORE:
https://lawleaders.com/
https://shelylaw.com/

what is an alternative business structure
what is an abs law firm
how to set up an abs law firm
can a non lawyer be a partner in a law firm

segments.text: In 2021, Arizona implemented regulations
allowing the creation of alternative
business structures. An alternative
business structure or ABS is basically a
law firm that's owned in whole or in
part by someone who's not a lawyer. In
my work, I advise and help a lot of
ABS's. Our team consults with ABS's as
they apply and afterward when they're
doing business. Over the past few years,
as the environment around ABS's has
started to get more clear, I've learned
about some of the biggest risks that
face ABS's. And I'm going to go through
a few of them. First is conflicts of
interest and ethical challenges. The
involvement of non-awyer owners in law
firms raises concerns about potential
conflicts between profit motives and
ethical obligations. For instance,
investors might prioritize financial
returns over clients best interests. The
State Bar of Arizona is especially
concerned that attorneys could be
pressured to make decisions that could
compromise their professional judgment.
It's really important that ABS's follow
a core principle of attorney
independence to avoid ethical
violations.
A second is regulatory oversight and
compliance. ABS entities are law firms.
Like other law firms, they're subject to
stringent regulatory requirements to
ensure ethical conduct and protect
clients. Non-compliance can result in
severe penalties, including license
suspension or revocation. In fact, there
have been a couple recent disciplinary
decisions related to ABS's and their
compliance attorneys. Neither I nor my
clients want to get anywhere near such a
disciplinary action. The third issue is
quality of legal services. Some people
are concerned that the drive for
profitability in ABS law firms might
lead to cost cutting measures that
compromise the quality of legal
services. Critics argue that some ABS
firms focus on high volume, lowcost
services, possibly neglecting complex
legal needs that require more
personalized attention. My personal
opinion is that lawyers already face
that sort of pressure and I'm not sure
that it's much different in the ABS
context, but I can understand the
concern. Fourth is client
confidentiality concerns. Non-awyer
ownership raises questions about the
protection of client confidentiality.
Unlike attorneys, non-awyer owners are
not bound by the same professional
obligations of confidentiality, which
could increase the risk of unauthorized
disclosure of sensitive information. At
Denton Peterson Dunn, when we represent
ABS's, we draft confidentiality policies
that will help protect client
information. And when we train
compliance attorneys, we always address
this important issue. Fifth is the
possible impact on traditional law
practices. ABS entities, which are often
backed by big capital and technological
resources, pose a new competitive
challenge to traditional law firms,
especially small and solo practices.

taking over the world and that finance

software and new finance injections are

lawyers could be good for most clients.

metadata.title: Navigating the Arizona ABS Program: Rule Changes and Rising Opportunities
metadata.author: The Heart of Law Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Prepare to venture Prepare to venture into the uncharted territory of Arizona's legal landscape, where the rulebook is being reshaped, and the status quo is bravely defied. In this transformative episode of The Heart of Law, our astute host, Mirena Umizaj, invites Ethics Attorney Lynda Shely, the esteemed founder of The Shely Firm, to shed light on the intricacies of the Arizona Business Structure (ABS) program and its groundbreaking 2021 rule changes. Together they discuss the elimination of Ethics Rule 5.4 and how it has acted as a powerful catalyst, propelling Arizona lawyers to forge collaborative partnerships with non-lawyers, igniting a new era of innovation and opportunity in the legal landscape. 

With an impressive private practice spanning over two decades, Attorney Lynda Shely has consistently delivered exemplary representation to numerous law firms while also providing invaluable ethics advice to over 2,000 firms nationwide. However, her influence extends far beyond her thriving practice. With pivotal roles in prominent committees and organizations, including the Arizona Supreme Court's Alternative Business Structure (ABS) Committee, Attorney Lynda Shely stands at the vanguard of the ABS program's development and implementation, driving the advancement of innovative approaches to legal practice.

As the episode unfolds, Attorney Lynda Shely takes a moment to reflect on her personal journey to becoming an ethics attorney, navigating the delicate balance of career and motherhood while raising her three children. Her story serves as a testament to the determination and resilience required to carve a path in the legal profession. Reflecting on her experiences, Attorney Lynda Shely unveils her instrumental role in spearheading the groundbreaking initiative that allows Arizona lawyers to establish law firms with non-lawyers as owners or investors. Addressing misconceptions, she acknowledges lawyers' concerns about potential conflicts of interest. However, she assures listeners that the Arizona ABS program is designed to maintain integrity by safeguarding lawyers' control over legal decisions. She sheds light on the rigorous regulations and meticulous approval process that enable non-lawyers to hold ownership stakes in law firms while respecting the professional autonomy of lawyers in client representation and case selection.

As the conversation progresses, the focus shifts to the intriguing realm of mass torts and its intersection with Wall Street. With artful emphasis, Mirena highlights the profound significance of this intersection, succinctly stating, "this is where the rubber meets the road." Her words resonate as Wall Street ventures into the domain of mass torts, actively investing in law firms through financial loans, seamlessly integrating themselves into the very fabric of the debt structure. In parallel, Mirena and Attorney Lynda Shely explore the ever-evolving landscape of technological advancements, honing in on the transformative impact of chat GPT and its wide-ranging implications for the legal field.

As the final moments of the episode unfold, the spotlight shifts toward the legal landscape in Utah, where uncertainty looms over the issue of non-lawyer ownership. Mirena's mention of Utah's shifting stance from considering partnerships to potential felony charges raises eyebrows and prompts reflection. In response, Attorney Lynda Shely expresses her disappointment in these attempts to restrict innovation and courageously advocates for the embracing of change. She acknowledges that "change is scary,", particularly in the legal profession, where risk aversion often prevails. However, she reminds us that it is precisely this embrace of change that propels progress and allows the legal profession to adapt and better serve its clients.

metadata.shortDescription:
We wrap up this season with a long-time friend of the show, Allen Rodriguez. is a legal product development strategist who has been serving the legal industry for over 20 years. Over the course of his career, Allen has built a reputation for creating innovative #legalservices products as well as developing highly effective law firm business and marketing strategies.  Allen is a valued speaker on the topics of law marketing, legal services product development, and future of law issues. He has provided consulting and marketing services for companies such as McKinsey & Co., Coleman Research Group, LexisNexis, and Littler.

Before starting The Singular Law Group under the Arizona alternative business structure for #lawfirms, Allen founded law innovation agency ONE400 and was the Director of Attorney Services at LegalZoom. While there, his work contributed to a substantial portion of overall revenue at the company and helped LegalZoom move from a provider of “do-it-yourself” legal services to a comprehensive legal solutions provider, incorporating attorney-fulfilled work across all U.S. jurisdictions.

Additionally, this was a special evening event on #VeteransDay and Allen is a United States Army veteran. We were honored to have him join to tell us about the Singular Law Group on such a special day. 

For those considering building a law firm in Arizona, that allows for non-lawyer ownership, you're going to want to catch this replay. Allen doesn't only give us the vision of Singular Law Group, he also lays out the exact steps he went through to apply to the Arizona bar and the efforts it took to be approved to offer legal services under the ABS model. 

Thanks for spending time with us this season... we'll be back in the future! 

More about Allen Rodriguez & Singular Law Group: 

Allen Rodriguez on Twitter: https://twitter.com/allen_rodriguez. 

Allen Rodriguez on LinkeIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/allenrodriguez/

The Singular Law Group: https://singular.law/. 

ONE400: https://one400.com/.

The future of Non-lawyer ownership of law firms is an ever-changing landscape that is rapidly evolving as new technology, regulations and policies are continually being developed and implemented. Law firm marketing strategies need to evolve.
As the legal industry moves into the digital age, law firms must adapt to the changing environment or risk being left behind. An intense digital law firm marketing strategy is the start. The most significant change in recent years has been the growing acceptance of non-lawyer ownership of law firms. In the past, the American Bar Association (ABA) Model Rules of Professional Conduct prohibited non-lawyer ownership of law firms in an effort to prevent outside interference with a lawyer's independent and professional judgment. However, in recent years, a handful of states have begun to allow non-lawyer ownership of law firms. Arizona is leading the way in this area, having eliminated its Rule 5.4 in January 2021. Under the new rules, entities with non-lawyer ownership must first seek regulatory approval to become an “alternative business structure” (ABS). Similarly, Utah has implemented a seven-year “regulatory sandbox” pilot program to experiment with alternative business structures. California, Michigan, North Carolina and Washington, D.C., are also exploring revisions to Rule 5.4.
In any event, it’s worth keeping an eye on the developments in law firm ownership. The future of law is here, and the only way to stay ahead of the curve is to be prepared.
