metadata.title: The HITECH Act: Electronic Health Records and Meaningful Use
metadata.author: CaptureBilling
metadata.shortDescription: This short educational animated video made by Capture Billing highlights the key features of the HITECH Act, Meaningful Use, and Stimulus Money for EHRs and what it means for you and your practice. Video produced in collaboration with Manny Oliverez at http://mannyoliverez.com. For help with your medical billing call us at 703-327-1800 or visit us at http://www.CaptureBilling.com .

segments.text: If you are like most doctors you've probably heard something about a government incentive program
encouraging physicians to implement electronic health records,
however you're probably a little fuzzy on the details.
Well,you're not alone the let's take a closer look and see if we can help you make sense of it all.
On February seventeenth two thousand nine,
the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act
also known as the Stimulus Package
was signed by President Obama into law.
Contained within it's pages is new legislation known as the Health Information Technology
for Economic and Clinical Help Act
That's a mouthful so we'll just call it the HITECH Act.
So what exactly is the HITECH Act;
and how does it affect you, a physician?
Well very simply it uses financial incentives to encourage physicians to adopt Certified Electronic
Health Records
or EHRs.
Through the increased use of EHRs the government hopes to achieve the goal of a national health
information network
that will result in improved quality of care,
patient safety and lower costs.
What kind of financial incentives are we talking about here?
Perhaps as much as thirty four
billion dollars.
So now you're probably asking yourself
two questions.
One, how do I qualify for this money?
And two, just how much of that thirty four billion is available to me?
Well the answers to both of these questions are actually quite simple.
To qualify for a piece of the HITECH money
there are two things you will need to do.
First
your practice must purchase and use a government certified EHR.
Secondly
your practice will need to demonstrate
meaningful use of this EHR.
This means that you will have to prove to the government
that the EHR is being properly implemented
according to their criteria.
This criteria is detailed in a list of twenty five requirements issued by the Department of Health
and Human Services.
It is broken down into two sets of objectives and measures;
a core set
and a menu set.
A core set consists of fifteen
non-negotiable objectives
that all physicians must comply with.
In the menu set however,
providers are free to choose five items from among a menu of ten to implement.
In all this means physicians must meet twenty total objectives in order to demonstrate
meaningful use.
Fail to meet even one of these meaningful use requirements
and you become ineligible for the incentives.
Now that you know how to qualify,
let's find out how much of that thirty four billion you can get your hands on.
The answer to this depends on which incentive program you're eligible for.
HITECH provides two separate programs,
one for Medicare
and one for Medicaid.
With Medicare physicians can earn up to seventy five percent
of their Medicare allowable charges
up to a maximum of forty four thousand dollars.
With Medicaid
close to sixty four thousand is available to physicians
who see more than thirty percent of Medicaid patients.
That number is reduced to twenty percent if you're a pediatrician.
Keep in mind
this incentive is for each eligible provider within a practice.
For example;
have five providers on the Medicaid program and your practice can receive up to three hundred
and twenty thousand dollars in incentive funds. Unfortunately though the
HITECH Act is not just about handing out free money.
Delay
or even decide not to implement a certified EHR
and you will be penalized.
Not only will you lose out on the incentives,
but the government will also begin decreasing your reimbursement rates
by as early as twenty twelve.
So as you can see at its core the HITECH Act is not that complicated at all.
Simply purchase and use a government certified EHR,
meet all the meaningful use requirements
and you'll be eligible for the HITECH incentives.
And on a final note beaware of the fact that commercial insurance carriers are
already talking about jumping on the meaningful use bandwagon
and requiring providers to meet the same criteria
for their pay for performance programs.
Hopefully this has given you a clear understanding of the HITECH Act
and what it means to you and your practice.
Over the next several years EHRs will change the way
we as health providers keep patient records.
Change is coming fast;
act now to make sure that you don't miss out on your portion of the HITECH money.

metadata.title: MPT Podcast 8: HIPAA - Changes in HITECH and the Impact on Your Practice
metadata.author: emedikon
metadata.shortDescription:
In this Medical Practice Trends video podcast, Mike Meikle of Hawkthorne Group Consulting discusses recent changes in the enforcement of the HITECH Act and how medical practices should be prepared. Subscribe to the audio version on iTunes 
https://itunes.apple.com/us/podcast/medical-practice-trends
/id286494996?mt=2&ign-mpt=uo%3D4
Transcript:
Dr. Polack: This is Peter J. Polack, M.D. with Medical Practice Trends and in our podcast today our guest is Mike Meikle of Hawkthorne Group consulting firm.   So welcome Mike!
Mike Meikle: Good afternoon sir!  
Dr. Polack: Today we are going to be talking about recent changes in the enforcement of the HITECH Act.  So this is something that physicians want to really pay attention to, although right now it doesn’t seem to be an issue, we need to be aware that there’s certainly some significant potential penalties – is that right?
Mike Meikle: That’s correct - $50,000.00 per record breach. 
Dr. Polack: Well, can you talk to us a little bit about this recent case that occurred and what are the implications for the typical medical practice?
Mike Meikle: Certainly.  Very recently, or up until this year, the HIPAA – the Health Information Portability and Accountability Act, which has been around since 1996, though didn’t have a lot of teeth in the overall law, most medical practices and even large healthcare providers sort of recognized it was there about protected health information but they really didn’t put in their standard business process and practices to be concerned about it.  
But with the advent of the HITECH Act in 2009, the enforcement of HIPAA has become more prevalent, and in February of this year, Health and Human Services assessed a $4.3 million penalty against Cignet Health in Prince George’s County, Maryland and then two days later, HHS levied another one million dollar settlement against Massachusetts General Hospital in the same type of HIPAA privacy complaint.  
Dr. Polack: What exactly did they do?  Was it one of these accidental breach of information where someone took a laptop and lost it or what exactly happened in the case of Cignet?
Mike Meikle: Well with Cignet, the issue basically revolved around the fact that the organization was denying 41 patients access to their medical records when they had requested them, and this was between September 2008 and October 2009.
 So what the patients did, and the HITECH Act and HIPAA encourages this, they filed individual complaints about this to Health and Human Services.  Then of course HHS decided to investigate.
Well, what really added fuel to the fire was that Cignet refused to cooperate with HHS when HHS requested records from Cignet.  Instead of sending the 41 records to the organization they backed up a truck full of thousands of medical records and had HHS sort through them for the 41 they needed, and then they basically stonewalled and obfuscated and kind of skated around the issue and finally HHS got so fed up that they went ahead and penalized them for the $4.3 million.  
So that was a huge wakeup call to the healthcare provider – large healthcare provider industry.  It was just unheard of for this level of penalty to be levied.  
Dr. Polack: And this was a civil penalty, right?  This is not just a fine or a fee.
Mike Meikle: Yeah, it was a civil monetary penalty.
Dr. Polack: And in the case of Massachusetts General?
Mike Meikle: Well this is another interesting issue, and like you had just mentioned, so how did it get lost – was it stolen?  Was the laptop taken?  Did somebody leave a backup tape in a car?  Well, what really happened here was an employee of Mass General left documents on the subway and in the documents there was protected health information of 192 patients that had been diagnosed with HIV and AIDS and also had medical record numbers, health insurance and policy numbers, date of birth, of course with name, and they were never recovered.
 So HHS stepped in and levied the one million dollar fine on Mass General and then of course they had to do a corrective action plan and they had to basically do a whole comprehensive set of policy and procedure adjustments to protected PHI because this is not in the actual business practices of the organization.
 So not only did they get this one million dollar fine but they had to retool their business processes and technology processes to protected PHI which they hadn’t been addressing.  So there was an additional cost which is now reported........

records like in the case of Mass General being kind of carelessly left in a subway.
So what organizations have to do, healthcare organizations, is to train their employees
about PHI – Protected Health Information or e-PHI – the electronic Protected Health
Information, how to properly work with the information, how to protect it, understand
it and also impart on the employees the risks and the ramifications of losing PHI to the
organization, how they can really undermine the viable business model of an organization
if they have too large of a breach, and that once again it’s a business process and training
your employees goes a long way.
And of course with the technology piece, if you have electronic information encryption
of your storage media and also an effective Asset Management Program.
So if your laptop walks away you actually know your laptop’s gone, or how many laptops
you have in your practice – do you know?
Well you should know and making sure that those hard drives on the laptop are encrypted
and also have the ability potentially to do a remote wipe of device, an ability to track
where that device is if it happens to fall out of a physician or nurse’s hands and
that you can actually know where it’s gone.
If someone logs onto the internet you know where it is.
You can remote wipe it.
So once again, there’s a lot of ways technology can facilitate compliance but the basic training
of your employees is very important.
Dr. Polack: Okay, well very good.
Thanks very much.
Mike Meikle: No problem, sir.

metadata.title: HITECH ACT - 2010 Changes in HIPAA Law
metadata.author: lawofmedicine
metadata.shortDescription:
S. Sandy Sanbar, MD, PhD, JD, presents the 2010 changes in HIPAA Law
pursuant to implementation of the 2009 Health Information Technology
for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act. This is particularly
important for physicians and health care providers who utilize
electronic health record systems.

segments.text: This article deals with the high-tech
act, the changes in HIPPA law in
Physicians and other health care
providers who utilize electronic health
record systems will have to comply with
updated HIPPA privacy and security rules
as early as 2011 under a proposed rule
published by the Health and Human
Services Office for Civil Rights on July
The
rule implements the 2009 health
information technology for economic and
clinical health act. That's the
high-tech act provisions aimed at
creating a secure foundation for sharing
electronic protected health information
in the emerging landscape of healthcare
reform.
The High-Tech Act strengthened and
expanded the scope of the HIPPA privacy
and security rules, enhanced the HIPPA
penalty provisions, provided for HIPPA
enforcement by state attorneys general,
and established a federal data breach
notification law.
The heightened safeguards and compliance
requirements along with increased
penalties for
non-compliance pose significant hurdles
not only for existing covered entities
but also for a significant number of
additional organizations in the healthc
care industry.
The HIPPA privacy security and
enforcement law
changes involve covered entities, that's
physicians and hospitals, and their
business associates, both of whom must
comply with the language of the
high-tech
act. The changes include the following.
Number
one, access to electronic health
records. Covered entities that use
electronic health records must provide
patients with a copy upon
request. They can charge a reasonable
fee for complying with the request such
as a copy labor costs. Number
two, minimum necessary rule.
Covered
entities are required to use or disclose
only the minimum necessary amount of
protected health information required to
complete a covered function. That is use
a limited data set or the least amount
of protected health information
necessary to accomplish the intended
purpose. Number three, business
associate
agreements.
Previously, business associates were
required to comply with HIPPA related
privacy laws through a contract with a
covered
entity, but they were not responsible
for HIPPA compliance.
Now, business associates are bound by
the HIPPA laws and must have policies
and procedures documenting the
same.
Specifically, they must amend their
business associate agreements to add
language that the business associate
must comply with the HIPPA rules,
including the breach notification
requirements and include details on how
the business associate will restore and
safeguard protected health
information. Number four, request for
restrictions.
Covered entities must allow individuals
to request restrictions on how their
protected health information may be
disclosed, but are not required to honor
such requests. For example, a patient
who pays out of pocket can request that
his health care provider not disclose
information about his medical condition
or treatment to his employer or insurer.
Under the old privacy laws, a governed
entity was required to accept the
patients request but did not have to act
upon
it. Effective 2010, however, covered
entities must honor requests not to
disclose protected health
information for purposes of payment or
health care operations only if the
patient pays the entire cost of
treatment out of pocket.
Number five, marketing, fundraising,
communications.
Currently, in
2010, covered entities may not engage in
marketing activities that use a
patient's protective health information
without authorization.
However, an exception exists whereby
covered entities and their business
associates can encourage patients to
purchase or use a health related product
or services without
authorization. For example, a
cardiologist can send materials to his
patients encouraging them to use a
certain cholesterol reducing drug.
This exception applies even if the
covered entity is paid by a third party
that is the drug manufacturer to engage
in such marketing. Under high-tech, such
activities are still permitted but with
additional limitations.
Specifically, the marketing
communication must a describe a
healthcare related product or service
that is provided by or included in the
plan of benefits of the covered entity
making the communication. That is an
insurance company cannot market a drug
that is not covered.
B relate to the treatment of the
individual and
C relate either to the case management
or care coordination for the individual
or to the recommendation of alternate
treatments or providers.
Additionally, covered entities can
continue to receive payments in exchange
for these
communications, but the communications
must relate to a drug that the patient
is currently prescribed, and the payment
must be reasonable.

metadata.title: What is a Multidistrict Litigation, or MDL?
metadata.author: Searcy Law Video
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, attorneys Brenda S. Fulmer and C. Calvin Warriner III explain the intricacies of multidistrict litigation and how this unique process may apply to your potential case.

An MDL is a type of consolidation that occurs when dealing with defective drugs, medical devices, and any other tort that impacts a large number of people. This allows a single judge to focus on and commit a single case, resulting in faster and more consistent rulings.

For more information contact us below:

West Palm Beach, FL 33409
Toll-free: (800) 780-8607

En Espanol: (800) 220-7006
https://www.searcylaw.com/

whether civil actions pending in various federal districts should be transferred to one Federal District for pretrial proceedings if so it selects the presiding judge the judge who handles these coordinated actions is called the transferee judge while the courts where the actions were originally filed are called the transfer or courts the individual case is aggregated in the MDL proceeding are sometimes referred to as the transferred actions or the Constituent actions it is possible for the panel to create MDL proceedings on its own initiative if the panel considers a transfer on its own initiative it will issue a show cause order to all counsel in the actions it is considering consolidating these counsel have 14 days after the date of the order to enter an appearance and 21 days in which to file a response to the panel's proposed transfer if counsel do not respond within 21 days the panel will assume the party agrees to the transfer it is more common however for an attorney for a litigant to create an MDL counsel for any party one of the plaintiffs or one of the defendants may file a motion for transfer with the panel the moving party asks the panel to send all cases involving specified common questions of fact to a Judicial District for the coordination of all pretrial proceedings if the panel determines that the transfer will be more convenient for the parties and witnesses and finds that it will promote the just and efficient conduct of all transferred actions it will grant the motion the motion to transfer that is filed with the Judicial Panel for multi district litigation must explain why aggregation will be more convenient just and efficient and must identify all constituent actions the panel is being asked to transfer the movement must identify each constituent case on a numbered schedule that provides each action involved listing the full name of each party the district court and division where each action is pending the civil action number of each action and the name of the judge assigned to each action this list will be the source of the panel's service list after the move it provides this service list the clerk of the panel will notify the council for all parties in the Constituent cases about the motion filing and activities in the MDL proceeding any party identified on the service list has 21 days to respond to the motion to transfer and a failure to respond is considered consent to the motion it's also possible that later actions will be filed that fit in the parameters of the cases that have been joined in the MDL proceeding should this happen any council representing a party in that MDL proceeding must notify the panel of those other actions if any of the new cases raise the issues stated in the panel's transfer order the panel will transfer these new cases into the MDL the panel's rules call these actions tag-along actions considerations in creating an MDL the panel considers three issues in evaluating whether to issue a transfer order and in determining what that order will say first the cases must share one or more questions of common fact these must be material contested and factual that the disparate cases may share some legal issues is insufficient second transfer must advance the just and efficient handling of the actions the panel will examine the number of cases involved the number of shared questions of fact and the nature of these questions the statutes and rules governing MDL s do not establish a minimum number of cases in the MDL but the panel will take the number of cases into consideration it also must consider the potential to avoid duplicative discovery conflicting rulings unjust delay or needless complication these first two issues focus on whether an MDL somewhere is a good idea next the panel must also consider where to make the transfer the panel will try to transfer the cases to a district judge who can manage the cases in a way that is cost effective efficient and fair to all parties the panel considers the geographical location of the pending cases and the residence of the parties to determine the most convenient district to handle the actions the inquiry of the panel as to the transferee court also includes one whether the proposed district has adequate transportation and hotel facilities to handle counsel from across the country who may participate in the case to the business location of the defendants in relation to the proposed venue three the location of witnesses and evidence in relation to the proposed venue for the presence or absence of other MDL s in the district and five the competence and interest of the proposed transferee judge in handling the MDL affecting the transfer to MDL when the panel orders the transfer of the constituent actions into an MDL the clerk of the panel serves the order on all Council on the service list and sends the order to the transferee court as soon as the clerk of the transferee court files the order the transfer takes effect at that point the transfer or court's jurisdiction ceases and the transferee Court acquires exclusive jurisdiction from that point forward all pretrial proceedings will take place under the supervision of the MDL court this includes discovery and dispositive motions such as motions to dismiss and summary judgment the MDL Court also considers evidentiary motions such as dough bear motions which help determine what scientific and expert testimony will be allowed an often critical determination in mass tort actions the MDL Court is not authorized to try the transferred cases but instead is supposed to remand them to the transfer or courts for any trials that take place however no trial and the transfer or courts can take place until the panel remands the case after the MDL judge has suggested to the panel that it remand those cases the manual for complex litigation issued by the Federal Judicial Center posits that early organization of the case is critically important as soon as the MDL is established the usual practice is for the transferee judge too quickly schedule a status conference with all lawyers involved in the litigation this conference will involve a variety of case management matters to be included in the first case management order one of the most important issues for the MDL court to address is which of the many lawyers representing various plaintiffs will take the lead in managing the aggregated proceedings it is the MDL judges responsibility to choose counsel for leadership positions typically the MDL judge will appoint interim lead or liaison counsel to be spokespeople for the plaintiffs until the MDL judge is able to appoint permanent leadership the judge will need to appoint the plaintiff steering committee which is responsible for the management of the plaintiffs side of the case during pretrial proceedings under the management of that committee there are other leadership roles for example the liaison count handles administrative matters and assists in the coordination of communications between the court and other counsel the liaison counsel usually practices in the transfer or judges district and therefore is conveniently local finally the MDL judge will establish committees to do tasks such as discovery briefing and recruiting expert witnesses MDL judges use two primary methods to select the counsel who will fill the leadership roles in one method the MDL judge invites the lawyers to apply for leadership positions and the judge evaluates the candidates to decide which counsel to select alternatively the MDL judge directs the plaintiff's counsel to file a proposed leadership slate either way the MDL judge ultimately decides which council will take various leading roles another early step in the case usually includes the judge ordering the parties to establish a common benefit fund for the purpose of paying reasonable attorneys fees costs and expenses and to establish rules for the management of that fund initial discovery in MDL cases in a typical non MDL lawsuit plaintiffs are required to make certain disclosures about their claims at the beginning of the case this same requirement manifests in MDL Xin required plaintiff fact sheets fact sheets are court approved standardized forms that seek basic information about plaintiffs claims such as when and why the plaintiff used the product at issue and the injury the plaintiff claims to have suffered the court will also require all the plaintiffs to produce their medical records identify all treating physicians and identify all potential witnesses in some cases the court will also require plaintiffs to produce their employment and educational histories the fact sheets require the same level of completeness as interrogatory answers and other forms of discovery the plaintiffs must sign a declaration at the end of the fact sheet which states the answers are true and correct to the best of their knowledge thus making inaccurate fact sheet responses grounds for perjury charges or other punishment as false statements to the court the court also might require plaintiffs to submit what is called a Lone Pine affidavit which is from a treating physician supporting a plaintiffs claim of injury failure to complete fact sheets in a timely fashion unless excused for good cause may cause the court to dismiss a plaintiff's claim for failure to prosecute defendants also may be required to file fact sheets for each plaintiff providing basic information defendants may have about the claimants or their claims these fact sheets need not be completed until after the plaintiffs file theirs as MDL mass tort actions perceived past these initial stages the MDL judges and litigants often try to introduce class-action procedures into the aggregated action to resolve the cases as a group and to use class action procedures for more detailed discovery this may include the class action procedure of selecting Simbel whether cases to try in the transferee court rather than to remand them to the transfer or courts the results of these bellwether cases may show the parties their potential risks and benefits and facilitate settlement in our next module we will discuss many of the ways in which MDL procedures and class-action procedures are combined in mass tort actions

metadata.title: Trying Cases and Settlement [Multidistrict Litigation (MDL) Conference]
metadata.author: The Federalist Society
metadata.shortDescription:
Multidistrict litigation (“MDL”) accounts for nearly half of all civil cases in federal courts. Although MDLs were designed to be efficient mechanisms for “coordinated or consolidated pretrial proceedings,” in some instances they have become one-sided forums known for lacking the basic protections afforded to all other cases by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (FRCP), the Federal Rules of Evidence and appellate review.

Luncheon Panel: Trying Cases and Settlement

12:30 p.m. - 1:45 p.m.

Moderator

Jeffrey B. Clark, Partner, Kirkland & Ellis LLP
Participants

John Beisner, Partner, Skadden Arps LLP
Brian Jackson, Partner, Butler Snow LLP
Chris Seeger, Founding Partner, Seeger Weiss LLP
Jonathan D. Selbin, Partner, Lieff Cabraser Heimann & Bernstein, LLP

As always, the Federalist Society takes no position on particular legal or public policy issues; all expressions of opinion are those of the speaker.

metadata.title: What Are the Stages of a Lawsuit in an MDL? Part 1 (Explained for Clients)
metadata.author: Nigh Goldenberg Raso & Vaughn PLLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn about the phases of a multi-district litigation (MDL). Mass tort cases against pharmaceutical and medical device companies are typically consolidated nationwide into an MDL. After consolidation, attorney leadership for the litigation is decided. Following the litigation leadership selection, which Nigh Goldenberg is frequently a part of, orders are put in place directing how to file a lawsuit in the MDL, serve the lawsuit and discovery request. The MDL discovery process can be very lengthy in order for the attorneys to go through millions of pages of documents to determine what the defendants knew or should have known regarding the dangers of their products. The strength of a pharmaceutical or medical device case largely depends on the knowledge of a danger or defect in the product and the company's failure to warn of such risk. Following an extensive document review, the leadership attorneys begin taking depositions of key witnesses, such as corporate representatives, sales representatives, and corporate leadership.

0:35 Formation of the MDL leadership attorneys.

1:32 Discovery Phase - Obtaining documents from corporate defendants and reviewing the documents.
2:22 How many documents are typically produced in an MDL?
2:42 Discovery Phase - Depositions of corporate witnesses.

metadata.title: The New Proposed Federal Rule 16.1 and Its Implications for Multidistrict Litigation
metadata.author: Sullivan & Cromwell LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of S&C’s Critical Insights, Bill Monahan, Head of S&C’s Products Liability & Mass Torts Group, and Shane Palmer, an associate in the Firm’s Litigation Group, examine the new proposed Rule 16.1 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, which the Judicial Conference of the United States’ Advisory Committee on Civil Rules recently voted to adopt as the first rule governing multidistrict litigation. They discuss the original proposal for Rule 16.1 that was published last year, the defense and plaintiffs bars’ reaction to the proposed rule, and the final proposed rule that was adopted last month and its implications for MDLs.  
 
Since Congress passed the Multidistrict Litigation Act in 1968 and created the MDL process, there have been no specific rules dictating how judges should manage MDLs, beyond the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure that apply in every federal civil case.
 
In 2017, the Advisory Committee established an MDL Subcommittee to consider whether new rules should be added to address the unique challenges of MDLs. Rule 16.1, which is designed to guide MDL courts in addressing the various and complex issues unique to MDL proceedings, is the first proposed rule to come out of the MDL Subcommittee’s efforts.

segments.text: Welcome to S&C’s Podcast Series, “S&C Critical Insights”.
I’m Bill Monahan, Head of S&C’s Products Liability and Mass Torts Group and a partner
in the Firm’s Litigation Group.
Joining me today is Shane Palmer, an associate in the Firm’s Litigation Group.
Today, we’re going to talk about the new Rule 16.1 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure,
which the Advisory Committee recently voted to adopt as the very first rule governing
multidistrict or MDL litigation.
We’ll be discussing the original proposal for Rule 16.1 that was published last year,
then we’ll talk about the defense and plaintiffs bar’s reaction to the proposed rule, and
then the final rule that was adopted in April, last month, and its implications for MDLs
going forward.
To provide some context for our discussion, Shane, would you start us off by describing
the existing guidance that’s currently out there for conducting pretrial proceedings
in an MDL?
The short answer is that there is no official guidance.
Since Congress passed the Multidistrict Litigation Act in 1968 and created the MDL process, there
haven’t been any specific rules dictating how judges should manage MDLs, beyond the
Federal Rules of Civil Procedure that apply in every federal civil case.
So, in the absence of official guidance of MDLs, courts and parties have turned to sources
such as the Manual for Complex Litigation, which includes recommendations for how to
structure and manage large, complex cases involving many parties.
Relying on the Manual for Complex Litigation and other sources of unofficial guidance,
for years MDL courts have adopted a range of procedural devices designed to create efficiencies
and to reduce the costs and complexities of MDL proceedings.
These include the use of master consolidated pleadings, along with plaintiff fact sheets
to plead facts relating to specific parties, processes for appointing plaintiff steering
committees to act on behalf of other counsel and parties for purposes of coordinated discovery
and pretrial motions, and processes for selecting specific cases to serve as bellwether trials
to resolve key factual disputes that in theory, can inform global settlement negotiations.
In recent years, the number of cases that are transferred to MDLs has ballooned.
Five years ago, about half of all pending federal civil cases were part of an MDL, and
today, five years later, that figure is closer to 70 percent, which is really a remarkable
statistic.
The proliferation of MDL cases combined with the until now, lack of any specific rules
for how MDL should be managed, has raised a number of concerns for both judges and parties
and their lawyers.
One, because there are no mandatory rules governing MDL proceedings and judges are given
significant discretion in managing pretrial proceedings, there is significant uncertainty
about how any given MDL proceeding will be carried out.
Especially in the early stages of litigation before pretrial schedule has been set or a
case management order has been issued.
Another significant issue is that, where there are a very large number of individual cases
consolidated in an MDL often with little screening at the front end, there is an increase potential
for meritless cases to fly under the radar when the MDL lacks a procedure for the early
vetting of individual claims.
The practical reality is that the large number of cases being filed creates a significant
risk of driving settlement numbers up, of compensating meritless cases, and also running
the risk of impeding settlements and settlement negotiations, given the proceed value of cases
that in reality, are not cases that should be paid or should be part of any settlement.
In response to these and other concerns, in 2017 the Advisory Committee established an
MDL Subcommittee to consider whether new rules should be added to the Federal Rules of Civil
Procedure to address these and other unique challenges of MDLs.
The new rule, 16.1, which Shane is going to talk about now, is the first proposed rule
to come out of that Subcommittee’s efforts.
So in June 2023, the Judicial Conference Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure, published
proposed amendments to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, which included the addition
of this new rule, 16.1.
The new rule focused on the early stages of MDLs and introduced four provisions intended
to provide a framework for the initial management of MDL proceedings.
So first, the proposed rule recommended that the MDL court schedule an initial management
conference very early in proceedings.
The proposed rule states that the conference is intended to “develop a management plan
for orderly pretrial activity in the MDL proceedings.”
This generally happens already and so this rule would really just be formalizing an existing
practice.
Second, the MDL Court was given discretion to designate so-called, “coordinating counsel”
to assist the court with the initial management conference and to work with plaintiffs or
with defendants to prepare for the conference.
We’ll talk more about this provision in a bit.
Third, the proposed rule suggested that the MDL court order the parties to meet and confer
in advance of this initial management conference and submit a joint-report covering a variety
of recommended topics.
Those topics included some of the same items that are addressed in a joint-rule 26(f) report
that the parties would submit before an initial Rule 16 scheduling conference in a typical
civil litigation.
Those topics include for example, a proposal for a discovery plan and a potential for early
settlement discussions.
But the topics for this MDL initial management conference also included several items that
are peculiar to MDLs, including among other things, one, whether plaintiff’s leadership
counsel should be appointed, the procedure for their appointment, their role in pretrial
and settlement activities, and the means for their compensation.
Two, discussion of how and when the parties will exchange information about the factual
bases for their claims and defenses.
And three, whether consolidated pleadings should be prepared and how to handle the filing
of new actions in the MDL.
There’s other things enumerated in the proposed rule, but those are just some examples.
And then finally, the proposed rule recommended that MDL courts enter an initial MDL management
order following this conference, addressing the matters discussed in the parties’ report
and any other matters in the courts’ discretion.
Again, this generally happens already, so this would just be formalizing existing practice.
One thing to note, the proposed rule was entirely advisory in nature, so rather than imposing
mandatory requirements on courts and the parties, the rule used permissive language instructing
that courts should or may take certain steps to guide the MDL at the outset of the litigation.
In terms of reactions to the proposal, many lawyers in the defense bar were supportive,
including in particular, the recommendation that MDL courts consider how and when to exchange
information about factual support for plaintiffs’ claims.
It is a reality of many MDLs that meritless cases get filed and effectively parked in
MDLs for years without any meaningful screening or assessment.
And some on the defense side reacted to the rule by arguing that it should include even
more stringent requirements for earlier screening of individual plaintiffs’ claims to combat
the proliferation of meritless cases.
On the other side, the plaintiff’s bar was generally critical of the proposed rule.
In particular, many plaintiffs, attorneys, and advocacy groups reacted negatively to
the inclusion of the coordinating counsel role, arguing that this might give a very
small number of lawyers too much control over key decisions before leadership appointments
were made by the court.
Similarly, some plaintiffs’ counsel complained that the coordinating counsel role could erode
non-lead plaintiff’s autonomy over their individual clients’ claims.
And still other plaintiffs’ counsel complained that a blanket rule applicable to all MDLs
regardless of their size and complexity was inappropriate and would limit MDL judges’
flexibility.
So, let me now talk about the final rule that was ultimately adopted.
Last month, in April, the advisory committee voted to adopt a final version of Rule 16.1
that removed the provision giving the court leeway to designate coordinating counsel to
assist the court and the parties in preparing for the initial MDL management conference,
but it left most of the proposed Rule intact.
Even without that coordinating counsel role, however, once the Rule goes into effect, the
parties in an MDL will still need to coordinate in advance of the initial management conference
to meet and confer about the topics that Rule 16.1 recommends should be covered in that
conference.
So practically speaking, the plaintiffs in an MDL are ultimately going to need to act
through some sort of representative committee in carrying out that coordination at the front
end.
And, in any event, because the final Rule doesn’t prohibit the use of a coordinating
counsel for the initial scheduling conference, MDL courts can still decide to use coordinating
counsel in specific cases at their discretion.
The Advisory Committee also declined to adopt comments calling for stronger language on
a mandatory basis that would require MDL plaintiffs to provide earlier substantiation of individual
plaintiffs claims, but Rule 16.1 does retain the suggestion that the court should order
the parties to address in their initial report how and when they will exchange information
about the factual bases for their claims and defenses, and it recommends that the MDL court’s
initial management order address this issue as well.
As such, defense counsel will soon have a procedural vote to request more stringent
procedures for inquiring into individual plaintiffs’ claims and the bases for them at the outset
of litigation.
Thanks, Shane.
That last point has important implications for defendants’ ability to deal with baseless
claims earlier in MDL proceedings before there’s been any meaningful settlement negotiations.
Currently, delay is not uncommon in the ability to assess the merits of individual plaintiffs
claimed injuries.
Sometimes not until around the time of the bellwether process and often that’s too
late to have any real value in terms of vetting cases for global settlement discussions and
other reasons.
But now that the proposed Rule explicitly endorses the earlier exchange of information
about the parties’ claims, there are a couple of strategies that might be helpful to weeding
out baseless claims early on.
First, for MDL cases that have been filed, defense counsel may want to push in the initial
case management conference for the court to allow early briefing of some threshold relatively
straightforward issues around individual plaintiffs and their injuries.
While more complicated issues around, say causation, that would require expert testimony,
are more typically appropriate and going to be saved for later in the proceedings.
There could be early on some discrete relatively simply issues that defense counsel can target
based on relatively limited disclosures from plaintiffs.
For instance, where the plaintiff didn’t use the product at issue or where records
show that the plaintiff experienced the injury before having used or meaningfully used the
product that allegedly caused the problem.
One additional opportunity to press for earlier discovery is where the parties’ negotiate
the tolling of statutes of limitations for individual cases that have not yet been filed.
Typically this is sometimes called the census registry.
As part of that tolling process, the parties sometimes agree to put in place a registry
for plaintiffs or potential plaintiffs to identify themselves and the nature of their
injuries in order to obtain the benefit of tolling.
At this stage, defense counsel can press for more information and documentation, perhaps
with the benefit of the new proposed Rule here, maybe even some medical records to substantiate
the injuries that are being put on the census registry in order to be eligible for tolling.
Plaintiffs’ counsel will of course remain subject to the requirements of Rule 11 and
comparable rules under state law that conduct a reasonable inquiry into the facts alleged
in a complaint and to represent that those factual contentions have or are likely to
have evidentiary support and if plaintiffs’ counsel fails to put in that work to investigate
the merits of their claims at the outset, they’re going to be risking Rule 11 sanctions.
That’s another tool in addition to the ones I just mentioned available to defendants for
trying to deter unmeritorious claims.
So, the final Rule now will go to the Judicial Conference of the United States for approval
and then on to the Supreme Court.
Finally, the Rule would need to be reviewed and approved by Congress.
With the time it will take to go through that final review process, the Rule won’t come
into effect until sometime in 2025 or later.
But between now and then, MDL courts will almost certainly be looking to the proposed
Rule for guidance.
Thanks for joining me Shane, and thank you all for listening to S&C Critical Insights.
We hope it was interesting.
For more information about our practice please visit us at www.sullcrom.com.

metadata.title: How AI Is Changing Mass Tort Lead Generation
metadata.author: The Leads Warehouse
metadata.shortDescription:
🔥 Artificial intelligence is changing how law firms evaluate mass tort leads, process potential claimants, and scale their intake operations. As AI makes intake faster and more efficient, it is also changing the economics of mass tort lead generation and increasing the importance of high-quality claimant data.

👉 Full breakdown: https://theleadswarehouse.com/why-ai-is-increasing-the-value-of-high-quality-mass-tort-leads/

📌 What You’ll Learn (Mass Tort Leads & AI)

In this 3–4 minute TLW Mass Tort Market Brief, you’ll learn:

• How AI is changing mass tort intake
• What a mass tort lead is
• The three primary types of mass tort leads
• How signed case campaigns work
• How long-form mass tort leads are qualified
• How co-reg real-time mass tort leads create scalable volume
• How AI can increase intake capacity
• Why AI may allow firms to process more claimants without proportionally increasing staff
• How AI can help firms analyze campaign performance
• Why lead quality still matters even with better technology

Mass tort lead campaigns generally include signed cases, long-form leads, and co-reg real-time data, each with different economics and intake requirements.

📂 Category: Mass Tort Lead Generation

This video builds topical authority around:

• Mass tort leads
• Mass tort lead generation
• Mass tort marketing
• AI for law firms
• Artificial intelligence in legal marketing
• Legal lead generation
• Mass tort intake
• Signed mass tort cases
• Long-form mass tort leads
• Co-reg mass tort leads
• Real-time mass tort leads
• Law firm marketing

This video is part of TLW’s ongoing analysis of mass tort lead generation, legal marketing, claimant acquisition, and lead conversion.

🔗 Resources & Next Steps

https://theleadswarehouse.com/

► Schedule a strategy discussion with James Schulze:
https://theleadswarehouse.com/jim/

segments.text: Artificial intelligence is changing mass
tort marketing. Law firms can evaluate
potential claimants faster, process more
cases, and make better decisions about
where to spend their marketing dollars.
And that is changing the economics of
mass tort lead generation.
Mass tort intake can involve reviewing
medical records, claimant information,
treatment histories, exposure details,
and other documentation. AI is helping
intake teams organize and summarize that
information, identify any missing
documentation, and flag potential
qualifying cases much faster.
So, what exactly is a mass tort lead?
It's a consumer who may qualify for
legal action involving things like
pharmaceutical injuries, defective
medical devices, toxic exposure,
environmental contamination, or product
liability.
Mass tort lead generation generally
falls into three major categories:
signed case or full intake campaigns,
long-form leads, and co-registration
real-time leads. Each offers a different
combination of qualification, consumer
intent, volume, cost, and work required
by the law firm.
Signed case campaigns go furthest
through the intake process. The claimant
is qualified, intake is completed, an
attorney is engaged, and a retainer is
executed. These cases cost considerably
more, but much of the intake work has
already been completed.
Long-form leads collect detailed
information before the lead reaches the
law firm. That can include diagnosis,
injury, prescription history, treatment
timelines, exposure, and other
qualifying criteria. The additional
information helps firms screen and
prioritize potential claimants.
Co-reg real-time leads offer another
approach. They can provide scalable
volume and lower acquisition costs, but
typically require more filtering,
qualification, and intake work from the
law firm.
And this is where AI starts changing
mass tort marketing. If technology
allows the same intake team to
efficiently evaluate more potential
claimants, a firm's capacity to work
lead volume can increase without
necessarily increasing staff at the same
rate.
We've seen this firsthand. One large
national law firm we work with
traditionally focused on long-form and
full intake leads because of internal
volume limitations. After adding AI
processing capabilities, they didn't
replace those channels. They added
co-reg leads to create additional
volume.
AI can also help firms evaluate campaign
performance in real time, improve
outreach, test scripts, and identify
which torts are producing stronger
cases. That matters because mass tort
marketing isn't simply about generating
the most leads. It's about finding
qualified claimants and controlling the
cost of acquiring signed cases.
AI doesn't make a bad lead good. What it
can do is help law firms process
qualified opportunities faster and at
greater scale. As intake becomes more
efficient, high-quality mass tort leads
become even more valuable. The firms
that combine good leads, strong intake,
and smart technology may be able to
build larger case inventories more
efficiently than ever before.

metadata.title: Billion Dollar Lawsuits: When Litigation Finance Met Mass Torts
metadata.author: Bloomberg Law
metadata.shortDescription:
Mass tort litigation has become a booming industry, with billions of dollars at stake for plaintiffs, lawyers, and investors. 

The litigation finance industry has taken notice, pouring money into these lawsuits attracted by the potential of high returns. In 2023, for example, litigation funders funneled nearly $17 billion into lawsuits like the Camp Lejuene and 3M earplug cases. These suits are driven by extensive digital advertising campaigns to identify potential claimants. 

For the law firms bringing these cases, this can lead to massive paydays. Lawyers typically taking 20-40% if they're successful, and that can amount to billions of dollars in high-profile cases.

metadata.title: Making Millions Off Other People’s Lawsuits: How Litigation Finance Works
metadata.author: Bloomberg Law
metadata.shortDescription: For centuries it was considered taboo for a third-party to have a financial stake in a lawsuit. Today, thanks to an industry re-examining the relevance of legal doctrines from feudal times, a new crop of firms have sprouted to invest in lawsuits for profit. The concept, known as litigation finance, has quickly spawned  a multi-billion dollar industry that is getting the attention of the country’s largest law firms. In this video, Bloomberg Law’s Roy Strom gives a peek inside this growing practice and explains what it means for the future of the business of law. (Reporting by Roy Strom, video editing & graphics by Virginia Gilles, Senior Producer: Andrew Satter, Executive Producer: Josh Block.)

metadata.title: Lawyers Explain Litigation Finance | How Lawsuit Funding Levels the Playing Field in PI Cases
metadata.author: Dolman Law Group
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of the David and Goliath Podcast, Matt Dolman and Stan Gipe of Dolman Law Group based in Clearwater, FL, sit down with Casey Gard to break down the reality of litigation finance and its growing impact. They discuss lawsuit funding, tort reform, and how private capital is helping level the playing field between plaintiffs and powerful insurance companies.

With over 30 years in finance and 25+ years as an investment manager across hedge funds and private equity, Casey brings a unique perspective to the legal world. Focused on litigation finance through his family office, he shares how capital is deployed, common misconceptions about the industry, and why funding is critical for firms handling complex, high-stakes cases.

Available on Spotify, Apple, YouTube, and other fine retailers where podcasts are sold.

metadata.title: How Litigation Finance Can Help Lawyers and Law Firms
metadata.author: TownCenter Partners Litigation Finance
metadata.shortDescription:
At first glance, a lawyer may feel reluctant to work with a third-party funder, even if the client is eager for help in financing the case.  But a closer look at litigation funding reveals that it offers several significant advantages for building a better law practice.

metadata.title: The August 2026 Mass Tort Power Rankings: What to Acquire, What to Watch, and What Is Settling
metadata.author: Jon and Marc
metadata.shortDescription:
In Episode 51 of Tort Talk, Jon Robinson sits down with mass tort litigator Joseph Fantini of Rosen Injury Lawyers to break down the official August 2026 Mass Tort Power Rankings. With major developments across consolidated litigations, Jon and Joe provide an actionable roadmap for plaintiff law firms looking to optimize case acquisition, assess docket maturity, and capitalize on approaching settlement cycles.

From mature litigations nearing resolution to high-upside emerging opportunities in medical devices and pharmaceuticals, discover which dockets warrant aggressive investment and which are facing procedural hurdles like arbitration enforceability.

In this episode, we cover:

1.) The official August 2026 Top 10 Mass Tort Power Rankings

2.) Why Hair Relaxer could follow the Talc settlement trajectory for uterine, endometrial, and ovarian cancer claims

3.) Updates on the upcoming Bard PowerPort bellwether trial on August 18

4.) The resurgence of Tylenol following the Second Circuit's decision reinstating expert testimony

5.) Why Video Game Addiction is flying under the radar as a top cross-selling opportunity for personal injury, family law, and disability firms

6.) Key requirements for filing Uber and Lyft sexual abuse claims before resolution windows close

7.) Emerging medical device opportunities in Olympus Scopes ahead of MTMP

7.) Ones to Watch: Early movements and MDL forecasts for Kratom and Online Gambling Addiction

8.) The reigning champion: Which litigation holds the undisputed #1 spot?

Chapters: 
00:00 - Introduction and August Power Rankings Overview 
00:59 - #10: Tylenol (Second Circuit Decision and Expert Strategy) 
02:13 - #9: Bair Hugger (Settlement Rumors in a Mature Docket) 
03:05 - #8: Bard PowerPort (Previewing the August 18 Bellwether Trial) 
04:23 - #7: Roblox (Arbitration Clauses and State Court Traction) 
06:05 - #6: Olympus Scope (The Hottest Emerging Tort Heading into MTMP) 
07:44 - #5: Weight Loss Drugs / GLP-1s (GI Injury vs. NAION Vision Loss Tracks) 
08:56 - #4: Video Game Addiction (Why This Tort Is Flying Under the Radar) 
11:00 - #3: Uber Sexual Abuse (Liability Picture, Filing Proof, and Looming Settlements) 
12:54 - #2: Hair Relaxer (Settlement Trajectory and Viable Injury Criteria) 
14:05 - Strategic Framework Behind the Power Rankings 
14:56 - Ones to Watch: Kratom and Gambling Addiction 
17:40 - #1: The Undisputed King of the Power Rankings 
19:23 - How Law Firms Can Efficiently Acquire and Sign Mass Tort Cases

#MassTorts #TortTalk #LawFirmGrowth #PersonalInjuryLaw #LegalMarketing #HairRelaxer #GLP1 #MedicalDeviceLitigation #MDL #triallawyers 

About The Jon & Marc Podcast

The Jon & Marc Podcast is for lawyers who care about growth and the bottom line. Jon and Marc interview leaders in plaintiff law to break down how major cases are built, how firms scale, and how strategy plays out behind the scenes. If you want to understand how the biggest players in the space think and operate, you’re in the right place. New episodes every week.

Joe, thanks for joining us. I know we've got a lot of progress that has happened in the world of mass torts over the past week. You excited to get into the power rankings? >> Hey, it's Mark. Before we dive into this episode, we just want to say that we built our our digital around one simple idea. Law firms do not need more random marketing activity. They need more signed cases. That's why we handle everything from advertising to social media with a founder-led approach that keeps the strategy tight and the work accountable to a real outcome. Stop chasing vanity metrics and get more cases. Go to rrdigitalmedia.com for more information. Let's get back to the episode. >> Yeah, glad to be here with you. Excited to go over the power rankings, kind of give a picture of where we're at right now and what we're thinking we'll see for the rest of 2026. >> Let's get right into it. Coming in at number 10, one that has not cracked the top 10 in a very, very long time, we have Tylenol. Fresh off the second circuit's decision, we've been hearing a lot of buzz, but really haven't seen much movement yet. Joe, why is this one that people should be paying attention to here at number 10? >> Yeah, like you mentioned, we were waiting for almost 2 years to get that decision out of the second circuit. It came down in our favor and allowed our experts to come back in. So, there's definitely big fight to still be had about these cases and we're going against J&J, who we know has a history of dragging all the litigations out, but I feel like this is a good opportunity for people to get involved in this case. The liability seems pretty clear, especially after the decisions that we had in previous trials. New cases are getting harder and harder to come by. So, I think these cases don't hang on, you know, this time next year in 2027. They've made a lot of changes to their platform. So, definitely get the cases on file, but I think we'll be hearing about a settlement in this one maybe in the next 6 months. >> That would be fantastic, especially if they've actually put things in place to prevent this from from happening any further. metadata.title: Litigation Finance - The class action perspective
metadata.author: Addleshaw Goddard
metadata.shortDescription: What does the future hold for class action litigation funding? Watch on as Stephen O'Dowd from Harbour Litigation Funding shares his views on the risk management option transforming the global disputes market.

segments.text: [MUSIC PLAYING]
Hello, my name is Stephen O'Dowd,
and I'm a senior director of litigation funding at Harbour.
Very much, a global concept.
There's an interchanging of terminology,
which can be confusing.
So you might hear these claims variously described
as class actions, group actions, mass litigation,
collective redress.
But the ability of a group of people
who have all suffered a common harm to collectively bring
their claim, that ability has existed outside of the United
States for a long time.
Perhaps, a newer phenomenon is the facilitation
of class actions through the introduction of legislation.
Genuine class action regimes that allow a single claimant
to represent the interests of a much wider group.
Taking examples outside of the US, Australia and Canada,
they both have generic, genuine, and quite mature class action
regimes.
And the UK, the UK has a class action regime.
It's restricted only to competition litigation claims,
but nevertheless, it's a genuine regime.
So very much, a global concept.
Class actions are typically large,
both in scale and the amount of damages at stake, which
means that they're expensive.
Both expensive in terms of your own side
legal costs and in some countries, you have the loser
pays principle.
So if you get it wrong, if you're
unsuccessful in your claim, generally, you
will have to pay a large portion of your opponent's costs,
as well.
The ability to shift that cost burden onto a litigation funder
is really important in the context of a class action.
And in my experience, even the largest,
well-resourced institutions would generally not
use their standard litigation budget
to participate on the claimant side in a class action.
They tend to look for a risk management option,
such as litigation funding.
I've no doubt that class actions will
continue to develop and grow globally in the coming years.
Why do I say that?
Well, even the largest, most sophisticated
institutional clients are becoming more familiar with
and more comfortable with participating
on the claimant side in class actions.
And in some cases, they feel compelled to participate
because the behaviour of the defendant has been
so egregious.
Then from an investment perspective,
I've said before, these claims tend to be large.
The damages are significant, which
can make them an attractive investment proposition
for litigation funders.
And with all of this happening, the experience and expertise
of lawyers and the judiciary develops, too.
All those ingredients lead to growth.
But I'm not somebody who agrees with some of the alarmists who
say that there has been or will be
an explosion of class actions.
That the floodgates have opened or that they're about to open.
If you take Australia as an example,
some alarmists have been saying that
about that regime for a long time,
but the statistics don't back it up.
Another issue or a reason that there hasn't been or won't
be an explosion is, I've mentioned it,
the loser pays principle, which applies in Australia
and some other countries.
The price of getting it wrong is significant,
which is a check and balance against frivolous claims.
And also, I find that countries can
be cautious about introducing legislation
for class action regimes.
They tend to set the threshold quite high for those claimants
being allowed to proceed.
Take the UK as an example.
The class action regime for competition claims
is into its fourth year and not a single claim has got up yet.
Not a single claim has been certified,
which I think is quite telling.
So I expect growth and development,
but measured growth and development.

metadata.title: Litigation Finance Market Process
metadata.author: The National Law Review
metadata.shortDescription:
Commercial litigation funding is a powerful tool that provides financial support for legal claims, but securing and structuring funding requires a deep understanding of the legal agreements involved. This episode is designed to help attorneys navigate the complexities of litigation finance agreements, ensuring their clients secure funding on favorable terms while mitigating risks.

This session covers the different uses of litigation funding, the process of obtaining financing, and the essential legal provisions in prepaid forward purchase agreements. Attorneys will gain insights into payment structures, recourse vs. non-recourse agreements, termination clauses, confidentiality protections, and dispute resolution mechanisms to ensure clarity and enforceability in these contracts.

Download the free slide deck (PDF) here: 
https://financial-poise-video-webinars.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/2026/COMMERCIAL_LITIGATION_FUNDING_-101/2-Litigation-Finance-Market-Process/2-Litigation-Finance-Market-Process.pdf

metadata.title: Mass Tort Update 2026: Roundup Settlement, PFAS Litigation & Uber Cases | Steve Smith
metadata.author: Cut to the Chase Network
metadata.shortDescription:
Mass tort litigation is heating up in 2026 — and this episode breaks down the cases making the biggest impact right now.

From a major proposed settlement in the Roundup litigation to growing momentum around PFAS “forever chemical” cases, and ongoing lawsuits tied to Uber safety concerns, this episode gives you a clear, insider view of where things stand.

Gregg Goldfarb is joined by Steve Smith of Broughton Partners, to unpack the latest updates, explain what they mean for claimants and attorneys, and highlight why this year could be a turning point for mass tort law.
Join Gregg and Steve on "Cut to the Chase" as they discuss:
What the proposed Roundup settlement means and why some attorneys are concerned about case values

How PFAS contamination became a nationwide legal and public health issue
Why 2026 could bring major resolutions across multiple mass tort cases
The reality behind Uber lawsuits and ongoing safety concerns
How mass tort litigation is evolving for law firms and claimants

KEY MOMENTS
Uber lawsuits teaser and what’s coming in this episode
Why 2026 could be a major year for mass torts
Roundup settlement update and proposed payout structure
Why who you partner with in litigation matters
PFAS cases explained: “forever chemicals” and water contamination
The scale of PFAS exposure across the U.S.
Camp Lejeune updates and what’s changing
Uber lawsuits: safety concerns and allegations explained
How mass tort opportunities are evolving for law firms
How to get involved in mass tort litigation

Steve Smith is the VP of Business Development at Broughton Partners, where he helps law firms navigate and scale within the mass tort space.
With over 20 years of experience in sales, marketing, and business development — including more than a decade focused specifically on legal marketing — Steve has worked closely with many of the nation’s top firms on case acquisition, intake strategy, and mass tort growth.
Through his work, he specializes in connecting law firms with qualified claimants, vetted litigators, and data-driven strategies that help firms expand into complex litigation while managing risk.

The resources mentioned in this episode are:
Learn more about the proposed Roundup settlement, including the tiered payout structure, residential-use claims, and non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma cases discussed in this episode.
Explore PFAS “forever chemicals” litigation, including firefighter exposure, drinking water contamination, and the push toward a broader resolution of these cases.
Learn more about Camp Lejeune water contamination claims and how changes to the statute of limitations have allowed affected individuals to pursue legal action.
Watch the film “Falling Waters” referenced in the episode for background on early environmental contamination litigation and how these cases first came to light.
Stay informed on Uber-related litigation involving passenger safety concerns, background check practices, and ongoing multidistrict litigation.
Learn more about Paraquat litigation and its alleged link to Parkinson’s disease, including both MDL and state court case developments.

Contact Steve Smith at Broughton Partners if you are a law firm interested in entering or expanding within the mass tort space:
Email: steve@broughtonpartners.com
Phone: 954-224-1733

Learn more about Broughton Partners’ consortium model, which allows law firms to diversify across multiple mass tort cases with shared resources, vetted partners, and strategic guidance.

Want to hear more mass tort updates, and legal issues shaping our communities, affecting everyday people? Subscribe to Cut to the Chase: with Gregg Goldfarb.

If you or a family member has a case involving Camp Lejeune, PFAS, NEC, or Depo-Provera, you've probably seen headlines about deadlines and settlements and wondered where your claim actually stands. In Part 2 of this conversation on Climate Change Environment Science & the Law with Gregg Goldfarb, host Gregg Goldfarb sits down again with Stephen Smith, Vice President of Broughton Partners, to unpack four more mass tort campaigns that are all reaching critical moments.

Smith explains why Camp Lejeune finally has real momentum, now that a federal judge has given plaintiffs' leadership until the end of October to reach a deal with the DOJ or risk being replaced. He also clarifies why no new Camp Lejeune claims can be filed, since the window Congress opened has now closed. On PFAS, he walks through how firefighting foam (AFFF) seeps into soil and drinking water, why 131,000 cases were filed when only 60,000 to 70,000 were expected, and how an upcoming Daubert hearing on two additional injuries could shift negotiating leverage before a possible global resolution.

On NEC, Smith explains how two defendants agreed to pay just under $1 billion, why state court cases have succeeded where the federal MDL has not, and why the details of case values are still unknown. And on Depo-Provera, he breaks down the science linking the birth control shot to brain tumors called meningiomas, with more than a 5x increased risk, and shares his expectation of average case values between $150,000 and $200,000 for qualifying claims.

Throughout, Smith and Goldfarb stress that deadlines, qualifications, and venue all matter, and that claimants should talk to their own firm about where their specific case stands.


WHAT YOU'LL LEARN

- Why a federal judge's October deadline could force a Camp Lejeune resolution
- Why new Camp Lejeune claims can no longer be filed
- How firefighting foam contaminates drinking water across the country
- Why 131,000 PFAS cases were filed, and how that number has been cleaned up
- What a Daubert hearing is, and how it could change PFAS negotiations
- How to find out if your water is contaminated with PFAS
- Why NEC cases in state court have outperformed the federal MDL
- What the science shows about Depo-Provera and brain tumors
- What Depo-Provera claimants might expect, and when


TIME STAMPS
0:00 - Intro
0:15 - Camp Lejune case updates
4:17 - PFAS Water Contamination Ligitagion
13:24 - NEC - Pre-Term Babies Settlement
14:23 - Depo-Provera Litigation and conclusion


Stephen Smith is Vice President of Broughton Partners, a mass tort marketing and consulting firm, where he has spent nearly 20 years advising law firms and claimants across major litigations including Talc, Roundup, Hernia Mesh, Social Media, Camp Lejeune, PFAS, NEC, and Depo-Provera. Known industry-wide as "The Mass Tort Mentor," he works to help claimants get connected with qualified representation and to help law firms navigate complex, evolving litigation. 


Contact / Follow Stephen Smith: 

Firm: https://www.broughtonpartners.com/
Phone: 954-224-1733 
Email: steve@broughtonpartners.com
 

Want more conversations that cut through the noise on science, climate, and the issues shaping our future? Subscribe to Climate Change Environment Science & the Law with Gregg Goldfarb for new episodes every week.

metadata.title: Hernia Mesh Lawsuit 2026 Update | How to File a Hernia Mesh Lawsuit
metadata.author: Drugwatch
metadata.shortDescription:
Thousands of people who received hernia mesh implants have filed lawsuits after serious complications. A free hernia mesh case review through Drugwatch can help you learn if you qualify for a lawsuit: https://www.drugwatch.com/hernia-mesh/lawsuit-help/   

Some of the biggest issues patients face include chronic pain, infection, mesh migration, adhesions, bowel obstruction, hernia recurrence and the need for revision surgery.

In August 2026, a federal jury awarded $88 million to an Alabama man and his wife in the first Covidien hernia mesh bellwether trial. However, the judge said that the amount may be reduced. The case involved claims that the man's bowel became stuck to mesh and that he required additional surgery.

Hernia mesh lawsuits involve manufacturers including Bard/Davol, Atrium and Covidien/Medtronic.

You may be eligible for a lawsuit if you had hernia repair surgery with mesh and later experienced serious complications. Qualification can depend on the type of mesh used, your injury, medical history, surgery dates, available records and the filing deadline in your state.

Drugwatch’s free case review is confidential, and there is no obligation to file a lawsuit.

This video provides general information and is not medical or legal advice. A case review does not guarantee that you qualify for a lawsuit or receive compensation.

segments.text: In August, 2026, a federal jury awarded $88 million
to an Alabama man and his wife
in the first Covidien, Hernia Mesh Bellwether trial.
Larry Patterson said his bowel became stuck to the mesh
manufactured by Medtronic, and he needed another surgery.
The verdict was based on the facts of that one case,
and every lawsuit is different.
Thousands of people who got hernia mesh implants
have filed lawsuits after suffering serious complications.
More than 26,000 hernia mesh lawsuits
are pending in federal court against companies
including Bard Duvol, Atrium, and Covidien Medtronic.
These cases are grouped into separate
multi-district litigations, or MDLs, for each manufacturer.
An MDL lets one court manage similar lawsuits
from people all across the country.
Hernia mesh is an implant used to strengthen weak tissue
during hernia repair, but some people say their mesh
caused painful and serious health problems.
Complications include bowel blockages,
a hernia returning, infection, mesh failure,
or mesh moving out of place, organ damage,
long lasting pain, and scar tissue.
Hernia mesh lawsuits say some manufacturers sold
defective implants and did not properly warn patients
or doctors about the possible risks.
You may qualify for a hernia mesh lawsuit
if you had a hernia repair with Mech
and needed another surgery afterwards,
or if you're scheduled for another surgery
to repair damage.
You may also qualify if you had serious complications
that required medical procedures other than surgery.
Your medical and surgical records
can help show which mesh brand you receive
and document your complications.
Filing deadlines may apply and qualifications depend
on the facts of your case.
Settlement amounts and jury awards vary based on
the mech brand, the severity of injury,
and the details of each individual case.
There is no set payout.
For example, Bard Davol paid $184 million
to settle about 2,700 hernia mesh cases back in 2011.
In 2024, Bard's parent company, Becton Dickinson,
reached a settlement covering nearly 38,000 cases.
The amount paid to each plaintiff was not disclosed.
Jury awards have ranged from hundreds of thousands of dollars
to $88 million against Medtronic
in the Patterson Covidien case.
While past results don't guarantee similar outcomes
in future cases, you may still qualify for a lawsuit
if you were injured after hernia mesh surgery.
Drugwatch has advocated for your legal rights since 2009.
We've connected more than 20,000 families
with experienced lawyers to protect their rights.
And Drugwatch offers a free case review
if you've been hurt by defective hernia mesh.
If you qualify, an experienced hernia mesh attorney
will contact you to discuss your legal options.
These attorneys typically work on a contingency basis.
That means you usually pay nothing unless you win your case.
However, you may have to pay certain fees
such as court costs.
It's important to ask the attorney
about any out-of-pocket costs.
If you've been injured by mesh,
you have a limited time to file a hernia mesh lawsuit.
A lawyer can tell you if you qualify.
Go to drugwatch.com/hernia-mech/lawsuit-help.
Or click that link in the description below
to see if you have a case.

metadata.title: Hernia Mesh Lawsuit Update: Covidien Verdict, Bard Settlement, and What Comes Next | Timothy O'Brien
metadata.author: Cut to the Chase Network
metadata.shortDescription:
Larry Patterson went in for a routine hernia repair. He came out, eventually, with several inches of his bowel removed.
Timothy O’Brien, board-certified trial attorney and shareholder at Levin Papantonio, just won $88 million for Patterson and his wife Tammy against Covidien, a Medtronic company. It is the largest compensatory award in fifteen years of mesh litigation, and the first of roughly 2,500 cases to reach a jury. The mesh, Symbotex, sits right against your intestines behind a collagen barrier meant to last 30 days. Covidien’s own internal testing showed it was gone in under seven. They knew in 2003.
O’Brien walks Gregg through the evidence that turned the trial, where sales staff swore to doctors the barrier lasted a month while R&D said otherwise in writing. He also maps the hernia mesh lawsuit landscape, from the Bard settlement covering 33,000 claimants to why Medtronic Covidien is the last major manufacturer still fighting, and what a bellwether verdict actually means for the thousands of people still waiting on their own cases.


Join Gregg and Timothy O'Brien on Climate Change Environment Science & the Law as they explore:  
What You'll Learn
Why a generation of surgeons stopped doing tissue-to-tissue repair, and what that traded away
How Symbotex’s protective barrier was supposed to work, and how fast it actually disappeared
The 2003 document that locked in the depositions and became the case’s spine
Why sales and R&D were telling two completely different stories about the same product
