And they knew back in 2003 and that was our key document that really unpacked the deposition testimony where they really got locked in where they had to say, "Yeah, it's gone or no longer working within 7 days." >> Okay, so you know, lots of people have hernias. And from what I understand, and I haven't done a survey of everybody that's gone and had a hernia repaired and what their doctor's telling them. But for the most part, from what I understand, people go in, they see their doctor, that you have a hernia that needs to be repaired, we're going to put this mesh in it, and there are different manufacturers, different mesh products out there. So people end up getting involved in the litigation and they don't even really know who the manufacturer of the product is. They're getting interviewed by their lawyers and they're saying, "Which Who's the manufacturer?" Well, the lawyers figure it out later on when they get the medical records. But that part that plays into I think a little of the confusion when people have a hernia mesh case and they're seeing that there was a settlement and then they're hearing there's a trial verdict. So let's just kind of break this down like how many different manufacturers were there? Are they all settled? Were their products okay? I mean, just give me a general lay of the land. >> So, there were three major manufacturers and two of which are still on the market today. The number one is Bard or Becton Dickinson, and that's the one where it's been a very large settlement involving 33,000 claimants that I led with Kelsey Stokes out of Ohio. And they that by market share had the largest number of claimants, and that's still in administration. So, most of the folks have not been received their funds yet who were Bard claimants, but it pays out over the next 2 years. So, that that's the number one by market share. Very close behind that is Medtronic Covidien. So, that's the case I just tried. And Medtronic Covidien actually was in a settlement posture with us for years, and they had us on what's called a tolling agreement where they said, "Don't file your cases. Let's see if we can get a settlement working. Let's get them all under one roof, and then we'll look at them and we'll try to settle them." And then they had a change in the general counsel, and they just said, "Okay, we're pulling the tolling agreement. We're not going to settle." So, that's when this MDL was formed, and that's why we're a little behind the rest of the MDLs that have settled. The third manufacturer is Johnson & Johnson or Ethicon, and they had multiple products. One was called Physiomesh, which was actually a recalled product, and that was an MDL that was based out of Northern District of Georgia or Atlanta. And then the two other major products they had were called Proceed and PHS or Prolene Hernia Systems, and those were in an MCL or a massive state court litigation in New Jersey that Kelsey and I led with some other folks, and we resolved those, got a settlement in about two two and a half years ago, and that is almost done being funded. The Physiomesh also settled, and that's completely funded. So, really the only major manufacturer with any sizeable market share that's left that has not resolved is Medtronic Covidien, which is what we're fighting now. >> Okay, so just for those out there that are like, "Okay, I'm starting to understand. My case didn't settle." From what I understand, there's 2,400 cases, Covedien cases, in the multi-district litigation. >> Right, it's probably closer to 2,500. We get about I think we're on the order of about 100 a month are being filed there, but yes, that's the rough ballpark. >> All right, so in this case, well, you know, I'm just kind of throwing out some terms that people are like, "What what is what is that all about?" This was the first bellwether trial in that multi-district litigation to go forward. >> Yeah, so just a a bird's-eye view of what a bellwether trial is, it's not these are not class actions. If you have a hernia mesh case, you've got your own case. So, your case theoretically would either settle or be tried. It's not a class action where there's one trial, and then boom, it it locks in the the judgment for everybody else. So, this is kind of a a test case to see how is a jury going to react to lines of evidence, to the experts, to the scientific issues. So, yeah, this is the first Covedien test case. It's a very real case. It's a very real judgment, a real verdict, real consequences, but it is just one man's case. >> All right. And so, when you say bellwether, that's sort of like a test case. It's a real case, but it's designed to show all the people in the litigation, the lawyers, and the the clients what could happen one way or another, but it doesn't necessarily mean that the next bellwether trial is going to be another big victory for the plaintiff. >> That's a good way of looking at it. And of course, there's some efficiencies that happen in the second and third cases because the judge has ruled on a lot of common scientific issues, and a lot of those rulings will carry over downstream for the next case to be tried and so forth, but the actual case-specific stuff, so the client-specific stuff, is all very individual. And so, for For in our Patterson case, we actually had the implanter come to trial, the person who made the decision. And in the next case, that may not be that way because they may not be available to try. So, you you be you have to take a deposition of them. And their decision, the reason why they chose a mesh may be different than the doctor's decision-making in the Patterson case. So, there's very individual issues. But the very first bellwether case, by far I think most people who try these cases will tell our viewers is the most important because it sets the tone and also it sets it really creates a body of rulings which kind of become law of the case for the other similar cases that follow. >> All right. So, you did mention that prior to this trial, Covidien expressed interest in resolving all the cases and that they had a change of heart. Since this trial, is there any update on that? Or are they like, "Hey, we're going to take an appeal. We're fighting this tooth and nail. See you at the next trial." >> They are definitely going to appeal. You know, it costs a few hundred dollars and a one-page piece of paper to file the notice of appeal. But in so far, at least in their their press releases, they indicate they're going to appeal. We've had a settlement special master that was appointed several months ago by the judge. And so, obviously we've been working to see about a resolution. But frankly, I think both parties, over the last several months, all of their attention has been devoted to trying this case that we just tried. So, it remains to be seen whether this will motivate Minneapolis, where Medtronic is located, to take settlement a little more seriously than they have in the past. >> All right. So, when are the next bellwethers? Are there any new bellwethers that are set for trial? >> So, the judge indicated the last trial, toward the end of the Patterson trial, that she wanted to try the next one in the fall of this year. So, in just in a few months. We are actually having a meeting with a judge later this week to talk about the scheduling of the next trial. I'm not sure when her calendar is going to have 4 weeks where she can try it, but my expectation is that it would be late this year or sometime before the summer of next year. And those cases have already been worked up, so there was a bellwether pool where there was a small group of cases that were selected by the court to be the pool of bellwether cases. So, we know what cases are coming up next. >> So, I think this is a good point to end this discussion. My main issue here is I know there are people out there that sometimes maybe they're able to talk to their attorney about their case and it's a short conversation. So, this is designed to really kind of give a little bit of more of a global nature to the discussion and you're not going to get like a 2-minute talk here or whatever. Tim, I'd like to shout out to your co-counsel. You did not try this case alone. Who were you with? >> So, Kelsey Stokes who I mentioned earlier, she really did the overwhelming majority of work on the experts and she was masterful at it. So, she tried the case, we split the witnesses evenly. I got to have the fun doing openings and closings. We both selected the jury together. So, we were pretty equal trying this case, but she did the unfun stuff which is putting experts on and direct examination, both our regulatory expert, our causation expert, and then taking the cross-examination of their biomaterials expert. So, Kelsey and I were the two trial attorneys for this case. >> All right, and Kelsey is with Mark Lanier's outfit, right? >> She is correct and for purposes of the Medtronic litigation, she's actually got her own firm called Stokes and Hogs that does nothing but the Medtronic Covidien litigation just simply as a carryover from her prior firm. So, she is with Mark Lanier's office, but she tried this case as a partner in Stokes and Hogs. >> All right, is your firm Levin Papantonio accepting new Covidien cases? >> We're actually accepting new Bard cases, too, although because of the Bard settlement, it's not just wide open in terms of Bard cases. Uh you have to be pretty selective because in Bard, now we have to file pretty soon after you file all the lawsuit, you have to file an expert report, a case specific expert report. But obviously, there's no settlement on Covidien, so yes, we're accepting Covidien hernia mesh cases as we speak. >> All right. So, folks, if you've had a hernia repaired and then you had that dreaded revision and removing some of your intestines or whatever, what's the best way to get in contact with you, Timothy? >> Yeah, so you you can always go to levinlaw.com. That's levinlaw.com, or you can email me directly. That's tobrien@levinlaw.com. And we'll be happy to get some basic information and get your medical records together so we can see A that you had a mesh and B what your damages are, and then see be able to advise you on what your legal recourse is from that point forward. >> All right. This is Timothy O'Brien, shareholder with Levin Papantonio, board-certified trial attorney. Thanks for coming on short notice. I wanted to get this out there because in part, I wanted some of this information, too. So, hopefully, we're clearing the confusion and all that. And Tim, get back to work. You got a lot to do, all right? >> All right. It's good seeing you, Greg. >> All right. Everybody listen, share this episode because maybe your friend or a loved one had that dreaded hernia operation. They're like, "Oh my god, what am I going to do?" And you know, maybe the only thing you can do is go to court and get compensation. >> [music]

metadata.author: Napoli Shkolnik
metadata.shortDescription:
Andrew Croner discusses the next phase of PFAS litigation as cases move beyond AFFF firefighting foam exposure and toward individual personal injury claims. 

Learn how the AFFF MDL is shaping future PFAS lawsuits, why medical documentation is becoming increasingly important, and what individuals should know about pursuing claims involving kidney cancer, testicular cancer, ulcerative colitis, thyroid disease, and other PFAS-related conditions.

segments.text: Hello, everyone. Welcome to another episode of Tort Talk with Joe Fantini of Rosen Injury
Lawyers. Joe, as always, appreciate you taking time out every week to come in and share with us
what you've learned as it relates to the updates and insights and all things mass tort. Thanks for
having me, Susan. Yeah, so I know a couple of quick updates that I wanted you to share would
be around both Talc and the CPAP cases and that litigation. Share with us what you've learned
over the last week. Yeah, some big developments in both of those cases. We'll start with CPAP.
So recently it was just announced that CPAP entered into a settlement to resolve all of the
personal injury claims. The settlement is for $1.1 billion. There's approximately
58,000 cases involved. Under the terms of the settlement, we need to get 95% participation,
which a little bit lower than what we usually see, about 98%. Phillips isn't going to be involved in
the administration of the settlement. It's going to be up to leadership to kind of categorize and
award different amounts. And then also everybody has an additional six months to come forward,
whether or not a claims on the registry or have been filed, to bring forward another claim.
Supposedly the settlement's going to be funded in 2025. So this was a really surprising development
because we haven't even served our expert reports which were due at the end of May. So everybody's
really excited about this settlement and we'll learn more in the coming weeks about the specific
injuries to be included. Awesome. Tell us a little bit about Talc. Yeah, another big development in
Talc. As everybody knows, J&J previously had the two unsuccessful bankruptcy petitions. They were
both dismissed at the end of last year. J&J moved and created a company and established it in Texas
for this two step, which we were expecting. Under the previous bankruptcies, J&J was proposing $9.8
billion to resolve the ovarian and Meso cases. Just this week, it came out that J&J has a new
plan to file a third bankruptcy, a pre packaged bankruptcy. So here are the terms, as I understand
it, it's going to be about $6.5 billion to resolve all the ovarian cancers, with an additional about
4 billion for a total potential of $11 billion paid out over 25 years. This is only going to
include the ovarian cancers. J&J said that 99% of the claims involve ovarian cancers. The Meso
cases, they said they've already resolved 95% of them. They're continuing to do firm inventory
settlements with the Meso cases, they're not going to be part of the bankruptcy. This one's going to
be a little bit different because J&J indicates that they have 75% approval of the potential
claimants, and the claimants have until July 26 to opt in and affirmatively say they're in favor of
this plan. So we're going to see a little bit of fighting between some of the plaintiff attorneys
who feel like this isn't enough and the plaintiff should get more, and those who are in favor of
it trying to bring an end to this ten year plus litigation. So we'll have more developments over
the next three months. We're really interested in seeing if this is going to finally end this
nightmare of a litigation for everybody. Yeah. And exciting that they're, like you said, that there's
movement. And so I appreciate sharing about those two litigations. What is going on with AFFF,
and especially as it relates to the CMO that was released. Yeah, AFFF. As everybody knows, we've
had the water drinking settlements, and those have been really powerful in the class action.
So now we're focusing more on these individual personal injury cases. And there's a recent order,
case management order number 28, that everybody needs to pay attention to. Essentially,
this order allows you to file a case that's not one of the top tier injuries. So if you don't
have a testicular, a kidney cancer case, ultra colitis, thyroid or liver cancer, you're able to
file a case, then you're going to have to dismiss the case without prejudice, but it will toll for
four years from the date of the filing. So that's going to allow additional time for leadership and
the signs to evolve for maybe some of these other cancers that we're looking at, like prostate, down
the line. So we'll see an uptick of filings in the next couple months here, and then we'll see a
number of dismissals. So don't get concerned about that. But what we're really focusing on then is
getting these bellwether trials going, and we're looking at our first trial here in 2025. So really
focus on those tier one injuries. That's what everybody seems to be paying attention to. Really
good ones, the super strong ones are testicular and kidney. So that's where we'll see the first
trials next year. But a lot of excitement right now, a lot of attention being paid to
the AFFF litigation. Yeah, that is exciting. And lastly, give us an update on Hernia Mesh. Bard,
my favorite litigation that there ever was. We'll say. So, as everybody knows, in the MDL,
the judge canceled the fourth bellwether trial, ordered the parties to mediation. This has been
ongoing for a couple months now. And, and what we're hearing is they're supposed to report back
to the MDL judge by May 24 that they're at an impasse. I'm hearing that we're making some
progress in this mediation. Everybody's hoping for a global settlement that's going to include
the MDL and the Rhode island cases. As we sit here today, there's been no resolution reach, but they
continue to work together. And I'm hopeful before that May 24 deadline when the judge indicated
there could start being some remands that will have a settlement. So stay tuned for that. We'll
keep you updated, of course, every week here on tort talk, if there's a settlement reach in
the next couple of days. Awesome. Well, Joe, as always, thank you so much for taking a moment to
connect with me and share the updates and insights with industry. Thanks for having me, Susan.

metadata.title: Navigating Mass Tort Settlements: The 95% Participation Threshold & Depo-Provera Rules
metadata.author: Jon and Marc
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of Tort Talk, Jon Robinson, Marc Rioux, and Joseph Fantini analyze key mass tort updates leading into Mass Torts Made Perfect. They cover Spinal Cord Stimulator JPML petitions for Abbott and Nevro, the 95% participation threshold for the $5.5B Talcum Powder settlement, Judge Rogers' Depo-Provera administrative docket rules, and California JCCP momentum in Video Game Addiction litigation.

Timestamps: 
00:00 - Introduction & MTMP Fall Outlook 
00:43 - Spinal Cord Stimulators: Abbott, Nevro, and Boston Scientific Tri-MDLs 
02:11 - SCS Case Volume Estimates & State Court Filings 
03:38 - Talcum Powder: The 95% Settlement Threshold & $3B Payout Timeline 
05:18 - Tracking Down 70,000 Claimants & Deceased Plaintiff Procedures 
07:09 - Depo-Provera: Administrative Docket Rules & Nov 30 Lone Pine Deadline 
08:53 - Video Game Addiction: How the California JCCP Works Without an MDL 
10:30 - Target Defendants, Microsoft Rumors & Inventory Settlement Frameworks 
12:39 - Pre-MTMP Predictions: Searching for the "Bell of the Ball"

#MassTorts #TortTalk #SpinalCordStimulator #TalcSettlement #DepoProvera #VideoGameAddiction #LegalMarketing #MassTortsMadePerfect #LawFirmGrowth #PlaintiffLaw

About The Jon & Marc Podcast.

The Jon & Marc Podcast is for lawyers who care about growth and the bottom line. Jon and Marc interview leaders in plaintiff law to break down how major cases are built, how firms scale, and how strategy plays out behind the scenes. If you want to understand how the biggest players in the space think and operate, you’re in the right place. New episodes every week.

segments.text: Welcome back to Tort Talk. We are back
for another week. I'm joined by John
Robinson and Joe Fantini as we turn the
page on summer and look forward to mass
tort MDL perfect. We'll cover some
significant developments in the world of
mass torts. Joe, John, thanks for being
here.
>> Here's probably the most important
question you can ask your marketing
agency. Who are they really optimizing
for? Because if the answer is internal
margins or shareholder expectations,
that changes how strategy gets built.
Our RR Digital stays independent so we
can optimize around one thing, law firm
growth. That means cases, clients, and
revenue. If you're rethinking your
marketing partner, visit
rrdigitalmedia.com
and let's start the conversation.
>> Moving into our first mass tort of the
day, spinal cord stimulators. One MDL
was formed for Boston Scientific in June
and now there are two petitions pending
before the JPML for Abbott and Nevro
manufacturers. What's going on with that
one, Joe?
>> Yeah, like you mentioned, Mark, we
already have one MDL that's involving
specifically the Boston Scientific
manufacturer and now we have a petition
that's going to be heard at the
September 24th JPML hearing. Basically,
it it follows exactly what was alleged
in the Boston Scientific that these
specific manufacturers with their
specific product caused these injuries.
It could be burns, it could be ongoing
pain, it could be paralysis, it could be
perforation, a lot of problems with
them. But earlier, everybody remembers
the the panel denied a request to
centralize all the spinal cord
manufacturers into one MDL. So it looks
like we'll end up with three specific
MDLs for each manufacturer. I think
ultimately this works better for the
plaintiffs and the litigation helps
speed it up because each litigation can
have its own nuance and allegations. So
took a little bit longer than we would
have hoped for these to get centralized,
but I'm expecting both of these
petitions to be granted and by October
we'll have two new MDLs that everybody's
going to be talking about at MTMP.
>> Yeah, exciting to see how these goes. Do
you have any idea what the volume of
these might be?
>> Yeah, so we it looks like Boston
Scientific is the biggest one right now.
There's about 30 cases pending in the
MDL. It's really early. I think we're
going to see a parallel state court
action popping up for Boston Scientific.
It seems like that's going to be in
Massachusetts. All told, I think we can
get above 10 to probably 15,000
between each one of these litigations.
So, I don't think anyone individually
will get above that 10,000 threshold,
but combined, I think we're looking at
15,000 plus cases. So, definitely a lot
of people impacted. There's a lot of
cases out there to to be had and
for people that really, you know,
suffered some pretty severe injuries.
>> And then, are there any other
manufacturers outside the two that are
being petitioned right now?
>> There there are a couple, you know,
smaller manufacturers out there, but but
it looks like, you know, the market
share's really dominated by by these
three players. So, I don't think we're
going to have another, you know, MDL
after we get these two formed. This is
probably going to be the end of it. So,
these are just kind of your old-school
traditional medical device cases where
you're going to go, get the product ID,
look at the implant sticker log and the
operative report and see which was the
manufacturer and then that's going to
tell you which litigation and where to
really file the case at.
>> We're going to talk about the talcum
powder cases. We had a settlement in
July and then it's been relatively quiet
since. What's been going on with talc
and what's happening next?
>> Yeah, so a lot going on. This is kind of
the part that doesn't get talked about
as much. I know you guys did a good
podcast previously on the process after
there is a settlement, but we had this
uncapped $5.5 billion settlement that
got announced earlier this summer. And
behind the scenes all the law firms are
really working really, really hard to
get in touch with the clients, get them
to agree to participate in the
settlement. And what we're really
striving to get towards is this 95%
threshold. So, common in in mass torts,
we see the defendants put in this
participation threshold. So, they don't
want to face a number of lawsuits
outside of the settlement. They really
want the majority of the people, in this
case 95% or more, to agree to
participate in the settlement program
and then have it administered. So, if
we're able to to reach that threshold,
people are going to have deadlines
coming up here in the fall to get every
one of their clients in. You know, the
the terms of the settlement call that
before the end of 20 27, we could see $3
billion dispersed. So, right now it's
getting in touch with your clients,
making sure they understand the terms of
the settlement, making sure they
understand the matrix, agreeing to
participate. Then once they're in in the
settlement, we're getting ready to start
submitting records that are going to be
reviewed to see, you know, where
everybody fits in the puzzle. That's
going to be the next step that we're
going to be working on through the end
of this year.
>> Yeah, I don't want to underplay the
monumental amount of work that firms
have right now to get in touch with all
those claimants because it's been going
on for so long. Tracking everyone down
over this time, making sure
you have up-to-date contact information.
People have moved, a lot of people have
passed away cuz it's been going on for
so long. It is going to be a ton of work
for the firms
to get to that 95%.
>> Yeah, it's it's definitely a lot. You
know, there's 70,000 cases involved. And
like you said, Mark, these are cancer
cases. So, unfortunately, a lot of
plaintiffs passed away over the time.
There There's a mechanism in place, part
of the settlement, where you can submit
information about who's going to be the
potential rep to get them included in
this 95% threshold, but there There's a
lot going on. So, if you have cases, you
know, make sure you're reaching out to
the clients. They're getting the
documents and agreeing to participate.
Otherwise, they could be excluded, and
that could be a tough up hill battle
because like we saw, two of the main
plaintiff experts withdrew their
opinions before we announced the
settlement. So, a lot of people are
really encouraging the settlement to
most of their clients.
>> Is that 95% threshold a common number,
or is that more of an extreme
number used for in these types of
scenarios?
>> Actually, it's a little bit less than
what we see. You know, usually we see
97, 98% threshold. So, I think they gave
us a little bit of a of a break there
because
some of these people passed away, and
it's been going along so far. But, what
we talked about before is even if we
don't get that 95, I think if we get
close, we'll be able to still move
forward with it. So, we'll keep you guys
updated as the settlement moves forward
and and we can get to that threshold and
keep everybody updated on what they need
to do for their clients here.
>> Speaking of another settlement that has
moved forward, Depo-Provera.
There have been a flurry of orders. What
does everyone need to be aware of?
>> Yeah, so after there's a settlement
announced, make sure you're following
along on the docket. We We've seen a lot
coming out of Judge Rodgers. As we
mentioned, there's about 6,000 cases
that are involved in the settlement. We
have state court cases going on in about
a half a dozen jurisdictions. And what
just got entered this week was an order
about an administrative docket. So, a
little bit unique. We don't see this in
every mass tort, but basically, if you
submitted your case to be included in
the settlement, Judge Rogers created
administrative docket where you then go
and file your case on the administrative
docket indicating that it's only for
purposes of the settlement, you plan to
participate on the settlement, but then
for the cases that aren't included in
the settlement, so if you don't meet the
criteria, the plaintiff wants to opt
out, the deadline's going to be November
30th to file that case on the regular
traditional docket, and then you're
going to have to comply with the Lone
Pine order doing the fact sheet, getting
the expert report. So, a lot of work
going on in that case, you know, it's
it's much, much smaller, like I said,
6,000 cases compared to 70,000, but
still a lot of work to be done, and
Judge Rogers really moves the cases
quickly, so keep an eye on the docket
there cuz there's a lot of important
filings coming down about, you know,
what proof, what records you need to
submit, but you have a couple, couple
months, pretty much 2 months until you
need to decide in the settlement or
outside of the settlement.

metadata.title: Elmiron Lawsuit
metadata.author: Miller & Zois, Attorneys at Law
metadata.shortDescription:
An update on the ongoing litigation involving the prescription drug Elmiron including when these cases might settle and what their estimated payout value is.

MAY 2023 Update

As Janssen Pharmaceuticals continues to negotiate confidential settlements for existing Elmiron claims, the influx of new cases into the Elmiron Multi-District Litigation (MDL) has significantly decreased. Over the past 30 days, only three new cases were introduced into the class action lawsuit, bringing the current total to 1,891. This is the smallest increase in new cases since the MDL's establishment.

APRIL 2023 UPDATE

The majority of these lawsuits are expected to settle this year. 

SEPTEMBER 2022 UPDATE

The Elmiron class action lawsuit continues to grow.  There were 1,740 cases pending in the Elmiron class action MDL and another 169 pending cases in state court in New Jersey. 

AUGUST 2022 UPDATE

July ended up being a very slow month for the Elmiron litigation. After seeing record high numbers of new Eliron vision damage cases transferred into the MDL recently, no new cases were added after July 7. A status conference with Judge Martinotti was held on July 13 and resulted in an order regarding appointments to the Plaintiffs’ Steering Committee, but there were no docket entries in the MDL for the rest of the month afterward.

But there is an Elmiron trial coming in January 2022.  If these lawsuits get that far.  You could see a global settlement before that trial. 

WHO ARE THE DEFENDANTS TO PAY A POSSIBLE SETTLEMENT?

Teva Branded Pharmaceutical and related companies, Janssen Pharmaceuticals, and Johnson & Johnson are the defendants. We believe these lawsuits will be mostly resolved in 2023.  

WHAT ARE THE ELMIRON LAWSUITS ABOUT?
The Elmiron lawsuits are against the manufacturers of the drug Elmiron, primarily Janssen Pharmaceuticals, a subsidiary of Johnson & Johnson. Elmiron, also known as pentosan polysulfate sodium (PPS), is a medication prescribed for the treatment of interstitial cystitis (IC), a painful bladder syndrome.

In recent years, numerous patients who have used Elmiron have reported developing vision problems, specifically a unique form of eye damage known as pigmentary maculopathy.  There really is no doubt that Elmiron caused this condition. This condition affects the macula, the central part of the retina responsible for sharp, detailed vision. Pigmentary maculopathy can lead to difficulty reading, dark spots in the visual field, and, in some cases, blindness.

Research and case studies have suggested a link between long-term use of Elmiron and the development of pigmentary maculopathy. As a result, patients who have experienced vision problems after taking the drug have filed lawsuits against Janssen Pharmaceuticals. The plaintiffs argue that the company failed to adequately warn patients and healthcare providers about the potential risks associated with Elmiron.

The lawsuits generally seek compensation for medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, and other damages related to the plaintiffs' vision problems. In response to the growing number of lawsuits, the U.S. Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation consolidated federal Elmiron lawsuits into a multidistrict litigation (MDL) in December 2020. This MDL aims to streamline the legal process by allowing the cases to be heard by one judge, which can lead to more consistent rulings and potentially facilitate a global settlement in 2023. 

https://www.millerandzois.com/elmiron-lawsuits.html

There are now over 700 Elmiron eye damage cases in the MDL and the first bellwether trials are set for January 2023.

metadata.title: Top 10 Mass Torts to Watch in 2026 | Power Rankings for Plaintiff Firms
metadata.author: Jon and Marc
metadata.shortDescription:
Mass torts, legal marketing, and case acquisition signals are shifting fast.

In this episode of Tort Talk, Jon Robinson, Marc Rioux, and Joe Fantini track MDL posture, bellwether timing, and defense strategy across active mass tort dockets. Joe Fantini shares his perspective on what actually creates pressure: case workups, trial readiness, and the procedural fights that decide whether these claims reach juries.

Hair Relaxer stays at #1 with 11,000+ active cases and a bellwether timeline that likely pushes into 2027. Social media addiction sits at #2 while a live Los Angeles trial puts platform design, addiction mechanics, and big-tech credibility in front of a jury. Uber climbs into the top three after an $8.5M Arizona verdict, and that result starts changing how the next bellwethers get valued.

The rankings also flag where momentum is building and where it is cooling. Roundup hits a historic low at #5 with Supreme Court timing on the calendar. Roblox enters the list with early leadership structure forming and a looming arbitration fight. Older dockets like Bear Hugger show real movement again as cases get worked up for remand and trial settings begin to land.
If you are a personal injury lawyer, mass tort attorney, or law firm owner tracking litigation strategy, this episode breaks down what matters and what comes next.

Key Takeaways

-How Hair Relaxer’s numerosity and maturity keep it at #1 and what dates matter next
-Why Uber’s $8.5M verdict matters after a prior zero verdict and what a “2-3 more trials” path signals
-What Roundup’s April 27 Supreme Court oral argument date could do to intake strategy
-The Roblox arbitration push and the consent issues that may decide early motion outcomes
-What to watch in weight loss drug MDLs: 3,000 GI cases now and likely bellwethers next year
-How to interpret a $250K talc bellwether inside a 70,000-case MDL

metadata.title: Inside Abbott’s $675 Million NEC Deal and Meta’s High-Stakes Trials
metadata.author: Jon and Marc
metadata.shortDescription:
The landscape of mass tort litigation moves fast, and this week’s episode of Tort Talk delivers crucial strategic updates across major consolidated dockets. Jon Robinson, Marc Rioux, and Joseph Fantini break down Abbott’s massive $675 million NEC inventory settlement, trial pressure surrounding social media addiction, TikTok’s $400 million DOJ settlement, and the rapid emergence of spinal cord stimulator litigation.

Whether your firm is managing NEC inventories, tracking social media dockets, or evaluating entry into medical device mass torts, this episode provides actionable insights on case valuation, trial posture, and strategic filing decisions.

Chapters: 
00:00 - Introduction & Headlines 
00:31 - Breaking Down Abbott's $675 Million NEC Inventory Settlement 
02:43 - Acquisition Strategy & Case Valuations for Remaining NEC Claims 
05:10 - Meta on Trial: Tennessee State Court & 29-State AG Trial in Oakland 
07:00 - Regulatory Pressure & The End of the "Endless Scroll" Feature 
08:16 - TikTok’s $400M DOJ Settlement & Multi-Defendant Strategy Differences 
11:14 - Spinal Cord Stimulator Update: Boston Scientific MDL & Pending Petitions 
13:57 - Fall Mass Tort Preview: MTMP Las Vegas & Emerging Litigation

#MassTorts #NECLawsuit #SocialMediaAddiction #SpinalCordStimulator #LegalStrategy #TortTalk #LawFirmGrowth #PlaintiffLaw

About The Jon & Marc Podcast
The Jon & Marc Podcast is for lawyers who care about growth and the bottom line. Jon and Marc interview leaders in plaintiff law to break down how major cases are built, how firms scale, and how strategy plays out behind the scenes. If you want to understand how the biggest players in the space think and operate, you’re in the right place. New episodes every week.

segments.text: The weed killer paraquat may increase your risk of Parkinson's disease by two and a half times.
In 2025, major legal developments could help you get justice if you've been harmed by this powerful herbicide.
Big companies like Syngenta and Chevron face thousands of Paraquat lawsuits
in a special federal court process called a multidistrict litigation, or MDL.
MDL's groups similar cases together to help speed up and simplify the legal process.
More than 6,000 cases have been filed claiming these companies did not warn people that paraquat could cause serious brain diseases like Parkinson's.
Paraquat lawsuits have been working their way through the courts for several years.
Settlement agreements offered some relief to people who claimed they were injured by this herbicide.
In April, according to court documents, both sides in the MDL reached a tentative agreement to settle the litigation.
This could bring much needed relief to more victims nationwide.
In 2021, Syngenta and Chevron set aside $187.5 million for settlements.
In July 2025, Syngenta settled a key lawsuit in Philadelphia right before that case was set for trial.
This lawsuit involved a farmer diagnosed with Parkinson's after decades of paraquat use.
Settlements typically indicate that companies want to resolve lawsuits without going to trial.
A paraquat settlement could resolve thousands of lawsuits against the companies all at once.
While both sides hammer out the details of a paraquat settlement, there may still be time to file new Parakwatt lawsuits.
Paraquat is a potent commercial herbicide. Swallowing just one teaspoon can kill you.
It's banned in 70 countries outside the United States.
Paraquat is a restricted-use chemical in the US, meaning you have to have a special certification to apply it.
If you or a loved one worked with paraquat, lived on or near farms that used it, and you got Parkinson's, you might qualify for a lawsuit.
Talking to a paraquat lawyer is the first step, and Drug Watch can connect you with an experienced law firm at no cost to you.
Simply gather your medical records and any documents showing you worked with paraquat or lived where it was applied.
Deadlines and settlement talks are coming, so if you or a loved one have been diagnosed with paraquat-related Parkinson's disease,
you should speak to a lawyer right away.
For more than 15 years, Drugwatch has helped 20,000 families connect with some of the nation's top lawyers who offer free case reviews.
2025 is a big year for paraquat victims.
Visit drugwatch.com/parakwatt-help for a free case review and to see if you qualify for a paraquat lawsuit.

metadata.title: Grok's Image Lawsuits Explained: 13 Cases and One Panel Hearing on Dec. 3
metadata.author: Tesorb
metadata.shortDescription:
Plaintiffs asked a federal panel to put the Grok image-generation lawsuits in front of one judge. The Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation hears that request on December 3, 2026, in New Orleans.

Here is what SpaceX's 10-Q and the panel's own hearing order say: the 13 cases on the transfer motion (eight in Arkansas, five in California), what the JPML does and does not decide, the earlier ruling that kept a case out of Texas, Virginia's notice of violation, and what a December order could and could not do. The suits' claims are allegations, not court findings.

0:13 What the suits allege (per SpaceX's 10-Q)
0:53 The map: 8 in Arkansas, 5 in California
1:25 What the JPML does, and does not, decide
2:17 More from the 10-Q: the Texas transfer ruling, Baltimore, Virginia's notice
3:31 Timeline
3:55 December 3 in New Orleans
4:24 What the order could and could not do

Not legal advice.

Medical practice handles patient care
MSO handles operations, billing, and growth

metadata.title: What is the difference between mass tort, class action, and a MDL?
metadata.author: Randell C. Roberts
metadata.shortDescription: There is a lot of discussion in the media about mass torts, class actions and MDL’s, but a lot of people don’t understand the difference. A mass tort is simply a type of injury, while a class action and an MDL are methods for getting people compensated for that injury. A mass tort, as the name describes, involves a situation where a mass of people, hundreds or even thousands, are injured by the same defective product. The typical situation is when a prescription drug is recalled after it has harmed hundreds if not thousands of people. A class action and an MDL (multi district litigation) are methods for compensating people who are victims of mass torts. A class action, however, is significantly different from an MDL. In a class action, there is just one lawyer, one case, one judge and jury, and one verdict that applies to everyone, even though the class action has been filed on behalf of hundreds if not thousands of people. As a general rule, personal injury cases and wrongful death cases are not good candidates for class actions because each person’s harm or loss is different. An MDL is generally the better way to go if you’ve had a serious injury or suffered the loss of a loved one. In an MDL, each person has their own attorney, they file their own case before the judge and jury that’s appropriate for that case, and they each get their own trial. Now, the reason it’s called an MDL or a multi-district litigation is that when these cases, sometimes hundreds or thousands of them, are all filed across the country, the courts require that they be consolidated before one judge, just for the pre-trial proceedings. That is just for the proceedings where the evidence is collected and documented. That saves the clients a lot of time and expense, but at the end of that process, the cases are sent back to be tried by that client’s lawyer in the courtroom that that client chose and for the client to receive their own individual verdict. They’re not bound by what happens in other cases that were filed in that MDL or multi district litigation. As a general rule, we at Roberts and Roberts recommend that when you have the option that you go with the multi district litigation or the individual case as opposed to a class action to be sure that you receive the individual attention and compensation that you deserve.

metadata.title: What Are the Stages of a Lawsuit in an MDL? Part 2 (Bellwethers)
metadata.author: Nigh Goldenberg Raso & Vaughn PLLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn more about the phases of a lawsuit in a Multi-District Litigation (MDL). If you have a lawsuit filed in federal court against a medical device or pharmaceutical drug company, there is a high likelihood that your lawsuit will eventually be consolidated into an MDL. Found partner of Nigh Goldenberg Raso & Vaughn, Daniel Nigh, explains the bellwether phase of an MDL. The bellwether phase of an MDL is when a subset of cases filed in the MDL get selected to proceed to trial so that both sides can evaluate the general strengths, weaknesses, and values of the lawsuits filed. The bellwether phase includes taking depositions of the plaintiff (person injured and bringing the lawsuit), the physicians that treated them, and potentially family members or other fact witnesses.

metadata.title: Why is a Bellwether Trial Important?
metadata.author: Fleming, Nolen & Jez
metadata.shortDescription:
A bellwether trial is a trial that is conducted to help both sides in a mass tort litigation assess the strengths and weaknesses of their cases. The results of a bellwether trial can help both sides to better understand how a jury might rule on the issues in the case, and can also help to facilitate settlement negotiations.

metadata.title: Hair Relaxer MDL (Uterine Cancer Litigation)
metadata.author: Michael Stanisci
metadata.shortDescription:
Hair Relaxer MDL (Uterine Cancer Litigation)

What's Going On: On January 8, Judge Mary Rowland held a Science Day in the federal hair relaxer MDL in Illinois. Both sides got two hours to present their scientific evidence about whether chemical hair relaxers cause uterine cancer. Think of it as everyone getting on the same page about the science before the real legal battles begin. With over 11,000 cases now consolidated, this is one of the biggest MDLs in the country.

Why This Matters: Science Day sets the foundation for everything that follows. The judge is getting educated on the complex medical evidence before ruling on Daubert motions, which are challenges to whether plaintiffs' experts can even testify. Those rulings will determine which cases survive to trial.

What's Next: April 1 is the deadline for defendants to file their Daubert challenges. After fact discovery wraps in March, the court will pick bellwether cases for trials likely starting in 2027. This is a marathon, not a sprint.

What This Means for Your Firm: Most of your clients are Black women who've been dealing with this for years. They need you to balance aggressive litigation with genuine empathy. Guide them through the compliance requirements (Plaintiff Fact Sheets, medical records, expert reviews) while being sensitive to the trauma of a cancer diagnosis. This is about more than winning cases. It's about justice for women who were targeted by these products.

Not medical or legal advice

In this episode of Global Economic Press, Alex Brady reports on a $40 million jury verdict for Kimberly Divelbliss in litigation over a failed Bard implanted port catheter, brought by attorneys including Brandon Henry of Wagstaff & Cartmell (https://wagstaffcartmell.com/) . The jury found the device had design defects and that the defendants failed to provide adequate warnings.



The catheter fractured two years after implantation, sending a fragment into Divelbliss’s heart and leading to serious health complications and further procedures. The verdict was the first plaintiff victory in the federal multidistrict litigation; additional bellwether trials are scheduled.

metadata.title: Could the Year of the Settlement Have One More in Store?
metadata.author: Jon and Marc
metadata.shortDescription:
With under 50 days left in 2026, the mass tort landscape is moving at breakneck speed. In this week’s episode of Tort Talk, Jon Robinson and mass tort attorney Joe Fantini break down four massive updates reshaping consolidated litigation right now.

First, we dive into the surprise $7.35 billion AFFF personal injury settlement resolving up to 120,000 claims, including qualifying injuries, critical November 13 ID order deadlines, deduplication, and what Lone Pine requirements mean for future claimants. Next, we analyze the FDA’s landmark November 9 warning label update regarding NAION (non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy) and sudden vision loss on GLP-1 weight loss medications, and how it impacts general causation and discovery.

We also examine the aftermath of the third Bard PowerPort bellwether trial, contrasting infection claims against high-value fracture and migration cases, and unpack the joint proposal to wind down the MDL and begin remanding 500 cases at a time. Finally, we look at the latest from the Camp Lejeune bench trials, the proposed 25-injury census, and why rumors of an end-of-year settlement are heating up.

0:00 Welcome to Tort Talk & End-of-2026 Mass Tort Overview 
0:45 $7.35 Billion AFFF Settlement Breakdown & Top 6 Qualifying Injuries 
1:40 Critical ID Order Deadlines, Deduplication & Future Lone Pine Claims 
3:20 Weight Loss Medications: FDA Mandates NAION Vision Loss Warning Label 
4:15 How the FDA Label Change Impacts General Causation & Liability
6:22 Bard PowerPort Update: Third Bellwether Defense Verdict Explained 
7:15 Why the Bard PowerPort MDL Is Winding Down & Remanding 500 Cases at a Time 
8:55 Fracture & Migration vs. Infection Claims in Bard PowerPort 
9:21 Camp Lejeune Bench Trials & The Proposed 25-Injury Census
10:40 Will We See a Camp Lejeune Settlement Before the End of 2026?

#MassTorts #TortTalk #AFFFSettlement #PFAS #WeightLossDrugs #NAION #BardPowerPort #CampLejeune #MDL #PlaintiffLawyer #LegalNews #MassTortLitigation #PersonalInjuryLaw #BellwetherTrial #RosenInjuryLawyers

About The Jon & Marc Podcast.

The Jon & Marc Podcast is for lawyers who care about growth and the bottom line. Jon and Marc interview leaders in plaintiff law to break down how major cases are built, how firms scale, and how strategy plays out behind the scenes. If you want to understand how the biggest players in the space think and operate, you’re in the right place. New episodes every week.

metadata.title: Expert Testimony and the New Rule 702: Strategy and Implications
metadata.author: McGuireWoods LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
The Federal Rule of Evidence governing expert testimony — Rule 702 — just saw its most significant changes in almost 25 years. In this webinar, McGuireWoods attorneys will discuss the implications of the new rule, how federal courts are applying it and strategic considerations for litigants going forward.

Download slides: https://media.mcguirewoods.com/events/2024/Expert-Testimony-New-Rule-702.pdf

More about the webinar here: https://www.mcguirewoods.com/events/firm-events/2024/3/expert-testimony-and-the-new-rule-702-strategy-and-implications/

Videos may include attorney advertising and aren’t legal advice/opinion. Prior successes ≠ future results. © 2024 McGuireWoods LLP. All rights reserved.

Filevine offers client portals, secure messaging, and team collaboration features designed for operational legal work, status updates, document sharing, task coordination, and client communication. Both these platforms offer enterprise-grade security. Harvey is built for global law firms and Fortune 500 companies with strong data isolation and role-based access controls. Filevine is SOC 2 Type 2, HIPAA, ISO, CJIS compliant, and FedRAMP ready, meeting the needs of law firms, corporate legal departments, and government agencies. For most buyers, security won't be the deciding factor. Both are designed for sensitive legal work. Reporting and analytics. Harvey's reporting focuses on AI usage and governance, workflow processing history, document handling, auditability for AI interactions, and usage patterns. This helps firms understand how AI is being deployed and ensure proper governance. Filevine offers firm-wide operational reporting, matter progress, team productivity, billable hours, case outcomes, revenue tracking, and custom dashboards. The distinction? Harvey reports on AI usage and compliance. Filevine reports on business performance and operations. Integrations and flexibility. Harvey integrates tightly with enterprise document management systems like iManage and legal research platforms like LexisNexis. However, its integrations are selective and enterprise focused. Filevine offers broader SaaS integrations, QuickBooks, Salesforce, Microsoft Office, Google Workspace, Slack, SharePoint, DocuSign, and more. Over 2,000 potential integrations. Consider Harvey AI if you're a large law firm or a Fortune 500 legal team focused on complex, document-intensive legal work like M&A, investigations, or regulatory matters. You'll benefit most if you have innovation leaders or knowledge management teams ready to invest in enablement and governance. Harvey's enterprise pricing and selective go-to-market means it's not really accessible to smaller firms or most mid-market buyers. Consider Filevine if you need a unified legal operations platform that handles the full matter life cycle, intake, case management, deadlines, billing, client communication, and is designed for law firms of all sizes, corporate legal departments, and government agencies. Managing operational legal work across practice areas like personal injury, mass torts, family law, immigration, criminal defense, and corporate contracts. It's accessible to mid-market firms and provides transparent pricing. metadata.author: Justinian & Associates PLLC
metadata.shortDescription:
In our Whiteboard Series, our lawyers explain concepts and processes of law that they deal with on a regular basis. In this episode, Attorney Erik Walker discusses pharmaceutical law and "Strict Liability vs. Negligence." 

www.justinian.com
512-980-0000
Facebook/Twitter: @justinian
Insta: @justinianandassociates

segments.text: [Music]
good morning I'm Eric Walker vice
president of justinian and associates
and I'm here again today to talk to you
about some area of the law that we think
will be of interest to you our firm
specializes in pharmaceutical litigation
other kinds of personal injury lawsuits
and immigration law today we're going to
discuss pharmaceutical litigation in
particular pharmaceutical litigation is
very different than other types of
personal injury lawsuits the elements of
the claims that the plaintiff raises in
a pharmaceutical case are distinct and
that's what we're going to focus on
today and I want to begin by talking
about the kinds of claims that you can
make in a pharmaceutical case in
particular strict liability versus
negligence claims in any personal injury
suit you can allege negligence
negligence just means that the defendant
failed to act as a reasonable person
would in particular negligence is the
failure to act as an ordinarily prudent
person would facing the same or similar
circumstances so for instance if you're
a driver on the road and you run a stop
sign you were negligent if you're a
doctor who fails to meet the standard of
care for professionals in your field you
were negligent negligence means engaging
and unreasonable conduct and in a
typical personal injury lawsuit
negligence is the principal claim that
is raised but in a pharmaceutical case
you can also raise what's called a
strict liability claim strict liability
does not require any proof of
unreasonable conduct on the part of the
defendant strict liability is
essentially liability without fault now
you might ask why would we hold
companies liable if they didn't do
anything unreasonable and the answer is
fairly simple if someone is injured by a
dangerous product someone has to be
accountable for that the question is who
is going to pay for the injuries that
were caused is the individual
was injured going to pay for their own
injuries even though it was caused by
somebody else's product is society at
large taxpayer supposed to pay for that
damage or is the company that makes the
product sells the product and profits
from the product the entity that should
pay and as a society we have decided
that it is the company that is making
money from the product that ought to pay
when that product causes injuries even
though there may be no fault or no
unreasonable conduct by that company and
so we have what's called strict
liability in pharmaceutical cases and
there are essentially three kinds of
causes of action or claims that a
plaintiff can make under the strict
liability doctrine in a pharmaceutical
case they are designed defect
manufacturing defect and marketing
defect a design defect claim essentially
says that the product was defective li
made or designed in other words the
plans for the product the scheme for the
product the decision of what to do to
make the product was defective so if you
have a drug that has a dangerous
component that's a design defect if you
have any kind of product where too much
of one ingredient is planned in the
product that's a design defect if you
have a drug that is just deadly and
should never have been made in the first
place that's a design defect a design
defect says that the plans for the
original product were bad a
manufacturing defect says the plans for
the product were okay the design was
fine but the actual making of the
product did not conform to
specifications so you may have a product
that is perfectly safe if made properly
but in the factory somehow or another
something happens and too much of one
ingredient gets put in the product or
some defect occurs during the making of
the product that's a manufacturing
defect the third kind of claim is a
marketing defect and that simply means
failure to adequately warned there are
going to be pharmaceutical products
have risks there's no question about
that and there's no way to avoid those
risks but at the very least
manufacturers have to warn potential
consumers about those risks so patients
can make an informed decision as to
whether to take the product failure to
adequately warn individuals about the
risks of a product is called a marketing
defect these are essentially the three
causes of action that you can claim
under the strict liability doctrine now
you can also claim negligence for these
claims - you can claim that the design
defect the defect in the planning of how
the product should be made was
unreasonable same for marketing defect
and manufacturing defect but you don't
have to you can argue simply that these
defects existed and the manufacturer is
liable for them even if the manufacturer
didn't do anything wrong there are other
claims of course fraud breach of
warranty breach of consumer protection
statutes that are the kinds of claims
you can make in many different types of
torts but we're going to focus on these
causes of action that are unique to
pharmaceutical litigation principally in
pharmaceutical cases we focus on design
defect and marketing defect I have seen
some cases where there was a
manufacturing defect I remember one
litigation in particular where the drug
was simply made at a factory that had
very poor safety standards and literally
the deadly component of the drug was
multiplied by many times during the
manufacturing process and as a result
people died but generally speaking the
claims that we focus on our design
defect and marketing defect or failure
to warn the plaintiff argues either that
the product is just dangerous as it is
as it's designed or that the
manufacturer failed to adequately warned
of the dangers of the product and as a
result the plaintiff was injured now
once the plaintiff establishes one of
these claims or causes of action there
are various defenses that the
pendant can raise the manufacturer can
raise to the claims one is called the
state-of-the-art defense this is
typically raised against the design
defect claim and it says this we
produced our product based on existing
knowledge of the time and we conformed
to what everyone knew the risks of
products were at the time in other words
we made our product just like everybody
else did we did nothing wrong we did
everything right the problem with the
state-of-the-art defense is that it
really takes the design defect claim out
of the strict liability realm and puts
it into the negligence realm one of the
reasons we have strict liability as I
mentioned earlier is because
manufacturers are the ones who profit
from their own products and therefore
when someone is injured by a product and
we have to decide who to hold
accountable the manufacturer the injured
individual or the taxpayer who should
pay for those injuries it's the company
that makes the product and profits from
it that should pay for the injuries even
if the company did nothing wrong
this state-of-the-art defense
essentially says we did nothing wrong
which contradicts the whole premise of
strict liability so a number of states
reject the state-of-the-art defense they
have something called the hindsight
plane which says that we look in
hindsight at what the dangers are risks
of the product are we don't look at the
knowledge of the time and if a court is
being true to the principle of strict
liability it will reject the
state-of-the-art defense because it is a
negligence principle it asks the
question of whether the manufacturer did
anything wrong it doesn't suggest that
the manufacturer should be liable for a
design that and ultimately injured
people but there are a number of
different state courts in different
states that do recognize the state of
the art defense and will allow the
manufacturer to say we made our product
to conform to existing scientific
knowledge and we did not in any way
deviate from what the knowledge of the
time was regarding risks
and therefore we should not be held
accountable a second defense is called
the learned intermediary defense and
this argument is essentially this
prescription drugs are very complicated
they're very complex products and the
decision of whether to ingest the
products are decisions that should be
made between patient and doctor the
manufacturer shouldn't be interjecting
itself in that decision so what most
states recognize is that the duty of a
manufacturer to warn in a marketing
defect claim failure to warn the
manufacturers duty to warn extends only
to the doctor the learned intermediary
who would be the doctor in other words
the manufacturer in a prescription drug
case does not have a duty to warn the
patient directly the manufacturers duty
is limited to warning the doctor it is
then up to the doctor to transfer the
warnings or communicate the warnings to
the patient and the doctor and the
patient together will make the decision
of whether to use the drug this is an
important defense because it means that
the plaintiff has to prove that the
manufacturer failed to adequately warn
the doctor in the physicians Desk
Reference or any other materials that
are provided to the doctor and the
plaintiff then has to prove that if the
manufacturer had provided adequate
warnings to the doctor the doctor would
not have prescribed the product to the
patient there are many instances when
doctors say even if that warning had
been stronger I would have prescribed
the product and that's why this defense
is a very potent one for the defendants
and we're going to talk about it a
little bit more later on there's also a
statute of limitations defense this
essentially is a claim that the
plaintiff failed to file its suit on
their suit on time there are deadlines
for filing lawsuits in states throughout
the country and they vary from state to
state if the plaintiff fails to file
their lawsuit within a certain period of
time the lawsuit is barred under the
doctrine of the statute of limitations
the good news is that most states in the
country
have something called a discovery rule
the discovery rules is an exception to
the statute of limitations and it says
this even though the deadline for filing
suit may be two years that deadline
doesn't start at the time the person
used the drug or even at the time the
person necessarily was injured by the
drug it starts at the time the person
knew or should have known that the drug
caused their injury so for instance if
someone ingests a product in the year
1979 and they develop an injury in the
year 1985 and they file suit in the year
1987 their suit as timely even though it
was filed far more than two years after
they took the drug because they filed it
within two years of being injured or if
you have a situation where someone is
injured let's say in the year 20 2015
and they don't file suit until the year
2019 because they don't learn that the
drug caused their injury until the year
2017 and I'm sorry about all the dates
here the lawsuit is timely that the key
inquiry is did the plaintiff file his or
her lawsuit within the time period the
limit provided by law based on when they
discovered that the product caused their
injury did they filed their lawsuit
within the time limit based on when they
knew or should have known that the drug
caused their injury and so there's a
good defense to the statute of
limitations that plaintiffs have there's
another defense called fraudulent
concealment if the plaintiff can prove
that the defendant fraudulent
fraudulently concealed the plaintiffs
cause of action or claim then the
statute of limitations does not apply
the problem with the fraudulent
concealment claim and it is a claim that
is misinterpreted by many plaintiff
lawyers is we're not talking about plain
vanilla fraud here we're that the
defendant concealed the risks of its
product we're talking about a defendant
actively concealing from the plaintiff

If you’re still doing everything in your law firm, from answering phones to managing marketing, this episode is your wake-up call.

On this episode of the Legal Lead Sharks Podcast, I’m joined by Andrew Pickett, founder of one of Florida’s top PI firms. He didn’t inherit his practice, he built it from the ground up and scaled it to over $38 million recovered by mastering two of the most overlooked pillars in law firm growth: intake and systems.

We dive into why intake is often the biggest bottleneck in growing law firms, especially when you're spending thousands on SEO, Google Ads, Meta Ads, or TV commercials. If the phone rings and an untrained call center rep is the first impression your potential client gets, you just lost a lead that could have been your next million-dollar case.

Andrew shares how he made the leap from courtroom prosecutor to business-minded firm owner, why client experience is the foundation of his referral engine, and the exact systems his team uses to keep clients engaged throughout the case. We also cover the mindset shift required to go from overworked attorney to strategic leader, and the books that changed everything for him, including E-Myth, Fireproof, Buy Back Your Time, and 10x Is Easier Than 2x.

If you're a law firm owner stuck in the messy middle, trying to wear every hat, and wondering why you can't scale, this is the episode you need. Andrew drops real-world insights and step-by-step strategies that any firm can implement.

Listen in and learn how to build a firm that runs like a business, not a solo hustle.

What happens when mass-tort claims grow faster than verification?
