videos.full_text: Welcome to the sign for more injury finding, the podcast where we bring together the people, ideas, and innovation shaping the personal injury industry. I'm your host, Laura Moore, founder and CEO of Moore Injury Funding. My mission is to help bridge the financial gap between injury and resolution while supporting the attorneys, medical providers, and professionals who help injured individuals navigate the road to recovery. Today, we are discussing a topic that deserves more attention across the legal and finding industries, and that is protecting the integrity of personal injury claims and understanding the risks associated with law firm lending. When funding decisions depend on contingency fee or contingent fee receivables and the value of a law firm's case inventory, the quality and legitimacy of those underlying claims matter. Verification, documentation, fraud prevention, and ongoing monitoring can all play important roles in managing risk. Our conversation will explore how lenders can better evaluate case portfolios, how verification systems work, what happens when claims are challenged, and how the industry can balance financial protection with fairness to legitimate claimants. Today's episode, the guest is Ron La Sour, a former JP Morgan banker, UBS trading executive, and Marine officer. Now CEO of the Ethical Law Network, which is working to bring real diligence and ethics to mass tort litigation. Ron, welcome to my show. >> Thank you so much for having me, Laura. >> So, let's start with the big picture. What are most significant risks facing lenders who provide working capital to personal injury law firms, and why is the quality of a firm's case inventory so important to the lending decision? >> Well, there are two main risks in third-party litigation finance. And the first is um event risk, right? You're lending against a contingency fee uh lawsuit. And so, the the claim can either settle or not, right? So, event risk in that regard. Um there's a second element of of event risk that most law firms and and lenders don't consider, which is that if the law firm doesn't provide uh good client services, that that client can take their case to another law firm. They have the absolute right to do that. And so, unlike other um types of collateral, real estate, you know, the real estate's not going to walk away from the lender, right? So, so that is a huge risk that most law firms are not considering. The second risk is duration risk. And I think that you're finding many law firms getting into trouble because some of the larger mass torts um and even uh large personal injury cases are taking longer to settle than they expected, right? And so, there are some unethical lenders that are intentionally, we call it loan to own, where they'll they'll give a line of credit to a law firm, and then when the the mass tort J&J talc in particular, it's gone on for a decade, you know, if the lender, or rather if the law firm defaults on that loan, the lender will pressure that law firm to sell their entire law firm to satisfy the debt. And so, huge, you know, but I love litigation finance for that reason, because it has all these nuances and eccentricities. >> It's it's so amazing. Same here, Ron. We're all on the on the same boat, I guess, on the same side. Just it's amazing how, you know, it For me, it because it's it's really a a synchronization of finances, law, and medicine. So, it's just to me it's fascinating. Always been. Um how does lending against expected contingent fees differ from lending against more traditional forms of collateral? >> Well, I would say um lack of liquidity, right? There's no secondary market or limited secondary market for these type of loans, right? And um whereas in other in other types of collateral, right? Stocks, bonds, commodities, even now in real estate with um fractional uh you know, tokenization, there there's a secondary market, but in in litigation finance, uh many many law firms in order to satisfy these loans actually have to sell the law firm or the complete docket itself, which is very, very difficult to do, right? So, lack of liquidity, I think would be the the biggest differentiator right now. >> Mhm. The legal industry process or processes enormous volumes of personal injury and mass torts claims. From your experience, Ron, what challenges arise when law firms acquire claimants faster than they can verify their identities, documentation, eligibility? >> The biggest liability right now is the um e-signature process, right? And you'll hear many of the old-timers in mass tort kind of decry the the the aggregation of of these new law firms in mass tort. You know, they'll they'll say, "How can anybody handle a docket of 10,000?" And they have a they have a point. And so, the e-signature process has completely undermined the attorney-client uh relationship for that reason. And you have bad actors um who come in and intentionally file false claims through identity theft. And um the plaintiffs' lawyers, uh there was just a law firm who was sanctioned for that, well, you know, court found that they were um intentionally uh and unconscionably um uh ignorant of the of the process. Defense counsel is not motivated to root out false claims because they're trying to limit the total liability. Right? So so nobody is really um focusing on that element. Right? It's kind of the wild west right now. >> So what where where do you believe the greatest vulnerabilities are at intake, during case development, or when claims reach settlement? >> I wrote I wrote a a 30-page white paper on this and there are many uh points of failure along the along you know in the ecosystem. Um law firms uh are certainly at risk of um being taken advantage of of other bad actors. But uh you know, client intake is a huge issue. Many times law firms outsource that. Um and then you know, document verification. Many of these MDLs are not requiring documentation, right? They they they simply they have whole categories where documentation isn't there and they settle them for nominal value. And then actually the third-party administrators also uh in in the settlement of claims, you know, there are many there's a recent lawsuit against third-party administrators who are you know, taking fees to to put cases through. So it you know, you have to have eyes on the whole process. And there are there are five entities that kind of dance in this ecosystem. >> Mhm. And those uh five entities being what what are what are those? >> Uh law firm intake lead generation kind of thing, funding um the uh third-party administrators and and then actually the courts themselves who who are not incentivized to look for fraud. They're they're the courts themselves are incentivized to get the you know, get the case off the docket as quickly as possible. >> Mhm. Thank you. I appreciate that. Uh when we talk about claim on fraud, it's important to distinguish fraudulent claims from legit legitimate claims that may simply have incomplete documentation. How should lenders and law firms make that distinction without unfairly penalizing injured people? >> Through the verification process. Your point is is well taken. I'll use a I'm a veteran as you mentioned. I'll use the 3M hearing protection lawsuit as an example. Right? 240,000 claimants originally. Um, a $6 billion settlement. Um, they have a whole category for claimants without medical documentation. And so, recently the special master um, as the claims were being paid recognized that one law firm their medical records looked um, fabricated, which they were. And upon investigation, they found that 996 of the thousand claims that law firm filed were fake. They were Ugandan nationals. Right? And so, what happens is that for every illegitimate claim paid, it diminishes the value of a legitimate plaintiff's claim. Cuz you have a $6 billion settlement divided by 240,000 people, you know, that gives an amount. But if there are only 100,000 legitimate plaintiffs, then their their their settlement value has been been diluted. And the law firm doesn't care because they're getting legal fees on on legitimate and illegitimate claims. The funder is getting paid by the law firm, and so they're getting full value on their loan. Right? The defendant doesn't care because they they've been capped at $6 billion, right? And the only people who really suffer are the legitimate plaintiffs. >> That's that that's tough. That's a tough one. Uh, can you, Ron, explain how a portfolio containing unverified or fraudulent claims can distort underwriting, advance rates, borrowing bases, and cash flow projections. >> Certainly. So, I have the benefit of actually doing this where I was a non-attorney owner of a DC law firm. We acquired 15,000 transvaginal mesh cases. We borrowed money from a um a high-profile lender. I won't mention their name. And in that again, I have a Wall Street background. So, I was looking at kind of the um the exposure. And when I was looking at it, they were overexposed on the much lower value cases and underexposed on the higher value cases. So, there was a misalignment of risk to the collateral, number one. Number two, the transaction I'm referring to was um was highly flawed for a variety of reasons and it was a subject of a book, right? And so, um in that docket because my partner um I was a minority partner in the law firm and he was using Indian call centers, it came to our attention several years after the fact that more than 20% of the claims that we sold were fake. >> Oh my goodness. >> They were fake claims originated in India. Yeah, so and that law firm ultimately was it they took out $50 million to do our transaction. Um several they just the law firm Akin Gump uh Stuart Aiken, I'll use his name cuz it's publicly in the record. He declared bankruptcy to 250 million dollars. So, he kind of kept doubling down on a bad loan. >> Mhm. >> So, huge risk if you don't verify your docket. >> Absolutely. Absolutely. Uh what warning signs should a lender look for before extending a credit facility? >> The you have to you have to evaluate the law firm itself, number one. There are many many fake law firms and that's again a one of the one of the things that I cover in the white paper that I co-authored with a you know, an ethicist. You have these um fake District of Columbia law firms. District of Columbia is um a the jurisdiction in the country where it that allows non-attorney ownership, right, by an individual. And you have these shell law firms set up to aggregate, all right? And then they co-counsel with reputable law firms. So, if you don't if a lender isn't aware of every element of the the, you know, the case origination, who are the law firms, who are the referring law firms, who did you use for case origination, who's your intake, who, you know, medical records. There are many fail points along along the the route, and unsophisticated lenders get burned all the time because of that. >> In the legal funding space, we have this term called settlement leakage. What is settlement leakage, and why can it become such a serious financial problem when a lender already has advanced funds against expected case proceeds? >> So, settlement leakage is where the the um the funder doesn't um receive the expected return on investment, right? They've lent money against a docket with a finite number of cases with an expected settlement value, right? If either the expected number of cases diminishes, right, either through um client attrition or the identification of fake cases, right? And or the settlement value that is expected isn't achieved, then that's settlement leakage, and the funder may not get the the rate of return that they expected. >> How can a lender evaluate whether the projected settlement value of a portfolio is supported by reliable information rather than assumptions? >> Uh two ways. Either the the lender itself can acquire the subject matter expertise to, you know, underwrite these cases, uh you know, more thoroughly, or they could any funder could retain uh you know, an organization like mine that would you know, that can do a more um thorough underwriting. You know, and again, what what's that subject matter expertise? As I mentioned, I've I've originated over 50,000 cases and um you know, again, because of the nature of the transaction I was involved in, right? I I know I know the dark side of of mass tort litigation finance. And so, I can you know, the process that we put together uh completely shouldn't say completely, but but significantly mitigates the potential for fraud in a docket. >> Mhm. So, a problem with one group of claims can sometimes affect an entire law firm or or their portfolio. How can sanctions, disqualification, repayment obligations, or other consequences associated with problematic claims affect a lender's broader exposure? >> Well, the lender is taking credit risk um based upon that law firm's uh capability and reputation, right? So, if the law firm has different case types, right? Mass tort law firms may have um a portfolio of different mass tort cases. A problem with one of those mass torts affects everything. Again, I'll reference that law firm in in the 3M hearing protection. It's a personal injury law firm um that was dabbling in mass tort. And the fees and sanctions that it received because of the fake cases in 3M certainly is going to affect their reputation, number one. And number two, the um you know, the clients who are become aware that their law firm is unethical can take their claims to other law firms. And the lender is uh is the one left handing the bit, like you know, holding the bag. >> What lesson should lenders take from high-profile mass tort disputes when evaluating the integrity of a docket from your experience? >> They have to do a better job of underwriting. And, you know, now with with AI-assisted identity theft, it is very, very difficult to determine the legitimacy of any claim um solely by electronic means, right? Nobody you know, and and and I know it's a question coming up, but we've gone old school, and we we do what we what I refer to as belly-to-belly, boots-on-the-ground claim verification. So, it's something it's expensive, but it's it's less expensive than than sanctions or bankruptcy. >> Absolutely. Let's talk about clean docket certification. What is it? How does the verification process work? And what distinguishes um an independently verified docket from one supported primarily by borrower representations? >> So, clean docket certification is a process we came up with that uses both electronic um uh electronic uh means to verify a claimant's identity, and then, as I mentioned, we use the belly-to-belly, right? And And so, what we would do, and again, I I've done this before, um where we would we go through our process, and we would identify we don't we don't disqualify. We only identify for a law firm, you know, those claims that have a high likelihood of fraud, right? We, as non-attorneys, we don't have you know, we can't make legal advice. That's So, we we put that on the law firm, but we give them the tools uh to make that evaluation. Um our process is different, where if I verify your docket and give it a clean docket certification, I will act as principal and serve as the expert witness to defend your docket if it's challenged by uh defense counsel or the court. And our process, I believe, would would prevail, you know, in in any, you know, any challenge by the defense or the court. Or the Justice Department, because the Justice Department is getting involved in this. Um you know, the False Claims Act, you have many uh insurance companies that are now filing RICO claims against uh personal injury law firms for staged uh personal injury um claims. So, you know, the the law firms and lenders are are coming increasingly um uh under more scrutiny. >> Mhm. Mhm. Um you um have a brief run that describes data scrubbing, contact information validation, and in-person identification verification. How do these steps work together to improve confidence in the underlying records? >> Well, as I said, we we've we've built a matrix where we show all the points of validation, the databases from which we got that information, right? And more importantly, you know, putting a mobile notary on somebody's doorstep, that sets out a very, very high bar for for challenge. And more importantly, you know, you don't have to be perfect, you just have to be better than the the next guy. And so, in the in the universe uh of um mass tort claims or even personal injury claims, our process puts our clients head and shoulders above the competition. >> Mhm. Verification that's not just an issue of of loan origination. How should lenders monitor a docket throughout the life of a credit facility, particularly when new claimants are continually added or the composition of a portfolio changes. >> It's all about reporting. Right? You you you know So again, I worked on Wall Street and I was in prime brokerage, which is a a suite of services that investment banks offer to hedge funds. One of the services that we offered was portfolio mark to market. Right? And so you have to every every night we would have to mark to market the hedge funds portfolio based upon the market price. Claims, you know, mass tort claims, personal injury claims, as I as I mentioned, it it is a slow moving asset class. And so mark to market is is you know, you can do that less frequently. However, there are elements of how many touch points did you you know, is the law firm contacting that particular client every week, right? What is the status of the medical records? Lenders need to have transparency. They need to have, you know, look through ability in a case management system to monitor that. And if something falls off, right? Red, yellow, green. You have different benchmarks. Somebody's contacting, you know, if the law firm is contacting the client every week, then it's green. They haven't contacted them in 2 weeks, it's yellow. They haven't contacted them in 3 weeks, it's red. And then the lender can get on the law firm's ass, shall I say, to to make sure that they're doing what they have to do to maintain that collateral. So the lender need needs to take a more active role rather than a passive role. >> Clean Docket Assurance includes several forms of protection, including expert witness support, potential defense cost coverage, and in case replacement under specified conditions. Can you walk us through how these protections work and explain the circumstances in which each of them may apply? >> Certainly. So Clean Docket certification expert witness is if we are retained by a law firm and we verify your docket, I will act as the expert witness on your behalf to go through our process and defend the docket to defense you know to defense counsel and the court. Number one. Number two, we'll incur the illegal expenses to defend that docket. Right? I put I'm acting as principal rather than agent, right? Most companies are agent. Um they'll they'll provide a service and if they get screwed up, they can get sued and they can get sued civilly, but they won't take a proactive role in helping the client defend itself. And then we also do victim identification. Right? And so if we've identified a victim and we verified it and it somehow comes out that that victim has you know has not is not valid, then we'll replace the claim so that the the law firm and the lender don't suffer an economic loss. And I can if I'm verifying if I'm the one identifying victims, I have that latitude. Now, I don't under what conditions? If you've retained somebody else to do your to do your um victim identification lead generation process and intake process, and I'm and I come in and I verify that docket, well, I'm not going to do a claim replacement because you've already paid somebody else to do that work. Make sense? >> Yes, absolutely. Thank you so explaining it so thoroughly. I really appreciate it. Um you um you know, you you've been working with with macro macro level analysis of of master dockets and and you've been working with you know, variety of claimant pools. How can analyzing patterns across a portfolio help identify potential identity fraud, uh collusion, treatment mills, or other concerning trends that might not be obvious when reviewing individual files? >> Yes, we actually get more insight the larger the docket and can look across um cuz there are many different data points. We mentioned 100 different data points, right? And so victim um identity theft is similar to the identity theft that they're finding in government benefit claims right now, right? So, the larger the docket, the trends we can see how many plaintiffs are using the same physical address, right? How many How many plaintiffs are using the same cell phone number? Um dual representation, is that claimant represented by multiple law firms, right? So, so these looking across, you know, multiple law firms in the same mass tort gives us more insight and can help us protect more law firms from bad actors who are simply trying to game the system because there's no communication among law firms, right? So, again, in in the capital markets, right? There's insight. When when you trade a stock, right? Everybody knows who bought and sold, right? The transfer agencies. But there is no There is no system in litigation finance. Even the courts have no idea of dual representation until settlement where the third-party administrator who's actually paying the checks might say, "Oh, >> Mhm. >> John Smith is getting paid at this law firm and there's another claim by John Smith. And then that causes a whole administrative problem because neither law firm knew, and now they have to share the fee if it's a legitimate fee. >> Mhm. From your perspective, what responsibilities do law firms, lenders, investors, and verification providers each have in protecting the integrity of the legal funding ecosystem? >> This is an important point, and it it's one where uh you know, it all comes down to the lawyer, right? And and I will tell you um I am tremendously disappointed in the attorneys in mass tort, and I characterize them two two ways, and this will be This will be controversial, but um they're either cowards or criminals. Right? In the sense that every lawyer knows that identity theft is happening in mass tort. But in my experience, nobody wants to do anything about it. Because number one, lawyers don't want to criticize other lawyers. And many lawyers are in on the scam. So, they don't want to do anything about it to upset the apple cart. But at the end of the day none of the other players you know, I I'm I'm mentioning five, right? So, the lawyers are at the tip of the spear. All right? The lender, the lead generator, the third-party administrator, or the court can't touch that. You know, have no have no um interaction with that claim unless the lawyer submits it. So, the lawyer is the one responsible for it. And they're the ones that should suffer the consequences if any portion any party in that process you know, are involved in the corruption. Right? So, the lawyers and and the lawyers are are extremely adept at avoiding that responsibility. Because the bar associations are not supervising the attorneys. And who who suffers? Well, legitimate plaintiff suffers, as I said, because you know, legitimate awards are diminished by the fraud. And then if it's a publicly traded company right? Who's the defendant? The shareholders of that company. So, it's the little guy on either end that are suffering from the fraud and collusion in in personal injury and mass tort civil litigation. >> Looking ahead, how do you see technology independent verification and more rigorous underwriting changing the future of legal funding and law firm finance? What practical steps should lenders take today to strengthen their portfolios and build greater investor confidence? >> Uh rigorous transparency. And and um familiarity with the asset class. As I said, there's stupid money flooding third-party litigation finance. Private equity, um, is is chasing a return, but they don't have the subject matter expertise. None of them have originated a claim. None of them have, uh, experience with false claims. Right? And so, it really comes down to, um, are you an operator? Right? Have you done it yourself? And so, you know, I think the most successful lenders in the space will be those lenders that either retain an organization like mine, or hire people, hire attorneys, who've actually built a docket. And most lawyers have never built a docket over a thousand claims. The vast majority of them, uh, you know, have not. So, experience, and, and transparency. And more importantly, sanctions, because they're not going to do it willingly. And so, there needs to be the Justice Department has to really come down on these bad actors. >> Um, and Ron, if someone has a question for you, or want to go into depth and and to specifically in this topic, how they can locate you, and how they can get in touch with you? >> I try to be easy to find. Right? So, my website is t e l n dot law. Um, my email address is r s l at t e l n dot law. Or you can Google me and find me on LinkedIn. metadata.author: Optimize My Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
Episode Summary:
In this episode of Personal Injury Marketing Minute, host Lindsey Busfield sits down with Thaddeus Wendt, partner and CEO of Feller and Wendt LLC, to discuss the transition from litigation to leadership in the personal injury law sector. Thaddeus shares his journey from focusing on litigation to spearheading business development, highlighting the importance of adopting structured management systems like EOS and Fireproof. He explains the challenges and strategies involved in scaling a law firm, including the necessity of intentional growth, the role of data in decision-making, and the emotional impact of transitioning roles. Thaddeus emphasizes the value of collaboration and learning from industry leaders to overcome hurdles in law firm expansion. This episode is a must-listen for attorneys looking to grow their practice and gain insights into effective leadership and business strategies.

Key Timestamps:
00:00 – Introduction
0:54 – Thaddeus Wendt's Background
2:08 – Growth Challenges in Personal Injury Law
4:22 – Recognizing Industry Changes
6:23 – Transition to Business Development
9:01 – Implementing Management Systems
10:59 – Building Core Values and Culture
12:26 – The Power of Team Alignment
14:01 – Lawyers as Business People
16:14 – Leadership Transition in Law Firms
18:46 – Delegating and Trusting Processes
21:26 – Emotional Impact of Career Transition
24:46 – Learning from Industry Leaders
27:21 – Actionable Steps for Firm Growth
30:01 – Collaboration Over Competition

About the Show:
Personal Injury Marketing Minute is a podcast dedicated to exploring the dynamic world of legal marketing, specifically tailored for personal injury attorneys. Hosted by Lindsey Busfield, the show covers a wide range of topics, from business development and leadership to marketing strategies and industry trends. Each episode features insightful conversations with industry leaders, providing listeners with practical advice and innovative ideas to help grow their practice. With a focus on clarity and actionable insights, Personal Injury Marketing Minute is an essential resource for legal professionals looking to stay ahead in a competitive market.

For more information, visit our website:
https://optimizemyfirm.com/

#PersonalInjury #LawFirmGrowth #BusinessDevelopment #Leadership #LegalMarketing

metadata.title: How Litigation Funding Is Shaking Up The Legal Industry
metadata.author: OffshoreAlert
metadata.shortDescription:
How Litigation Funding Is Shaking Up The Legal Industry: Law firms are out of ideas on how to boost profits, other than rate hikes. Corporate clients are frequently unimaginative and reluctant to experiment with anything other than rate discounts. The Bench is conservative and concerned about control over cases, rather than promoting responsible access to the legal system.

This session will explore the notion that all of these issues are fully addressed by responsible risk sharing and that, arguably, funding is the only historically transformative and disruptive innovation since contingencies (1700s) and insurance (1800s).

THEME: Investment & Business Opportunities

Constantine Karides, Partner, Reed Smith (New York)
James Little, Founder & Managing Director, Drumcliffe LLC (Washington, DC)
Michael Weisz, Founder & President, YieldStreet (New York)
David Kerstein, Investment Manager & Legal Counsel, Bentham IMF (New York)
Emily Slater, Director, Burford Capital (New York)

Recorded Live on May 01, 2017 at The 15th Annual OffshoreAlert North American Conference on Financial Intelligence & Investigations, The Ritz-Carlton, South Beach, Miami Beach, FL

Learn more at: https://www.offshorealert.com/events/

metadata.title: How Litigation Finance Is Reshaping Law Firms (Capital, Risk & 10X Returns Explained)
metadata.author: ResTech Solutions
metadata.shortDescription:
The Future-Ready Law Firm: Modernizing Law Firms, Managing Risk & Driving Growth
Navigating Law Firm Operations, Security & Innovation

Most law firms focus on winning cases.

But what if the real leverage is in how you finance them?

In this episode of Future-Ready Law Firm, David Levine sits down with David Kerstein, Managing Director of Arcadia Finance, to unpack how litigation finance is transforming the business side of law.

From non-recourse funding structures to the 10X rule, budgeting sweet spots, and the intersection of AI, capital, and risk, this conversation reveals how forward-thinking firms are evolving beyond traditional billable-hour models.

If you’re a law firm leader thinking about growth, risk sharing, contingency strategy, or operational efficiency, this episode will challenge how you think about monetizing legal work.

What You’ll Learn:
• What litigation finance actually is — and what it is not
• How non-recourse funding works in real-world cases
• The “10X Rule” funders use to evaluate opportunities
• Why budgeting discipline determines funding viability
• How firms can monetize cases instead of just winning them
• Why AI is becoming a force multiplier in legal operations
• How capital strategy changes firm growth trajectories

Guest: David Kerstein
Managing Director, Arcadia Finance

🌐 Arcadia Finance Website: https://www.arcadiafin.com/
🔗 David Kerstein LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/david-kerstein-0b58513/

metadata.title: The 4 Mass Tort Developments Plaintiff Firms Should Be Watching | Tort Talk
metadata.author: Jon and Marc
metadata.shortDescription:
As always, mass torts are moving quickly. Plaintiff attorneys face new developments in case acquisition, MDL strategy, and litigation timelines.
The latest updates affect social media litigation, weight loss drug cases, and the Roundup class action settlement.

Major litigation is reaching key inflection points across several high-profile mass torts. The social media addiction trial has reached the stage where the defense begins presenting its case after the plaintiff rested. Weight loss drug litigation tied to semaglutide continues to gain momentum after a UK regulatory warning linking the drug to a rare vision condition.

At the same time, the hair relaxer MDL is approaching critical Daubert hearings that will determine which expert testimony survives. Those rulings will shape the path toward bellwether trials expected in 2027.

Another development affecting plaintiff firms right now is the Roundup Missouri class action settlement. With roughly 60,000 potential claims involved, firms now face a 90 day window to evaluate cases, obtain wet signatures for opt outs, and determine which clients may be better served pursuing individual litigation.

For plaintiff law firms handling mass tort inventories, these developments affect litigation strategy, client communication, and settlement positioning over the next several months.

metadata.title: Litify Intake Training: Manage Leads, Questionnaires, and Case Qualification
metadata.author: Litify
metadata.shortDescription:
This Litify training session explains how intake teams can organize potential client information, manage intake records, use questionnaires, and move qualified cases through the intake process.

In this walkthrough, you will learn:

- How the Litify Intake feature works
- How to navigate intake records and list views
- How to create and manage new intakes
- How to use dashboards to track intake activity
- How questionnaires help collect consistent case information
- How CQC rules help qualify potential cases
- How to move intakes through different workflow stages
- How to refer cases through the Litify Referral Network

A structured intake process helps law firms capture consistent information, improve reporting, and create a smoother workflow from the first client interaction through matter creation. Litify provides legal teams with connected workflows for managing cases, reporting, and operations in one platform.

Learn how to track intake performance and conversion metrics: https://www.litify.com/blog/how-leading-plaintiff-firms-use-litify-to-optimize-marketing-and-intakes?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organicsocial 

For more Litify training resources, visit Litify: https://www.litify.com/resources?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organicsocial

metadata.title: Mastering Mass Torts: True Cost, Feedback Loops and Vendor Relationships featuring Devin Downey
metadata.author: Case Works
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of The Leverage Report, Dan Miner, CEO of Case Works, sits down with Devin Downey, co-founder and CEO of Blue Sky Legal, to discuss key challenges in mass tort case acquisition and the importance of creating strong partnerships between law firms and marketing agencies. Devin shares insights from his experience in the legal and advertising industries, touching on critical issues such as case attrition, lead generation quality, and the evolving dynamics of case development.

00:00 - Meet Devin Downey, CEO of Blue Sky Legal
01:15 - Devin’s Background in Advertising and Law Firm Marketing
01:54 - The Problem of Siloed Case Acquisition and Development
02:53 - Case Fallout and Attrition Data
05:07 - Impact of Feedback Loops in Lead Generation
06:41 - Identity Validation and Fraud Prevention in Case Acquisition
08:55 - True Costs of Acquiring a Compensable Plaintiff
09:40 - Addressing Dual Representation in Mass Tort Cases
11:27 - The “Facebook Effect” and Media Saturation
14:03 - Challenges of Managing Client Relationships Over Time
17:06 - Quality of Leads and Transparency in Marketing
19:18 - Importance of Brand Experience for Plaintiffs
22:18 - Staying in Touch with Clients Throughout the Settlement Process
23:06 - Recommendations for Law Firms When Vetting Vendors
24:50 - Final Thoughts on Vendor Selection
25:34 - Conclusion

Key topics covered:
- The impact of case fallout rates on mass tort firms and how to reduce them
- Aligning marketing and case development teams to improve case outcomes
- The importance of identity validation in intake and preventing fraudulent signups
- Strategies to minimize dual representation and improve plaintiff communication
- Evaluating marketing partners and lead generation in the mass tort space

Whether you're a law firm looking to improve your intake process or a marketing partner aiming to align your efforts with law firm goals, this episode offers actionable insights and strategies.

Get the full transcript here: https://yourcaseworks.com/the-leverage-report/mastering-mass-torts-true-cost-feedback-loops-vendor-relationships/

Learn more about Blue Sky Legal here: https://blueskylegal.com/

Get in touch with Case Works here: https://yourcaseworks.com/contact/

metadata.title: Understanding Litigation Finance Underwriting, Part I
metadata.author: TownCenter Partners Litigation Finance
metadata.shortDescription: Understanding how litigation finance works requires an understanding of the process by which a prospective funder evaluates and chooses the cases in which to invest. Underwriting is what assures that litigation finance is an economically rational undertaking, not merely a bet on the outcome of a lawsuit. This is the first of two posts on the underwriting process and how it implicates the way in which funders work with lawyers. This post focuses on underwriting from the funder’s perspective, while the next post considers the underwriting process from the perspective of the funded claimholder.

First, it’s important to note that there is a difference between plaintiff and defendant litigation funding.  The market for defendant-side financing is still developing but any type of claim could be eligible for litigation finance.  Whereas, funding on the plaintiff-side is more common but can be limited based on the funder, either to cases that involve commercial damages claims or personal injury claims.

metadata.title: Litigation Finance Demystified: Investment Trends & Future Outlook | Interview with Sean Campbell
metadata.author: Alt Funds Network
metadata.shortDescription:
Find us online: https://altfunds.io/
Email us with topic ideas: info@altfunds.io
Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/show/5hmRIlxXPlw5xi7sTp1g0r?si=2047a7ddd14c4431
Apple Podcast: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/alt-funds-network/id1662025628

Connect with Sean - Valiant Finance website: https://valiantfinance.net/

Key topics of discussion:
Definition and Origins of Litigation Finance: Sean Campbell dives deep into the history of litigation finance, tracing its roots back to 1200 A.D. and its modern evolution with banks supporting law firms.

Understanding Mass Tort: Dive into the world of mass torts, distinguishing them from individual lawsuits, and discover landmark cases like the Johnson & Johnson talc baby powder scenario.

Investment Shifts in Litigation Finance: From hedge funds to banks and now, the emergence of dedicated litigation finance firms, understand the changing dynamics of major players.

Access for Accredited Investors: Unlock opportunities in litigation finance as Sean discusses pathways for smaller accredited investors.

Most Impactful Cases: Highlighting influential lawsuits like the 3M earplugs case showcases the potential impact and profitability of strategic litigation finance.

Private Equity's Role: Discover why the titans of private equity are gravitating towards litigation finance and the potential ROI attracting them.

Risk Assessment in Litigation Finance: Peer into the meticulous vetting process that ensures only the strongest cases get backed.

Returns and Profitability: Unpack the lucrative returns from successful litigation cases and why they’re reshaping investment strategies.

Future of Litigation Finance: Predictions, trends, and trajectories shaping the future of this burgeoning sector.

Ethical Considerations in Third-party Financing: Delve into the moral debate surrounding third-party lawsuit financing and its implications on the justice system.


Disclaimer:
Alt Funds Network LLC and and its affiliates, episode guests, and the companies they represent do not provide tax, legal or accounting or investment advice. This material has been prepared for informational and educational purposes only, and is not intended to provide, and should not be relied on for, tax, legal or accounting advice. You should consult your own tax, legal, accounting, and investment professionals before engaging in any transaction or making any financial or legal decision based on your specific situation.

metadata.title: Litigation finance Changes the Law Firm Landscape
metadata.author: TownCenter Partners Litigation Finance
metadata.shortDescription:
It used to be taken for granted that large firms did not take cases on a contingent fee basis.  If a plaintiff had a potentially valuable claim and wanted to pay a lawyer through a contingent fee, the only place to look was a boutique firm.   But litigation finance is changing all of that, and large firms are now being more aggressive about pursuing contingent fee cases.

metadata.title: How Is Compensation Awarded in a Hernia Mesh Lawsuit? | The Good Law Group
metadata.author: The Good Law Group
metadata.shortDescription:
If you suffer from long-term injuries as a result of your hernia mesh surgery, it’s reasonable for you to wonder how much of a settlement you might be entitled to. Most hernia mesh cases are part of a multidistrict litigation, or MDL. Bellwether trials help guide the court and give everyone a sense of what the future holds. They’re set up in a way where the plaintiff and defendant each pick three defendants and try the cases. Compensation is typically awarded to the plaintiff, but the amount varies. To learn more about how this process works, watch this short video.

metadata.title: Mass Torts VS Class Action | What's The Difference Between Them ?
metadata.author: Business Box
metadata.shortDescription:
Mass Torts VS Class Action | What's The Difference Between Them ? 

While both mass torts and class actions involve large groups of plaintiffs suing a defendant, they differ significantly in how they are structured and handled.   

Mass Torts:

Individualized Claims: Each plaintiff files an individual lawsuit, even though the claims may arise from a common event or product.   
Unique Circumstances: Each plaintiff's case is unique, with individual facts and damages.   
Flexibility: Plaintiffs have more flexibility in pursuing their claims, including the choice of attorneys and the ability to settle individually.   
Complex Litigation: These cases often involve complex scientific and medical evidence, making them more time-consuming and expensive.   

Class Actions:

Collective Action: A group of plaintiffs, represented by a class action attorney, file a single lawsuit on behalf of all similarly situated individuals.   
Commonality: All class members share common legal and factual issues.   
Efficiency: Class actions can be more efficient than individual lawsuits, especially when there are numerous similar claims.   
Limited Control: Individual plaintiffs have less control over the litigation process and settlement negotiations

metadata.author: Dolman Law Group
metadata.shortDescription:
Mass torts don’t involve one giant courtroom showdown. Instead, a few selected cases are tried to estimate values for the rest ⚖️

about mass tors, we're talking about
typically multidist litigation. So what

records. They then look at these records
related to these claims and decide what

metadata.title: Camp Lejeune Bellwethers Kick Off, Meta Drops Out, & Bard PowerPort Surges
metadata.author: Jon and Marc
metadata.shortDescription:
Mass tort litigation moves fast. In this episode of Tort Talk, hosts Jon Robinson and Joe Fantini break down the critical developments shaping MDLs across the country.

We dive deep into the long-awaited kickoff of the Camp Lejeune bellwether trials in North Carolina. With trial pressure building and conflicting court filings between plaintiff leadership and the Department of Justice, learn why the DOJ is seeking a Lone Pine order, how Tier 1 kidney cancer injuries might settle first, and why Tiers 2 through 4 could take years to resolve.

In Social Media Addiction litigation, Meta settled out of the newest personal injury trial right after being hit with a $25 billion privacy penalty in New Mexico. That leaves Snap as the sole defendant heading to trial. We examine how state-level school cell phone bans and youth restrictions in states like Florida and Pennsylvania are shifting the legal environment.

Plus, we cover the massive surge in Bard PowerPort lawsuits, with over 400 new cases filed in a single month following a $40 million plaintiff verdict, and inspect the infection-focused third bellwether trial. Finally, we break down the newly filed master long-form complaint in the Boston Scientific Spinal Cord Stimulator MDL and what the upcoming FDA preemption fight means for 2027/2028 trial schedules.

Chapters:
00:00 - Mass Tort Litigation & End-of-Year Overview
00:59 - Camp Lejeune: Kidney Cancer Bellwether Trial & DOJ Lone Pine Request
05:58 - Social Media Addiction: Meta Settles, Snap Stands Alone & Legislative Trends
11:00 - Bard PowerPort: 400 New Filings & Infection Bellwether Trial
13:00 - Spinal Cord Stimulators: Boston Scientific Master Complaint & Preemption Defenses
16:27 - Key Takeaways for Plaintiff Law Firms

#MassTorts #CampLejeune #SocialMediaLawsuit #BardPowerPort #SpinalCordStimulator #PlaintiffAttorneys #TortTalk #LegalStrategy

About The Jon & Marc Podcast
The Jon & Marc Podcast is for lawyers who care about growth and the bottom line. Jon and Marc interview leaders in plaintiff law to break down how major cases are built, how firms scale, and how strategy plays out behind the scenes. If you want to understand how the biggest players in the space think and operate, you’re in the right place. New episodes every week.

We got another one scheduled for December, and then one after that for February. So, a ton of pressure in this litigation. If we come out on top on this infection case, I think that pretty much puts a nail in this litigation and and will likely bring about a global. We'll see what happens. I don't know if there's enough time left for it to happen this year. We'll probably, if we get a good verdict, see the next case settle out and then probably in 2027 some sort of global. But, yeah, good developments there. We love to see a lot of trials. Like we talked about at the top, it's these trials that bring about resolution. So, we got to keep getting those trial dates. >> Here we are, you know, a little more than 2 months before the new year. As soon as Halloween happens, like we're into holiday season. So, things will start slowing down a little bit. It'll be hard to kind of make movement um on a bunch of different fronts. We do have some progress on spinal cord stimulators. So, on this Boston Scientific MDL, the plaintiffs filed a master long-form complaint. What comes next for this specific MDL and for others as well? >> Yeah, so everybody knows who's been following along, we have three different MDLs for the spinal cord, each of them with a specific manufacturer. So, the one for Boston Scientific, that was the first one formed. That was back in June. So, about 4 months later, we finally have the master long-form complaint. So, this is the allegations in the complaint that applies to every case, right? It goes into the background. It goes into the FDA approval. It goes into the studies. It goes into what they knew. It goes into their marketing. And what we're likely going to see is the defendants move to dismiss this case in response to it. So, in response to a complaint, you can file an answer or you can file a motion for dismissal. So, we're going to see that right away and it's going to really get into the arguments if there's a legally sufficient claim. So, it's going to really help actually some of the later MDLs because we're going to know the exact arguments that the defendants are going to be making in these spinal cord simulators. I'll tell you right now the argument's going to be it was approved by the FDA. The FDA approved it. We couldn't make any changes to the product. We couldn't make any changes to the update because it was approved by the FDA. Our hands are tied. This case is preempted. It should get dismissed. So, that's going to be the next battle that's happening probably in the first or second quarter of the next year. We'll get it a a decision on that, but while that's going on, now we're still working on this initial what we call housekeeping in the first 6 to 9 months of an MDL where the leadership is really working hard with defense counsel coming up with next the fact sheet, some information on how to exchange discovery, information on the parameters of a short-form complaint, things of that nature so that the cases can really start pick up and and get moving. So, a huge lift going into this master long-form complaint. They're going to continue to work on it, but it's going to be a good road map for those later MDLs once we get to this point. We'll see the same thing happen in those cases. >> Sounds like we have a ways to go on this case, right? Just a a lot of legal work to do. >> Oh, yeah. We're you know, years away from a bellwether. Could it be 2028? You know, the first bellwether if if we get a a good a truncated schedule, but yeah, we're we're focusing more on the legal arguments now, not even really getting into case specific. metadata.title: Hair Relaxer Lawsuit Update: Bellwether Trials, Cancer Claims & What Comes Next
metadata.author: Salenger, Sack, Kimmel & Bavaro, LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
Hair relaxer lawsuits continue to move forward in federal court, with approximately 12,000 cases currently pending in the mass tort litigation.

These cases involve allegations that certain hair relaxer and hair straightener products, including products made by companies such as L’Oréal, Revlon, and others, may be linked to serious cancer diagnoses in women who used them over time.

In this video, Jeffrey Kimmel of Salenger, Sack, Kimmel & Bavaro explains the latest updates in the hair relaxer litigation, including:

• What Science Day means in a mass tort case
• Why Daubert motions are critical for expert testimony
• When bellwether trials may begin
• How bellwether results can affect future settlement discussions
• Why L’Oréal executives may be required to testify
• What factors may make a hair relaxer cancer case stronger

The lawsuits currently focus on claims involving uterine cancer, endometrial cancer, and ovarian cancer. Stronger cases may involve long-term use of a qualifying hair relaxer product, documented product identification, and a confirmed cancer diagnosis in the medical records.

SSKB Law is continuing to follow the hair relaxer mass tort litigation and will provide updates as the bellwether trials approach.

Attorney Advertising. Prior results do not guarantee a similar outcome.

If you've been injured in an accident, by medical malpractice or by a defective product, contact us. Call 1-800-675-8556 or visit our website: https://hubs.li/Q04zly370

metadata.title: Year-End Mass Tort Settlement Watch: Hair Relaxer, Camp Lejeune, Uber & Roundup Updates
metadata.author: Jon and Marc
metadata.shortDescription:
Marc is officially back from paternity leave, joining Jon and Joe for a packed year-end Tort Talk litigation update! With just seven weeks left in 2026, the crew breaks down the breaking L’Oréal Hair Relaxer settlement in Illinois state court and evaluates which major consolidated litigation could be the next to reach a global resolution before 2027.

In this week’s mass tort roundup, Joe Fantini shares insider intel on L’Oréal’s Day-1 settlement in the four-plaintiff gynecological cancer trial in Illinois state court, and what that means for the nearly 13,000 cases pending in the federal Hair Relaxer MDL. Next, the guys examine the latest Camp Lejeune water contamination settlement rumors as parties battle over Lone Pine orders, census data across all 25 injuries, and the massive gap between $11 million bench trial demands and $500,000 Elective Option payouts.

Jon, Marc, and Joe also put the Uber Rideshare Sexual Assault MDL (4,600 cases) on high settlement watch after Uber settled its October MDL trial ahead of the January 11, 2027 bellwether, and unpack the critical post-Durnell Supreme Court preemption briefing in Roundup that could shape the future of Paraquat and pesticide litigation nationwide.

Chapters: 
00:00 7 Weeks Left in 2026: Another Mass Tort Settlement Coming?
00:58 Hair Relaxer Lawsuit Update: L'Oréal Settles First Illinois State Court Trial 
03:46 Camp Lejeune Litigation: $11M Trial Demands vs. $500K EO & Global Settlement Rumors 
06:56 Uber Sexual Assault MDL: October Settlement & January 2027 Bellwether Watch 
08:55 Roundup Litigation Update: Class Action Approval & Post-Durnell Preemption Briefing 
11:05 Closing Thoughts Ahead of Thanksgiving Week

Subscribe to the channel for weekly mass tort updates, MDL docket analysis, bellwether trial breakdowns, and plaintiff law firm growth strategies.

About The Jon & Marc Podcast.
The Jon & Marc Podcast is for lawyers who care about growth and the bottom line. Jon and Marc interview leaders in plaintiff law to break down how major cases are built, how firms scale, and how strategy plays out behind the scenes. If you want to understand how the biggest players in the space think and operate, you’re in the right place. New episodes every week.

videos.full_text: Welcome back to TortTalk. I'm your host, Mark Renfro, finally back from paternity leave, back with the boys, Joe Fantini and John Robinson. There is seven weeks left in 2026. I may have been out for a couple weeks, but we do have a little bit of time left. And with me, I am bringing some good news. Welcome back to TortTalk, everybody. John and Joe, how's it going? >> Good, Mark. >> Doing great. Missed you, bud. Missed you a lot. >> Good to see you here. >> I missed you guys, too. I I enjoyed the time away, happy to be back. And I'm happy to be back with news of another mass tort settlement about to break. John, what do we have coming up? >> Yeah, we had big news out of Illinois state court with L'Oreal settling the first hair relaxer case involving four women. Joe, tell us the details about this. This is like very recent breaking news. What's going on with L'Oreal? >> Yeah, this just happened earlier this week. So often times in mass torts, we have the parallel state court and MDL action going on. The Illinois state court got the trial first. So this was a multi-plaintiff trial. Involved four plaintiffs like you said. And on day one, before we really got rolling, we have a settlement. So that's obviously big news for 12,000 almost 13,000 plaintiffs in the MDL where we've had some great news coming down with regard to some expert rulings, pretty much all in the favor of plaintiffs letting the expert testimony come in. So there's serious pressure and momentum building towards a settlement. Like you said at the top, Mark, we're about seven weeks out. Not sure if we can get another settlement to join the year of the mass tort settlement, but it's possible and things are looking great in that litigation. >> These four women, do they all have the diagnosis? What types of cases were these hair relaxer cases? >> Yeah, so these were all gynecological cancer cases. So you know, way back when there might have been a little bit of a split in whether non-cancer cases were proceeding. These cases were cancer cases, gynecological ones. I'm unclear if they were all ovarian or uterine, but I know they were all gynecological. So definitely the same type of injuries we we have in the MDL. >> When is the next trial after this scheduled for? >> Yeah, the next trial isn't going to be until 2027 and then that's going to be in state court as well and then we don't have an MDL trial coming up until September of 2027. So we'll see some more pressure coming out of the state court venues. Would be great to get another settlement. Would be even better to wind that all together into a global for state and MDL. >> Awesome. Very exciting news. Moving on to I think this is now the last legacy mass tort, I'm going to call it because it's been around for a while. Camp Lejeune, two trials are done but no verdicts. Next trial is set for January 2027. You know, are we going to get a settlement anytime soon or are we just as far apart still? >> Yeah, this is the where the rumor mill is going very active here. You know, every other day I'm hearing from somebody about a potential settlement. They're far apart. It's going to be the tier ones. It's going to be all 25 injuries, but what I can tell you is both trials concluded. Like you said, these are bench trials, so we didn't get a verdict right away. Probably going to be a couple more months until we get a verdict. In the first trial, they asked for a little under $11 million in damages. In the second trial, we're still seeing what the exact amount they're asking for, but those numbers are big and I can tell you from the EO, if this case would have settled through the EO, it would have been about a $500,000 case. They want the Lone Pine order, and the plaintiffs, they just want to do the census to get a feel for who have these 25 injuries. So today it's not sounding like there'll be a settlement, but I have heard rumblings, you know, the past few weeks of something breaking very quickly. At first I thought it was just going to be tier ones. Now I'm more leaning towards a global with those 25 injuries. But John, what are you hearing? >> I could tell you from the Camp Lejeune standpoint, this is actually litigation that we had not been involved in at all. Any intel that we get is just from firms that we are working with who have already have an inventory of cases. >> Yeah, I I like I mentioned, John, I I heard it was going to be the tier one injuries, but now I 'm hearing something broader. So I I think that's what we'll ultimately get. And Mark, you mentioned we we got about a six-week gap until the next trial. trial

for example if there is a limited class

Constituent cases are transferred to the

metadata.title: March 2024 Bard PowerPort Litigation Updates with Berger Montague
metadata.author: Case Works
metadata.shortDescription:
Bard Port Catheter MDL Litigation Update: What Plaintiffs Firms Need to Know

The multidistrict litigation over Bard's allegedly defective port catheters continues to rapidly progress, requiring close attention from plaintiffs attorneys assisting harmed patients. In Case Works’ recent podcast interview with members of the leadership team, including attorneys from Berger Montague, we discussed critical updates on this litigation expected to move swiftly to bellwether trials by late 2025. 

With over 100 lawsuits consolidated in Arizona federal court, Judge David Campbell is moving this MDL forward at an aggressive pace. Leadership has been appointed, discovery is underway, and the initial bellwether pool is set. Attorneys assisting plaintiffs should closely track litigation developments to ensure their clients' rights are fully protected as we rapidly approach trial. 

Interested in connecting with the attorneys of Berger Montague?
Shanon Carson: scarson@bm.net 
Jennifer Elwell: jelwell@bm.net 
John Albanese: jalbanese@bm.net 
Or visit https://bergermontague.com/contact-us/

See the full video with transcript here: https://yourcaseworks.com/the-leverage-report/bard-powerport-cathedar-lawsuit-updates-with-berger-montague/

segments.text: Susan B. - Hello, everyone.
Welcome to another episode of the Leverage Report.
Really excited today.
I'm joined with the team from Berger Montague.
And before we dive in, because we're going to be talking about all things barred port
catheter and the litigation.
And you guys are going to be giving us updates before we dive in.
And I just start peppering you guys with questions.
Why don't I start off with a little bit of an introduction?
So we've got Shannon Carson that is here with us.
He is the managing shareholder and is the co-chair of the Consumer Protection and Mass
Tort practice group.
Shannon, we appreciate your time and being here with us today.
We're also joined by John Albanese, who is also a shareholder in the firm's Minneapolis
office.
And we also have Jennifer Elwell is the senior counsel in the Philadelphia office.
And both of you guys, I guess, Jenny and John, you're both members of the firm's consumer
protection and mass tort practice group.
Again, really appreciate your time connecting with me today and sharing all the updates
and insights about this litigation.
Shannon, we'll start off with you from a high-level perspective.
If you could just provide an overview for the listeners about this litigation, these
cases, and for those that may be unfamiliar with the topic and maybe just talk a little
bit about the firm's role in the case.
Shanon C. - Sure.
And first, let me just say thank you for having us today.
It's a privilege to be here and to appear on your show with John and Jenny.
In August 2023, a number of lawsuits that had been filed in federal courts around the
United States alleging injuries caused by Bard implanted port catheter devices were
all consolidated in a multi-district litigation, or MDL, proceeding before senior Judge David
Campbell in the District of Arizona for discovery and pretrial proceedings.
All of these consolidated lawsuits involve personal injuries arising from Bard's alleged
defective design, defective manufacture, sale, and marketing of their implantable port catheter
devices.
These devices include the Bard power port device and many other similar devices that
are sold under other trademarks and brand names by Bard.
The devices that are at issue in this litigation are typically implanted in the patient for
the purpose of permitting the intravenous transmission of chemotherapy for cancer patients.
And that's the vast majority of the cases.
They can also be used for other types of applications as well, which I think Jenny's going to talk
about in a little bit.
The defendants here include Cr Bard Inc.
Bard Access Systems Inc.
Bard Peripheral Vascular Inc.
And their parent company, Becton Dickinson and Company.
The lawsuits all allege that Bard has known about the problems with these medical devices
for many years, but has failed to provide adequate warnings and redesign their products
to make safer for patients to use.
And that would avoid the types of injuries that we're seeing in this consolidated group
of lawsuits.
Susan B. - Thank you for that, Shannon.
And would you share a little bit about, Berger Montague, their role in this case?
Shanon C. - Sure.
We're working with a consortium of law firms in this multi-district litigation that came
together in a very cooperative and productive way even before the MDL proceeding was established
in the District of Arizona.
And that group of firms has been working to put their joint resources to work in terms
of serving the plaintiffs in this lawsuit.
As is typical in MDL proceedings, there was a leadership application process and an appointment
process that was conducted right after the MDL was established in federal court, and
I was appointed to the executive committee in the MDL proceedings.
My colleague Jennifer Elwell, who's on with us today, also holds an appointment in the
MDL proceedings on the plaintiff's steering committee.
Berger Montague.
Our law firm is currently working actively, very actively in the litigation, both in all
types of facets, but on the law and briefing side in the litigation, on the bellwether
Committee on Science and expert issues.
And so we really are fully immersed in the litigation and all that is going on with all
the lawyers in the case.
We also have an active role in a parallel proceeding where some cases have also been
filed in state court, primarily in the state of New Jersey, although there are some cases
that have been filed in other state courts as well.
And we are working actively with the lawyers who are involved in the state court proceeding.
And we have a large dedicated team in this litigation beyond just John and Jenny and
myself, who's been involved since the beginning, from paralegals and investigators and experts
and so forth, that we are bringing to bear on this litigation.
Susan B. - Great.
That sounds awesome.
And John, I'm interested to hear a little bit from you on the products that are involved
in this case.
John A. - Sure.
Well, as Shannon mentioned, this case all involves Bard's port catheters and what?
Port catheters are devices that are used when repeated access is needed to the patient's
vascular system or veins.
So instead of getting repeated ivs or other needle sticks, you get a port catheter.
These devices are referred to as porticaths, sometimes called, they're sometimes called
metaports, and they're intended to provide repeated and long term access to the vascular
system for patients requiring repeated delivery of medications, iv fluids, nutrition, if they're
unable to take food, orally and blood products.
And they're also used if you need to have blood samples repeatedly.
The great majority of port catheters are used for chemotherapy treatment, and the catheter
is surgically implanted under the skin.
And the port catheter consists of two primary components, an injection port and the catheter.
The injection port is typically implanted in the chest, has a raised center where the
needle is inserted for medication delivery.
The catheter is a small flexible tube that's attached to the injection port and inserted
into a blood vessel.
Susan B. - Well, they sound like they're really helpful, but I guess, Jenny,
you're going to tell us what is the problem?
What's the problem with these port catheters?
Jennifer E. - So all of the catheters are made in part with barium sulfate.
And the lawsuits allege that barium sulfate was left exposed on the outer surface of these
devices.
And when the devices were implanted, the barium sulfate degrades, which causes divots and
cracks on the surface of the device.
These divots and cracks then become places where the catheter can fracture or break,
or where bacteria can hide or where blood clots can form.
And so sounds like those are the problems.
What exactly are the injuries associated with the catheters?
Jennifer E. - So there are a few categories of injuries.
One involves fracture of the catheter component, the tubing that's attached to the port reservoir.
When that happens, the device malfunctions, which can lead to medication leakage within
a patient's body, pain and damage resulting from a broken catheter.
It involves surgical procedure to remove the broken device and then another surgery to
implant a replacement.
Typically, this can cause a delay in treatment, which is most typically chemotherapy medication.
Then catheter fractures become more severe when a fragment of the catheter breaks away
and migrates to a patient's heart or pulmonary artery, causing life threatening situations
and possibly internal damage from the migrated fragment piece.
That migrated fragment must be retrieved by way of catheterization or an open heart surgery.
Possibly another category is poor catheter infections.
These infections are often severe, accompanied by a range of symptoms causing patients to
present to emergency rooms such as high fever, extreme weakness, pain, swelling, rashes,
delirium.
The patients are often then quickly hospitalized after they present to the hospital for treatment
of life threatening blood infections or sepsis.
The hospitalization typically involves emergency removal of the infected port catheter around
the clock, antibiotic treatment testing, addressing complications caused by the sepsis, and often
then continued antibiotic treatment at home.
Like the fracture injuries the patient often requires another surgical procedure to implant
a new replacement, and treatment could be disrupted, delayed in this entire process.
Another category involves pork catheter related thrombosis or blood clots that could result
in pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis in the proximity of the device, such as the
heart or internal jugular vein.
These clots can also prevent life threatening situations, and treatment often involves long
term blood thinners, possibly removal of the port catheter itself.
And lastly, an injury that may overlap.
Everything I've just mentioned involves skin erosion and tissue necrosis around the port
catheter site on a patient's chest.
Susan B. - Of the cases.
Jenny, this is just a follow on question to that of the cases that your firm is handling
now, do you see one or more of those injuries more prevalent than others?
Jennifer E. - There's been pretty even distribution amongst the fracture cases.
Infection and blood clotting.
There really has been.
Susan B. - John, we were talking about this earlier in the level of interest
in firms getting into this mass tort, and so know we've had lots of discussions about
helping firms work up the cases.
And so seeing this increase in interest of getting into the tort, what are the factors
that are contributing to the rapid growth in the number of plaintiffs?
John A. - There are a few things.
First of all, Bard is by far the market leader in selling these devices.
And the great majority of implanted port catheters in the country were sold by Bard.
So there are a lot of potential claimants out there.
Bard's port catheter mean they're used in medical facilities and homes throughout the
United States by thousands of patients every day.
And the US, the Food and Drug Administration, the FDA has received hundreds of adverse event
reports from patients implanted with Bard power ports.
But the company just continues to market the products as safe and effective without recalling
them, adjusting the product, or adding warnings to the label.
And we expect that the number of filed cases will continue to grow as more people discover
that the reason they were injured by their port was because it was defective.
One thing that's also leading to more cases being filed is that these catheters were approved
by the FDA under the 510K process, rather than the more rigorous pre market approval
process.
This means that unlike some other medical device cases, we don't anticipate any significant
issues regarding preemption that would limit claims against Bard.
Susan B. - Well, what's the current status of the case?
John A. - There are presently over 113 cases pending in the MDL.
The cases, as Jenny mentioned, are diverse as to injury and include catheter related
infections thrombosis or blood clots, catheter fractures, and those fracture cases include
cases where the catheter fragment has migrated and also where it also has not migrated.
The court has approved the short form complaint and plaintiff profile form to be used, and
there is a direct filing order so you can just file directly into the District of Arizona.
Discovery is underway.
The court has entered a case management order regarding the process for the selection and
discovery in the first set of bellwether cases.
The initial plaintiff pool for the bellwether process includes all cases filed by April
I know leadership is being intentional about what cases get filed prior to the bellwether
selection.
24 selected cases will then engage in bellwether discovery process, and final selection will
take place in early 2025.
We expect that many more cases will be filed before the April 1, 2024 deadline for bellwethers,
and then there will be cases that are filed afterwards.
Susan B. - Thanks for the update, John.
Jenny, you were just talking a little bit about some of the injuries and the issues
with the catheter.
Can you tell us a little bit about what practitioners should be looking for when they're evaluating
the cases?
Jennifer E. - Yeah, sure.
So evaluating the cases does require close review of the medical records to get the product
id, the diagnosis, the removal information, possibly replacement device information as
well.
The timeline between the port implantation and the onset of the injury can be important,
too.
There are also potential statute of limitations issues for those plaintiffs that were injured
outside the standard statute of limitations, which in most states is two to three years.
Depending on the state, we may be able to invoke the discovery rule to extend the statute
of limitations further.
Susan B. - And Shannon, I guess just from you started out talking to us about
the high level of the tort, what do you see as the future of this litigation?
Shanon C - Sure.
I think one thing is really clear about this litigation, and that is that it'S going to
move really quickly.
Everyone who attended that initial case management conference with Judge Campbell heard him speak
about his intention in terms of moving the case forward promptly.
And this is not going to be the type of MDL that languishes for a number of years.
Judge Campbell has really taken the reins of this litigation, is holding regular case
management conferences, and these cases are going to start to go to trial likely by the
end of 2025.
So by the end of next year, in terms of when we're going to start seeing bellwether trials,
I believe he has fast tracked the litigation, for example, by not permitting Bard to file
certain rule twelve motions, which is a little bit out of the ordinary.
And we expect overall that the next 18 months for everybody working on this litigation is
going to be incredibly busy.
And that it's very important for those who represent clients who are affected by this
litigation to know what's going on.
If they don't know what's going on, to get with a firm that knows what's going on and
really take all the necessary steps to make sure that their clients rights are protected
and are moving forward as quickly as they can.
And so that's what I expect to see here over the course of the next year or two.
Susan B. - Well, speaking of firms that know what's going on, you guys being
appointed to the leadership, if firms want to reach out, attorneys want to ask you about
the litigation, get advice, hear your suggestions about criteria and such.
How do they get in touch with you?
Shanon C. - Well, it's super easy.
They can reach out to any of the lawyers here, myself, Shannon Carson, my colleagues, Jenny
Elwell, John Albanese, any other lawyer who works in our mass tort department at Berger
Montague, and we will be happy to talk to them and completely inform them about what's
going on in the litigation in a way that's very detailed and up to date.
One thing that Berger Montague really prides itself on is these appointments are a privilege,
and it's our duty to be up to speed in terms of what's going on.
And it's an honor to be able to work with many firms who are working with us as cocouncil
or referral counsel in terms of talking about representation of potential clients.
So please, if anybody has a question about the litigation, do not hesitate to contact
any of us and we will be very happy to speak with you.
Susan B. - Wonderful.
Jenny.
Shannon.
John, I'm just so grateful for your time today, spending some time with me, sharing the updates
and the insights on this litigation, and just, again, really grateful for your time.
Thank you so much.
Jennifer E. - Thank you.
It's good to be here.
Bye.

Depo-Provera Lawsuit Updates: Bellwether Cases Explained

What is a bellwether case, and what role could bellwether trials play in the Depo-Provera litigation?

In this educational video, attorneys Ben Martin and Greg Vigna, JD, MD discuss the bellwether process and explain important concepts involved in ongoing Depo-Provera litigation. The discussion covers how bellwether cases are selected, why discovery and internal documents can be important during litigation, whether an individual case could potentially be selected as a bellwether case, the role of expert witnesses, and meningiomas.

If you are following the Depo-Provera lawsuits or have questions about how mass tort litigation and bellwether cases work, this video is intended to help explain the legal process and terminology in an understandable way.

00:00 – Introduction
01:32 – The Importance of Discovery & Internal Documents
01:43 – What Is a Bellwether Case?
02:31 – Could Your Case Become a Bellwether Case?
03:29 – Experts Involved in a Case
05:34 – Understanding a Meningioma

Topics discussed:
Depo-Provera lawsuits • Depo-Provera litigation • Depo shot • meningioma • bellwether cases • bellwether trials • mass tort litigation • MDL litigation • discovery • internal documents • expert witnesses • pharmaceutical litigation

metadata.title: Inside Mass Torts with Lacey Lewis from Trial Lawyers United
metadata.author: Certum Group
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of Alternative Litigation Strategies, host Kevin Skrzysowski speaks with Lacey Lewis, an attorney at Trial Lawyers United (TLU), about how the firm handles mass torts. Lacey explains why she moved from corporate labor and employment defense to representing injured people, and what she learned about creativity and grit when she started working on the plaintiff side of medical device MDLs. She describes TLU’s “Relentless Pursuit of Justice” philosophy and what being “trial-ready from day one” means when most MDL cases settle: telling each client’s story in every complaint and motion. Lacey goes through TLU’s main dockets, including Talcum Powder, Depo-Provera, Hair Relaxer, and Bard Power Port, and explains how the firm decides whether to take on a new tort. It weighs the strength of the science under Daubert and Rule 702, how serious and provable the injuries are, what the defendant knew, and where the litigation stands. The program concludes with the business side of mass torts: how contingency arrangements keep the firm’s interests tied to its clients’, and how TLU’s partnership with Certum Group gives the firm the capital and financial expertise to stay in the fight through bellwethers and appeals.

Guest: Lacey Lewis is an attorney with the law firm Trial Lawyers United where she advocates for individuals in high-stakes legal matters. Her background spans plaintiff advocacy, corporate defense, multidistrict litigation, and eDiscovery, giving her a practical understanding of how complex cases are built, managed, and developed from multiple sides.  Lacey earned her Juris Doctor, magna cum laude, from the University of Louisville Brandeis School of Law, where she was on Law Review, President of the moot court team, and competed on the TYLA National Trial Team. 

To learn more, visit certumgroup.com

metadata.author: Jersey Justice Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
On the latest episode of the Jersey Justice Podcast, attorneys Gerald Clark and Mark Morris sit down with Adam M. Slater, Esq., a Certified Civil Trial Attorney and partner at Mazie Slater Katz & Freeman, for a conversation about high stakes trial advocacy, Mass Torts, MDLs, and AI in the Legal Profession.

On this episode, Adam shares his path as a relentless Plaintiff Trial lawyer from early "trial by fire" losses and landmark appellate reversals to leading nationwide mass tort litigation against major pharmaceutical and medical device manufacturers. He breaks down why reading a jury, cross-examining live witnesses, and human instinct can never be replaced by AI in the courtroom.

Debunking myths surrounding "tort reform" and New Jersey’s strict Affidavit of Merit requirements to examining federal preemption and sliding scale attorney fee caps, this episode takes a hard look at what it takes to fight against corporate giants.

Tune In!
-----------------------
Learn more about Adam M. Slater, Esq. at mazieslater.com.
