metadata.title: Ben Martin & Sebastian Westerby | Depo-Provera Litigation, Mass Torts, and Case Acquisition Reality
metadata.author: Tort Experts
metadata.shortDescription:
Mass tort litigation is often misunderstood, especially the difference between class actions and large scale individual cases. In this conversation, trial attorney Ben Martin (Ben Martin Law Group) joins Sebastian Westerby to discuss how pharmaceutical and medical device cases are investigated, built, and litigated in complex mass tort proceedings.

The discussion centers on Depo-Provera litigation, including the scientific discussion around meningioma risk, the role of FDA warnings and drug labeling, and how failure-to-warn claims develop in pharmaceutical liability cases. Ben Martin explains how mass tort cases move from early investigation and medical literature analysis through individual trial preparation.

Beyond the legal framework, the conversation also explores operational challenges that affect large-scale litigation. Topics include fraudulent claim submissions, weak case verification systems, and the importance of disciplined intake when building case inventories in mass tort litigation.

With nearly four decades of trial experience, Ben Martin shares practical insights into how plaintiff firms evaluate cases, prepare individual trials within large dockets, and maintain focus on the people behind each claim.

Topics discussed

• Ben Martin’s background and national mass tort litigation practice
• The difference between mass tort litigation and class actions
• Depo-Provera lawsuits and the meningioma risk discussion
• The role of FDA warnings and pharmaceutical labeling in litigation
• Federal preemption arguments in pharmaceutical liability cases
• How plaintiff firms analyze science, causation, and medical literature
• Fraud and fake claimants entering mass tort case pipelines
• The importance of case verification and intake quality
• Why communication systems reduce client attrition in litigation
• Trial preparation and representing individual plaintiffs within large dockets

About the speakers

Ben Martin
Founder, Ben Martin Law Group. Trial attorney with nearly 40 years of experience representing clients in pharmaceutical, medical device, and complex injury litigation across the United States.

Sebastian Westerby
CEO of Tort Experts, a mass tort marketing and case acquisition partner supporting plaintiff firms and litigation portfolios. Tort Experts has managed $450M+ in legal client acquisition spend and focuses on inventory quality, intake verification, and acquisition systems designed to reduce fraud, improve contact rates, and keep legitimate cases moving.

Key takeaway

metadata.title: Filevine Demo & Tutorial: #1 Case Management Software for Legal Teams
metadata.author: Business Solution
metadata.shortDescription:
👉 Get Started with Filevine: https://businessolution.org/get/filevine/

This video is a full walkthrough of a Filevine project and shows how law firms can use Filevine to manage cases, organize information, track deadlines, handle documents, automate tasks, and control access across the firm. The demo is shown through the lens of a personal injury case, but the concepts apply across many practice areas, including family law, immigration, estate planning, employment, corporate counsel, and more.

You’ll see how Filevine organizes case data through custom and built-in sections, how the activity feed works as the central hub for communication, and how firms can manage texts, calls, tasks, reminders, emails, faxes, and client portal messages inside a single matter. The video also covers deadline chains, case calendars, one-off deadlines, document management, PDF editing, version history, sharing tools, automated task flows, customization options, permissions, and what implementation looks like for new Filevine customers.

If you’re considering Filevine for your law firm and want to understand how its case management workflow works in practice, this video gives you a broad look at the platform and its main capabilities.

Timestamps:
0:00 Intro and overview of a Filevine project
1:25 Data organization with custom sections and case information tracking
4:25 Activity feed overview for notes, tasks, texts, calls, and client portal messages
9:21 Deadline chains, reminders, and case calendar management
13:30 Document management, folders, uploads, and document actions
16:37 PDF editing, document locking, version history, and Filevine AI
20:16 Folder sharing, two-way sharing, and email replies inside Filevine
23:08 Task management, automated workflows, and phase-based task triggers
26:29 Customization of templates, phases, and fields
31:05 Permissions, teams, roles, and protected sections
34:39 Implementation, free trial, migration, and ongoing support

metadata.title: Filevine AI Demo: Revolutionizing Legal Case Management with AI-Powered Tools
metadata.author: Daya Naef
metadata.shortDescription:
In this comprehensive demonstration of Filevine's AI capabilities, we explore how artificial intelligence transforms legal case management across multiple practice areas. The demo showcases Filevine's integrated AI tools that streamline document review, automate workflows, and enhance productivity for law firms of all sizes.

Features Demonstrated

Validation AI
- Automated validation rules for case progression
- Custom requirements checking without programming knowledge
- Real-time verification of critical case elements
- Statute of limitations monitoring
- Flexible rule creation for different practice areas

Fields for Document Analysis
- Automatic document analysis on upload
- Zero-day retention for security compliance
- Pre-configured prompts for different document types
- Medical record analysis and chronology creation
- Automatic extraction of key dates and information
- Side-by-side document review capabilities

Document Generation with AI
- Integration with Filevine Doc Assembly (FVDA)
- Automated demand letter creation
- Temperature-controlled AI for accurate content generation
- Seamless incorporation of analyzed documents
- Custom template support

AI-Powered Deposition Analysis
- Automatic transcript review
- Red flag identification
- Sentiment analysis
- Direct page linking to source material
- Interactive editing capabilities

Sidebar AI
- Comprehensive case summaries
- Activity tracking and analysis
- Source-linked information
- Customizable prompt building
- Follow-up task identification

Doc Review Tool
- Ad-hoc document analysis
- Multiple output format options
- Background processing
- Flexible prompt selection
- Custom report generation

Benefits for Law Firms

- Significant time savings on routine tasks
- Enhanced accuracy in document review
- Consistent analysis across all cases
- Improved workflow automation
- Competitive advantage for smaller firms
- Secure and compliant AI integration
- Reduced manual data entry
- Comprehensive case oversight

Security and Compliance
- Zero-day retention policy
- Secure in-platform processing
- No external AI tool requirements
- HIPAA-compliant document handling
- Protected client information

This demonstration showcases how Filevine's AI integration provides law firms with powerful tools to automate routine tasks, enhance accuracy, and improve overall efficiency in case management. The platform's comprehensive AI capabilities make advanced technology accessible to firms of all sizes, helping level the playing field in legal services.

For more information about Filevine's AI capabilities and other features, visit the partner resource page or contact a Filevine representative.

metadata.title: The Intake Bottleneck We Were Missing #legaloperations #lawfirmmarketing
metadata.author: Modern Legal Ops | Building a tech forward firm
metadata.shortDescription:
More inquiries, one intake agent, and cases taking longer to convert.

We're tracking four KPIs—Time to Touch, Open to Offer, Time Under Review, and Open to Close— and they helped us pinpoint where the process was slowing down: attorney review.

A practical example of using KPIs to understand what’s happening inside your law firm. Start broad, measure the handoffs, and improve the process.

Where does intake slow down in your firm?

#LawFirmOperations #LegalIntake #LawFirmGrowth #MOLEOPS

- Reddit: https://www.reddit.com/user/moleops
- Inquiries: marketing@esquireengine.com

TRANSPARENCY & DISCLAIMER
I'm the founder of Esquire Engine and Director of Operations at Meyer Wilson Werning. When I show tools my company builds (like Scraiquill), I share them to explain the underlying operating problem and decision-making process so you can apply the lesson regardless of your tech stack. Everything shared on MOLE OPS is for educational and operational discussion, not legal representation or legal advice.

#LegalOperations #LawFirmMarketing #LegalTech

metadata.title: Tips and Strategies for Successful Mass Tort Management
metadata.author: Carlton Fields
metadata.shortDescription:
Mass tort litigation is unlike many other types of litigation – the cases are large, complex, and fast moving, and if you’re not organized and prepared early on, it can be hard to regain control. In this podcast, Carlton Fields attorneys Ryan Cobbs and Ashley Drumm discuss the  idiosyncrasies of mass tort management and share tips and strategies to help you maximize efficiency and direct resources toward winning — not just defending — your next mass tort engagement.

Carlton Fields Mass Tort and Product Liability Practice: https://www.carltonfields.com/services/practices/mass-tort-and-product-liability

metadata.title: Eliminating Meritless Claims [Multidistrict Litigation (MDL) Conference]
metadata.author: The Federalist Society
metadata.shortDescription:
Multidistrict litigation (“MDL”) accounts for nearly half of all civil cases in federal courts. Although MDLs were designed to be efficient mechanisms for “coordinated or consolidated pretrial proceedings,” in some instances they have become one-sided forums known for lacking the basic protections afforded to all other cases by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (FRCP), the Federal Rules of Evidence and appellate review.

Eliminating Meritless Claims

11:00 a.m. - 12:30 p.m.

Panelists:

David Bernick, Partner, Paul Weiss LLP
Honorable Eduardo Robreno, U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
Chris Seeger, Founding Partner, Seeger Weiss LLP
Andrew J. Trask, Senior Counsel, McGuireWoods LLP


Moderator:

Doug Smith, Partner, Kirkland & Ellis LLP
Participants

As always, the Federalist Society takes no position on particular legal or public policy issues; all expressions of opinion are those of the speaker.

metadata.shortDescription:
Mass Tort, Rebuilt: AI, Expertise, and the Future of Litigation  @thelegaltechfund  

Visit 👉 www.legaltech.com 

In this episode of In Studio, Gordon speaks with Matt Francis, Founder and CEO of Pattern Data, about how structured data and domain-specific AI are modernising mass tort workflows. From intake and evidentiary development to settlement allocation, Pattern helps law firms and claims administrators evaluate cases faster and with greater confidence. They discuss 7–10x efficiency gains, human expertise in edge cases, rising AI adoption, and why the future of mass tort will be defined by integrated platform infrastructure.

6 Episode Highlights:

🔹Matt explains what Pattern Data does and where it fits in mass tort litigation.
🔹The pre Pattern world: labour driven review, fragmented systems, and expensive rework.
🔹How the “lens” model connects intake, development, and settlement in one structured system.
🔹Achieving 7–10x throughput improvements while surfacing edge cases for human review.
🔹AI adoption shifts across courts, MDLs, and leadership firms.
🔹Looking ahead: platform infrastructure, better data, and “truth tellers at scale.”

Follow us 👉  https://www.linkedin.com/company/the-legaltech-fund/

#thelegaltechfund #masstort #litigation

#LegalTech #BusinessOfLaw #ai  #lawfirms  #thelegaltechfund 
This information is for illustrative purposes only. Statements and opinions are not necessarily those of The LegalTech Fund, and no assurance is made that projections or forecasts will be achieved. This is not business, investment, legal, tax, or accounting advice and should not be relied upon as such. Featured companies and individuals were not compensated, and the companies listed represent only a subset of current investments. Third-party names and logos do not imply recommendations, endorsements, or affiliations. This does not constitute an offer to sell or a solicitation to buy any investment interests.

metadata.title: $375M Social Media Verdict + $6M Trial: What Mass Tort Lawyers Need to Know (2026 Update)
metadata.author: LexHive Podcast (Formerly- The Legal Growth Lab)
metadata.shortDescription:
The social media addiction lawsuit just took a major turn.

In this episode, Michael Stanisci sits down with mass tort attorney Joe Fantini to break down the recent major verdicts that could reshape litigation against Big Tech :

1) A $375M verdict in New Mexico
2) A $6M individual plaintiff verdict in California
3) Ongoing litigation against Meta, YouTube (Google), TikTok, and Snap

We discuss what these outcomes mean for:

1) Mass tort lawyers evaluating new opportunities
2) Law firms considering entry into social media litigation
3) Parents and potential plaintiffs impacted by social media addiction

Joe also explains:

1) Key qualification criteria for cases
2) The expected scale (200K+ potential plaintiffs)
3) Why urgency is increasing now
4) How recent verdicts provide a roadmap for future claims

This is essential listening for anyone involved in:

1) Mass tort litigation
2) Product liability
3) Social media addiction lawsuits

🔗 Connect with our Host and Guest:

Host: Michael Stanisci
https://www.linkedin.com/in/michaelstanisci/

Guest: Joseph Fantini
https://www.linkedin.com/in/joseph-fantini/ | https://www.roseninjurylawyers.com


00:00 Introduction
00:18 Two Major Verdicts ($375M + $6M)
02:06 Market Opportunity (200K+ Cases)
03:59 Urgency: Why Lawyers Should Act Now
04:22 Who Qualifies for These Cases?
08:26 Key Evidence & What Happens Next

metadata.shortDescription:
Two weeks out from Mass Torts Made Perfect, Joseph Fantini joins Jon Robinson and Marc Rioux for the Pre-MTMP Mass Tort Power Rankings. In this episode, the team breaks down the shifting dynamics across the top 10 mass tort dockets, identifying where firms should allocate capital, which mature litigations are closing their doors, and which emerging torts are quietly building massive momentum.

We dive into the debut of Chlorpyrifos, an insecticide litigation following the Paraquat blueprint for Parkinson's disease, and evaluate why Weight Loss Drugs have cracked the top 3 following increased national coverage on GLP-1 eye injuries. We also detail the current status of Spinal Cord Stimulator MDLs, the timeline for Hair Relaxer expert rulings, Olympus Scope consolidation delays, and which mass tort continues to hold the #1 ranking spot indisputably.

If you are evaluating docket growth, case acquisition strategy, or looking for insights ahead of MTMP, this episode gives you the breakdown you need.

01:10 - #10 Bair Hugger: Legacy Litigation Update

06:09 - #8 Bard PowerPort: Bellwether Momentum & Case Acquisition Windows

23:40 - #1 The Undisputed Top Mass Tort
27:11 - Exclusive Tort Talk MTMP Listener Event Announcement

About The Jon & Marc Podcast.
The Jon & Marc Podcast is for lawyers who care about growth and the bottom line. Jon and Marc interview leaders in plaintiff law to break down how major cases are built, how firms scale, and how strategy plays out behind the scenes. If you want to understand how the biggest players in the space think and operate, you’re in the right place. New episodes every week.

So, we're we're we're following that same playbook where you kind of focus on certain defendants. You need to prove up through the gamer code, the gamer ID to see how long they were on the platform, things of that nature. So, Microsoft is the one right now that people are talking about the most. I'll report back if you know any details about a settlement, an inventory settlements confirmed with them, but that that's the one that seems to be the biggest target and the one that's going first right now. >> All right, we're about to enter the top five. Coming in at number five, we have the the recent push from spinal cord stimulators. We're waiting on the formation of two more potential MDLs. Are you behind these cases? Do you think that these really can go somewhere? >> I do. You know, I I believe in these cases. I I think both of those MDLs that you mentioned are going to get formed. I think it's going to be better for the litigation overall that we have three separate MDLs. You know, one focusing each on each of the different manufacturers. And then I'm expecting a really big state court play coming out of a couple different store uh states. And there'll be a lot of pressure on the defendants, right? The the issue in these cases now is is going to be this preeemption argument, how it was approved, the approval process. So, that's the fight that you really have to watch. We're probably nine months out from that really coming to a head and and probably not going to be until this time next year when we hear from any court on that. And then after that, you know, a lot more people are going to get excited. But I think this has good science. I think this has significant injuries. I think there's a large population of potential plaintiffs out there. It looks like there's viable defendants. So, this is one I'm hyping up. I I predicted last week this is going to be the bell of the ball at MTMP. So, I think everybody's going to be talking about it in a couple weeks. So, now's a great time to get involved. >> Any particular manufacturers here? Yeah, the the one that was first out and seems to have the most cases right now is Boston Scientific. So, they they control the market and then it seems like Abbott's going to be the next one. So, Boston Scientific, but when you're signing these cases, the plaintiffs aren't going to know which manufacturer they had. So, you got to get the records, prove it up. It's kind of just like hernia mesh. They know they had the mesh. You got to figure out the manufacturer and figure out where to send it. Following up spinal cord simulator, we have yet another medical device, Olympus Scopes, which six months ago we were talking about being the bell of the ball of MTMP. And now here we are entering a phase where it's starting to mature. There have been a ton of cases that have been acquired by the firms that have been pushing this forward. It however it is moving a lot slower than I think people expected it to. Are we going to see consolidation in an MDL by the end of this year or is this going to push into 27? Yeah, I think this one's going to push into 2027. So, we we just had at the end of September the JPML hearing. There's only one left. That's going to be in early December. So, usually for a motion to be heard for consolidation, it needs to be filed at least 30 days before the hearing. So, we're really getting up against that window. And so, for that reason, I don't think we're going to have the MDL formed. You really touched on it when we were out at Vegas in the spring. Everybody loved this litigation. Everybody was going nuts over it. Everybody wanted to get these cases and I think that's what we're going to see for P spinal cord stimulators at this MTMP. But I'm really surprised that it's not moving as quickly as we thought. Have you heard anything about maybe some reasoning behind that, Mark? >> I don't have the inside scoop on why things aren't moving. >> I see firms acquiring cases, right? I just don't know what's happening with them. I think that that there is some sussing out of like the tears and what is truly going to be a real case here. I've seen all types of injuries come through ranging obviously from as severe as death all the way down to like, you know, minor infection where people are are in and out of the hospital, you know, and then a variety of things in between. We've seen cases where people have developed HIV. We've seen cases where there there's been punctures um from the scopes which I think are are not going to be included if this winds up getting consolidated. So honestly I I do think this is just a a period where there's so many cases because they have so much market share Olympus that the cases just are are sort of going through assessment and identifying like what's the right path for them to be proceeded on. >> Yeah. And I I I honestly am happy to see that. I think sometimes the plaintiff's bar can get in a little bit of trouble when we we try to rush a little bit to get that MDL filed to be the first firm filing that I I think we're doing exactly like you're saying it's identifying what are the injuries, what are going to be the ones we can get supported by the experts. So the firms that are in the know, they're they're getting these cases. Uh they're stacking their dockets. So just because there's not an MDL doesn't mean that the case isn't viable. I think spring next year we'll have an MDL and it'll be off and running. But if you want to get a six-month head start, you know, reach out to John and Mark. I'm sure they'll be able to hook you guys up with some good marketing that that works. >> Yeah, we we have run uh a good amount of these. So, we we've seen types of injuries that have been coming through. And do remember, it's still a number four, right? It's not like we're talking about it. It's off the power ranking. So, only three cases above it. Uh we're going to move into the top three right now. At number three, we have weight loss drugs, which have been getting national attention for the the eye injuries. I saw it on Good Morning America. It is cracking the top three now for the first time. We're still waiting on a Dobert ruling on the gastrointestinal MDL, being as how it has now moved up to number three. Joe, do you think it's time for people to start really looking at the weight loss drug seriously? >> Because this had a ton of attention and it's been pretty quiet until it's back in the top three of the power rankings. >> Yeah. No, you're you're exactly right there, Mark. Right. like I guess was it two three years ago, people started talking about this case and how it was going to be the biggest case potentially ever out there just based upon how many people are using these medications. And then the litigation kind of went forward and then we had a a ruling that wasn't great for the plaintiffs, right? Where we were required to get this gastric emptying study to prove the gastroparesis about a year ago and that really slowed down the momentum. But I I think now we're really focused in on these injuries and having that requirement for that study. I think it's going to help the plaintiffs that have the cases filed because the defendants's arguments is kind of shot down a little bit. So we're we're waiting on this Dalbert ruling might have it before the end of this year, beginning of next year just because this product's still on the market. The defendants are making so much money. I think they're going to roll the dice and they're going to keep pushing it until we get, you know, closer to a bellweather, even a bellweather case tried, unlike some of the other litigations where they settle out because they have a new product on the market or they're not selling it anymore before that expert opinion comes down. But, you know, we're talking right now about these gastro injuries, but like you mentioned, John, everybody in the world is talking about those eye injury cases, and they weren't even on our radar a year, year and a half ago. So, this is one to get involved with. There's going to be a lot more cases coming down the pipe. So, this is one that's going to be in the top three. And I I think this is going to be hanging around for the next year, year and a half. So, there's time to get cases for sure. >> I'm interested to see how this plays out because not only is this pretty much the most popular drug in the United States, it's probably the most profitable drug in the United States currently as well. >> Yeah, that that's a factor, right? We'll see what the defendants do here. Again, it's it's going to be a business decision. Settle out the cases before the expert opinion comes down and the judge rules on it or push it all the way towards the bellweather trial. Maybe try one or two of the cases. So, we'll we'll keep everybody watching, but this could be the most talked about tour to Mass Tour made perfect. I know people have been talking about it for years. He's coming on our platform. >> Fair enough. Fair enough. That concludes another power rankings, but we do have some announcements to make, don't we, Mark? >> We do. >> We do. We have MTMP coming up in a couple weeks. We could talk masstorrs. >> We might even record a live episode. >> We might. We might. We are going to be putting uh we're going to be putting that out on our socials so that people can sign up to attend. This is a private invite only event. Tort talk listeners, make sure you put your name on the list. It is hardcapped. So, make sure that you get yourself on the list as early as possible. The three of us will be there. This is going to be on Wednesday late afternoon and we look forward to seeing everybody there. >> Yeah. Excited for the event. Excited to see everybody at MTMP and see how these rankings change just in a month because everybody knows a lot changes pretty quickly in the mass tour world. >> Yep. And I can't wait to do the postm episode to see what all the hot gossip was of the show. >> We'll see you next time on Tor Talk.

metadata.title: How Mass Tort Firms Manage Cases from Intake to Settlement | Matt Francis
metadata.author: Pattern Data
metadata.shortDescription:
A look inside how mass tort firms move cases from intake through development to settlement on a single connected platform.

Most firms historically operated with fragmented processes: intake in one system, medical records reviewed manually or through outsource vendors, case data spread across CRMs and spreadsheets. When it was time to act on the information, someone had to stitch it all together. Pattern Data founder Matt Francis describes a different approach: a single structured system, tailored per litigation, that holds critical case data across the full lifecycle.

Matt walks through three stages: screening at intake against gating criteria, deeper evidence development for cases that meet criteria, and settlement preparation that uses the same structured dataset to calculate eligibility and generate submission-ready work product. From The LegalTech Funds InStudio podcast with Gordon Crenshaw.

Explore the Pattern platform:
https://patterndata.ai/platform

See how Pattern handles settlement preparation:
https://patterndata.ai/solutions/settle

Full Podcast: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_HuCGlH6Wyw

#MassTort #CaseManagement #LegalTech #MDL #Settlement

metadata.title: How the MSO Model Helps Healthcare Businesses
metadata.author: Holt Law: For Healthcare Businesses
metadata.shortDescription:
The MSO model is one of the most powerful — and misunderstood — tools in healthcare business law. Short for Management Services Organization, the MSO structure allows healthcare providers to separate clinical operations from business management, protecting compliance while creating scalable growth opportunities. Yet most clinic owners either don’t understand how it works, or they try to set it up incorrectly and end up with major legal exposure.

In this episode of The David Holt Show, attorney David Holt explains exactly how the MSO model helps healthcare businesses. Whether you run a medspa, telehealth startup, or large clinic, you’ll see how this structure can safeguard compliance, attract investors, and give you the freedom to focus on patient care while your business scales.

Here’s what you’ll learn:
- What an MSO actually is and why it matters for healthcare businesses.
- The compliance advantage — how an MSO separates medical risk from business operations.
- The growth advantage — how MSOs make it easier to bring on partners, scale locations, and attract capital.
- The practical steps to set up an MSO without running afoul of corporate practice of medicine laws.

Instead of drowning in legal jargon, David breaks the MSO model down in plain English, with real-world examples from clinics that have grown successfully using this exact framework.

By the end of the episode, you’ll know whether the MSO model is right for your business — and if it is, how to set it up the right way the first time.

0:00 MSO Model: Splitting Clinical Practice from Business Management
1:48 Corporate Practice of Medicine: Why MSOs are Legally Necessary
3:07 MSO in Action: Avoiding Legal Pitfalls (Payroll & Marketing Consent)
4:33 Compliance Requirement: MSOs in California (51% MD Ownership Rule)
5:04 MSO's "Cheat Code": Attracting Investor Funding for Growth
5:58 Accelerating Growth: Scaling from One Location to Multiple Clinics
6:40 The No-Brainer: Why Every Clinician (Without an MBA) Needs an MSO
7:36 MSO Power: Compliance Tool vs. Legal Engine for Growth
7:55 Next Episode: The Legal Landmines of Using AI in Your Clinic

metadata.title: What is the difference between mass tort, class action and a MDL
metadata.author: Roberts & Roberts Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
Although the terms mass tort, class action and an MDL are very popular amongst people thanks to the many discussion in the media, still many people do not fully comprehend the difference between them. To help people in identifying and understanding these terms correctly, Personal Injury Attorney Randy Roberts of Roberts & Roberts elaborates each one of them with expertise in this video. 

Video Transcription:
There is a lot of discussion in the media about mass torts, class actions and MDL’s, but a lot of people don’t understand the difference. A mass tort is simply a type of injury, while a class action and an MDL are methods for getting people compensated for that injury. A mass tort, as the name describes, involves a situation where a mass of people, hundreds or even thousands, are injured by the same defective product. The typical situation is when a prescription drug is recalled after it has harmed hundreds if not thousands of people. A class action and an MDL (multi district litigation) are methods for compensating people who are victims of mass torts. A class action, however, is significantly different from an MDL. In a class action, there is just one lawyer, one case, one judge and jury, and one verdict that applies to everyone, even though the class action has been filed on behalf of hundreds if not thousands of people. As a general rule, personal injury cases and wrongful death cases are not good candidates for class actions because each person’s harm or loss is different. An MDL is generally the better way to go if you’ve had a serious injury or suffered the loss of a loved one. In an MDL, each person has their own attorney, they file their own case before the judge and jury that’s appropriate for that case, and they each get their own trial. Now, the reason it’s called an MDL or a multi-district litigation is that when these cases, sometimes hundreds or thousands of them, are all filed across the country, the courts require that they be consolidated before one judge, just for the pre-trial proceedings. That is just for the proceedings where the evidence is collected and documented. That saves the clients a lot of time and expense, but at the end of that process, the cases are sent back to be tried by that client’s lawyer in the courtroom that that client chose and for the client to receive their own individual verdict. They’re not bound by what happens in other cases that were filed in that MDL or multi district litigation. As a general rule, we at Roberts and Roberts recommend that when you have the option that you go with the multi district litigation or the individual case as opposed to a class action to be sure that you receive the individual attention and compensation that you deserve.

metadata.title: MSOs, Your Market, And Your Choice - PIMM 151
metadata.author: Optimize My Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
Episode Summary: 
In this episode of Personal Injury Marketing Minute, host Lindsey Busfield sits down with Tim McKey, CEO of Vista Consulting, to explore the evolving landscape of personal injury law firms through the lens of Managed Service Organizations (MSOs). Tim explains the structure and benefits of MSOs, highlighting how they separate non-legal operations from law firm entities, allowing for external investment and operational efficiency. The discussion delves into the financial and strategic advantages MSOs offer, such as attracting private equity and enhancing business acumen within law firms. Tim also addresses concerns about the potential downsides of MSOs, drawing parallels to the medical industry while emphasizing the importance of maintaining high-quality legal services. This episode is essential for law firm owners looking to understand new growth opportunities and competitive dynamics in the legal sector.

Key Timestamps:
00:00 – Introduction
00:12 – Meet Tim McKey of Vista Consulting
01:00 – Understanding MSOs in Law Firms
03:08 – Evolution of MSOs in Plaintiff Firms
05:02 – Financial and Operational Benefits of MSOs
07:43 – Private Equity Interest in Law Firms
09:06 – Growth Opportunities Through MSOs
11:00 – Addressing Concerns About MSOs
13:00 – Aligning Goals Between Lawyers and Investors
15:13 – Importance of Business Efficiency in Law Firms
17:19 – Navigating Competition in the Legal Market
19:22 – Awareness and Adaptation in Legal Practices
20:00 – Exploring MSOs and Consulting Services

About the Show: 
Personal Injury Marketing Minute is a podcast dedicated to exploring the latest trends and strategies in legal marketing, specifically tailored for personal injury law firms. Hosted by Lindsey Busfield, the show offers insights from industry experts on topics like growth strategy, business operations, and market dynamics. With a focus on clarity and actionable advice, the podcast aims to equip legal professionals with the tools they need to thrive in a competitive landscape. Whether you're a seasoned attorney or new to the field, Personal Injury Marketing Minute provides valuable knowledge to enhance your practice.

#PersonalInjury #LegalMarketing #LawFirmGrowth #MSO #VistaConsulting #TimMcKey #LindseyBusfield

metadata.title: What is a Mass Tort Lawsuit?
metadata.author: Dyer, Garofalo, Mann & Schultz
metadata.shortDescription:
Mass torts allow for more variability in the damages awarded to the plaintiffs than class actions but result in more suits. While only one suit need be filed in a class action, a mass tort typically consists of a large group of suits. Each plaintiff will have her own suit. 

Cases involving defective drugs and products are frequently handled as mass torts. While each plaintiff suffered harm from the same defective product or drug, the harm they suffered may be very different.

For example, a group of plaintiffs may claim they were all harmed by the same medication. Some of those plaintiffs may have suffered pain and discomfort. Others may have suffered so much pain that they couldn’t work. Others could have required hospitalization and racked up big medical bills.

They probably can’t be certified as a class — they all suffered different degrees of harm and had different sets of preexisting conditions. Each case will depend on the specific facts surrounding that plaintiff and that plaintiff’s use of the medication.

metadata.title: Funding the Fight: Inside Litigation Funding with Rocade Capital
metadata.author: The Heart of Law Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Adam Rosen knows litigation finance from both sides of the table.

Now Managing Director and Head of Underwriting at Rocade Capital, Adam began his career litigating mass tort cases at Ashcraft & Gerel. Today, he evaluates many of the same types of firms and cases he once worked alongside, giving him a unique perspective on what makes a law firm ready for outside capital.

In this episode of The Heart of Law, Mirena Umizaj Dumas sits down with Adam to talk about that transition and how his experience as a litigator shapes the way he approaches underwriting today.

They dig into Rocade Capital’s recent acquisition of Law Finance Group, bringing together two platforms that have deployed more than $2.3 billion, and discuss what lenders are really looking for when they evaluate a law firm. Adam explains why strong case-level data matters, where firms tend to fall short, and what separates a firm that is ready to raise capital from one that still has work to do.

The conversation also covers the growing political scrutiny around litigation finance, including proposed federal tax changes and North Carolina’s ban on third-party funding. Adam and Mirena also break down Management Services Organizations, including what they can solve for law firm owners and where firms may give up more control than they expect.

On a more personal note, Adam shares what it looks like to balance a demanding career with raising two young daughters and talks about his work with the Milestone Foundation, which provides emergency loans to injured plaintiffs while their cases are still pending.

Topics include:

• Adam’s move from mass tort litigation to underwriting
• The Rocade Capital and Law Finance Group acquisition
• What lenders look for before financing a law firm
• Why case-level data matters when raising capital
• The political and regulatory pressure surrounding litigation finance
• What an MSO can and cannot solve for law firm owners
• Balancing a demanding legal career with family life

Learn more about Adam Rosen:
https://www.rocadecapital.com

The Heart of Law is hosted by Mirena Umizaj Dumas, Founder and CEO of Mirena and Company, a litigation finance and law firm consulting firm serving plaintiff practices nationwide.

Subscribe for new episodes.

Listen on Spotify:
https://open.spotify.com/show/0eBF99x8OEZgC13keJ4DiX

Listen on Apple Podcasts:
https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/the-heart-of-law/id1558488701

Learn more about Mirena and Company:
https://mirenaandco.com

Podcast production by Bebo Hajec of EMH Group.Strategic Marketing. Without the Agency Overhead.https://www.emhgroup.co

metadata.author: Slarskey LLC
metadata.shortDescription: In this series from Slarskey LLC, Partner Evan Fried explores hot topics in the world of litigation funding. Today's episode features Evan's conversation with Benjamin F. Blum, Managing Director at Flexpoint Ford; and Joshua Meltzer, Managing Director & Head of IP Finance Group at Finitive. The group discusses the evolution of investors interested in the litigation finance space, the types of investment profiles available within litigation finance, and the different ways deals are structured - including single cases, portfolios, and the use of insurance. The group also explores the impact of recent rate hikes, how to create scale in litigation funding, and other market forces at play.

metadata.title: 2015 Fall Conference: Litigation Funding: Panel 3
metadata.author: NYU School of Law
metadata.shortDescription:
November 20, 2015
Sponsored by the Center on Civil Justice

This panel assessed the potential for litigation funding as a tool for collective actions by states and municipalities, as well as in private arbitrations after American Express v. Italian Colors.

Panelists:
Samuel Issacharoff, New York University School of Law (Moderator)
Brian Fitzpatrick, Vanderbilt University Law School
Catherine Piché, University of Montreal
Anthony Sebok, Cardozo School of Law
Thomas Coyle ’15, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen, and Katz

segments.text: - So, welcome back everybody.
Hope you all had a good lunch.
Our third panel is moderated by Sam Issacharoff,
here on my right.
Sam is one of the co-directors of the center
and he's also the Reiss Professor of Constitutional Law
here at NYU.
Sam, I promised, when everyone left for lunch
that the afternoon panels were gonna be
as spectacular as the ones in the morning.
So, you're on.
- Thank you.
I wanna start actually by taking a moment of privilege
to say something about the center
because I think that we can stand here quite proudly
after the morning session as being
a fascinating introduction
into the world of litigation finance,
at least for those of us who are not in that world.
This is a very unusual academic enterprise.
This was set up as essentially a joint venture
of plaintiffs and defense firms who decided to put up
a significant amount of money with a five-year commitment
and it has two unusual features
in terms of academic enterprises of this sort.
First, we are not naming anything after anyone.
So, this is not the you-pick school of laws.
Actually, for a certain price that is available.
If you need it, we can talk about it.
(audience laughs)
Here is our fourth co-director who just walked in,
Troy McKenzie, who just got fired
from the Department of Justice.
Is that why you're here?
- [Troy] I'm playing hooky.
- Playing hooky,
so Troy is one of the founding co-directors.
So, there's no honors given to anybody in particular
for the significant contributions we have received.
The other thing that's completely unusual about this
is that more than half of our board of directors
and the people who sustain this enterprise
had no prior institutional affiliation with NYU.
So, these are folks who gave of their time and their money
and they come to our board meetings
and they sustain our activities
despite the fact that this was not their institution.
This is simply a commitment that there needed to be a place
where we could have discussions like the one
we've been having and we will continue to be having.
So, this is a great achievement for us
as an institution and we're very proud
and very happy for the work of Peter and Linda
and for the support that we've had in this enterprise.
So, let me introduce this panel.
My first exposure to the world of entrepreneurial financing,
of litigation as a distinct area of legal enterprise
took place about five, six years ago,
the first time I was lecturing in Australia.
And I kept being introduced to this concept
of litigation finance that was increasingly
taking hold there and playing a very significant role
in shaping the kinds of cases that were viable
under the Australian system,
where there are not contingency fees,
there are uplifts, but there is fee-shifting
so that somebody had to immunize the lead plaintiff,
for example, in a securities class action.
And the world of litigation finance had taken hold there.
And now all of the sudden, you had financiers coming in
and essentially acquiring massive control rights
in the litigation and turning the original lawyers
who brought the case into hourly employees.
And it shifted all the conceptions of risk,
all the conceptions of how we want lawyers
to be running cases, and this was quite unlike
anything I had seen.
And one of the unfortunate problems of getting older
is that whenever you see something that's new, you react.
You say, well, that's bad.
Right?
Because that's not what I'm used to.
And that was my reaction.
Well, this is just wrong.
This is not the way we do it.
And then it made me think that there are three functions
that we assign to lawyers in the United States
and basically concentrate in the bar.
One is the selection of cases,
particularly on the plaintiff's side,
particularly in contingent cases,
but in all sorts of litigations,
we let the lawyers screen.
In fact, Rule eleven and other such responsibilities
require the lawyers to do the screening of the cases.
Then we do, we assign to the lawyers,
the power to prosecute and defend the cases.
Lawyers have a monopoly on the capacity to go to court
on behalf of a client, so that's a second function
that the lawyers perform.
And the third function that the lawyers perform
is that the lawyers and only the lawyers
can be the financiers, the outside financiers
with an equity stake in the outcome of the litigation.
So, the assumption that an American lawyer has,
going to Australia, is that those three functions
have to be integrated.
And to the extent that they're present in any given case,
in any given representation,
they have to be carried out by the same person,
the same institutional actor, the same group of lawyers.
The Australian response,
and it was fascinating to confront this,
was that each of these functions could be disaggregated
and that you can spin them off and that the market
could rearrange the rights and responsibilities
across these functions in a way that is,
perhaps, more efficient,
in a way that is, perhaps, more transparent,
in a way that is, perhaps, just plain different
than the way we do things like that in the United States.
And so, for me this was just completely eye-opening
and in several subsequent trips to Australia
or other bodies of lectures and so forth,
this has become a bigger and bigger part
of what I've been fascinated by.
And the first entrant into the field,
an outfit called IMF, was spectacularly successful
initially, partially because like any first mover,
they grabbed a lot of the low-lying fruit.
And so, they could do very well with relatively little risk
and my sense of going to Australia was that
the profits that the funders were making were out-sized.
Because there just wasn't enough competition
and it wasn't a deep enough capital bench.
And so, as I became more comfortable with this system,
my reaction was we need to get more of this is in,
not we need to restrict it in some way.
But actually this will be a much better functioning system.
There may be regulations that we have to put in
and all that, but this will be a better functioning system
when there's competition within it.
And what we see in the United States is the paradox is
as it comes here, we have a much deeper capital market,
so it is quite likely that we will develop
more competitive innovations than Australia,
which is a much smaller country,
even though we are a late arrival here.
And to say the obvious, the Australians then went
and colonized and they reverse-colonized England
and they took over Canada and so this has become
a dominant model and the Australians are big movers
in setting up litigation finance on the continent, also.
So that the experience that they have,
the several years headstart that they have
has become an entryway into a lot of other markets.
So, we should be paying attention in this country,
in particular, to foreign innovations,
which takes us to the panel for today.
So, this morning was basically about how we conceptualize
the relationship between capital and law
and how we try to figure out what rules apply from each
and which ones can colonize the other.
We're gonna go a little bit further this afternoon.
And this panel is about how we conceptualize the role
of capital investments in litigation
in ways that change the relationship of the actors
in the case, in ways that are designed to change
the relationship of the actors.
So, we have three papers.
And the first one is by Catherine Piche.
Catherine is a law professor at the University of Montreal
who specializes on matters of litigation, class actions,
big cases, and Catherine is also an LLM of this institution.
So, we're very proud of the institutional affiliation.
And Catherine is going to talk about a Quebecois innovation
in which public money is used to seed private litigation.
That is, public money is used to help finance
private class actions in areas of law
that the Province of Quebec finds to be under-serviced.
That's a radical conception for us,
using public funds for private litigants.
There is an article by Judith Resnik,
one of our graduates, also, who argues that the class action
is, in effect, a public subsidy
for certain kinds of litigation because it lowers
the transaction cost of creating the benefits and scale.
This is going one step further.
Following Catherine, we have Tony Sebok.
Tony is a professor at Cardozo.
Some of you heard him speak here on the floor this morning.
Tony is one of the real forces in examining the development
of litigation finance.
I know that he's not at NYU, but he's just down the street
at Cardozo and I know that when I started getting interested
in this area, it was his work as much as anybody's
that I turned to to help guide me through it.
And Tony's paper does the flip of Catherine's.
So, Catherine is how public money
can seed private litigation
and Tony's is on how private money can help seed
public litigation.
And so, if you think about parens patriae suits
as being a more natural form of aggregation
that doesn't have the perversity of plaintiff's lawyers
running the show, well the problem is
that states are underfunded
versus big institutional defendants.
And so, maybe private resources can help
to redress that balance.
The third paper is by Tom Coyle
and this is a point of particular privilege.
Tom was a star student in a course on complex litigation
I taught a couple years ago with Arthur Miller.
Tom is a recent graduate of this law school,
just last year, works at part-time.
Only about, what 300 hours a week?
At this small firm called Wachtell Lipton or something.
Lipton may have something to do with this room, I think.
And Tom wrote his third-year paper for Troy McKenzie
and then when Troy left, I took over the supervision of it
and I read this paper and I thought, this is just amazing.
This is a complete breath of fresh air.
This is the idea that sometimes private agglomeration
of claims can be superior to public.
And that is when we get to the question of Italian Colors
and the prohibition on class actions,
maybe the market can be there instead of the public sector
in terms of creating the economies of scale
necessary to prosecute some of these cases.
So, it's very exciting for me to be able to have Tom here
and unheard of that he got a day off from Wachtell
to be here with us.
And then the commentator will be Brian Fitzpatrick.
Brian is a professor of law at Vanderbilt.
Brian has an institutional affiliation with us,
he was an Olin Fellow here for a year
before he went into full-time teaching
and Brian is as shrewd a commentator
on the structures of legal representation as you will find
and it's always a pleasure.
He was here at our conference last year,
so it's a pleasure to have him here.
So with that, Catherine why don't you begin?
- Well, thank you.
Good afternoon.
I'm delighted to be here today and I thank the organizers
for having invited me.
It's quite a thrill to be talking about litigation finance,
a topic that is, from my perspective as a Canadian,
largely misunderstood, largely under-discussed
and so I find this really, really great.
So, I'm a professor at the University of Montreal
as Professor Issacharoff mentioned.
And so, Montreal is in the Province of Quebec
and as most of you, if not all of you know
it is a civil law system with very strong
common law influences and a mixed procedural law system.
So, importantly it also has a class action
and in fact, Quebec was the first Canadian province to enact
class action legislation
based on Federal Rule 23 back in 1979.
And it was at a very social time, so you will understand
and you will feel and you will see the social flair
and the social culture piercing from this,
well perhaps the model itself,
the model I'll be discussing today.
So, part of the uniqueness of the system
was that it provided for a Quebec Ministry of Justice fund,
an assistance fund, for class action litigation.
So that is principally what I'll be talking about
in the little minutes, the few minutes I have.
I do wanna say that third-party funding exists in Canada
and is prevalent.
It is a largely underground and secretive practice,
which means that we don't have all the information.
What we know is that all the big players are there,
the Lexfund and Therium
and all these big financiers are there.
What we know, as well, is that the courts
are quite receptive to these agreements.
They have approved a few financing agreements.
What is important to know is that most of Canada
has adverse costs that are quite astronomical
and so there's a real problem there
in terms of access to justice.
So, the larger cases are funded through third-party funding
and plaintiff firms extending the monies.
So that's for kind of the rest of Canada
and in terms of Quebec, we don't have adverse costs.
We have capped adverse costs,
so that's not really the issue.
The issue is the attorney fees, obviously,
and the expert costs.
So, what I will be talking about is,
and what I've talked about in my essay
is this public fund, assistance fund.
It's the (speaking in foreign language),
I'll call it the fund for our purposes
and my argument is that it is an effective,
obviously financing mechanism, but it also has
this oversight function that should be underscored
and that should be made clearer.
And I think this oversight function is beneficial
to the whole system in that it contributes
to class actions in Quebec, well to the (mumbles) system
that we have, to this positively active system that we have,
a system that is often correctorizes a class action haven.
So, in short, and that is a more social perspective,
but I do think that successful cases
should help finance unsuccessful ones
and I do think current cases
should help finance future ones.
And on top of that, I believe that assistance
should be provided to legitimate and promising cases
from entities that have the proper motivations.
And I do think our Quebec fund has these proper motivations.
So, this fund has a two-parted objective.
The first one, obviously, is to finance class litigation.
Essentially in terms of bringing those actions in
for in assistance and throughout the litigation
you can keep applying for further financing
all the way through appeals.
The second function is an informational objective
and essentially it means disseminating information
about class actions, which also is very important in my view
in terms of transparency notably.
So, the fund significantly in terms of statistics
has made close to 800 decisions in the last 10 years
and has funded one-third of those applications.
So, on a yearly basis, the market is obviously much smaller,
but we have about 500 active cases per year
and the fund finances one-third of these cases.
The fund also has a big surplus of close to 14 million,
which could help finance more and more cases.
The fund may, when the fund grants assistance,
it will pay expert fees outright and it will help
with attorney fees, as well.
Now a big caveat there, the attorney fees
are not market rate, we're talking about $100 an hour
for senior lawyers,
which is quite insignificant, but it's still there
and the idea is there.
And so, they pay for legal fees, costs,
and this without charging interest fees.
Also and importantly, you will only reimburse
in case of success, which means that the fund essentially
assumes the risk of litigation.
So, it is well-capitalized with yearly provincial subsidies
and warranties and importantly,
it is almost entirely self-sustainable
through these subsidies
that are essentially a couple hundred thousand dollars
a year, but importantly it does recuperate a percentage
of all recoveries in all cases, whether funded or not.
Which means that all cases help contribute to the fund
and all current cases help contribute to future cases
and to the bringing of future cases.
So, essentially the argument here is that
the fund should work obviously as an oversight mechanism.
It already does de facto, but I think its role
should be redefined and a specific notion in the law
should be placed there to have a much clearer role.
Of course, one argument is that it brings transparency
to the system with additional information, statistics,
data, claims rates data comes, I think,
better law and better cases.
The screening mechanism gives, of course, incentives to
even if implicitly bring better cases forward.
It's kind of a natural tendency to bring worthwhile cases
as when the case is funded, there's a note in the docket
and there's a signal sent that this case may just be
more worthwhile.
Also, an incentive to be continuously competent
in terms of council, as you can keep applying
for further assistance throughout the litigation.
So, that's significant, as well.
It would bring more legitimacy to the fund
in terms of an actor of change that the fund has intervened
and made representations in a number of cases
in order, notably, to have this percentage regulation

videos.full_text: - So, welcome back everybody. Hope you all had a good lunch. Our third panel is moderated by Sam Issacharoff, here on my right. Sam is one of the co-directors of the center and he's also the Reiss Professor of Constitutional Law here at NYU. Sam, I promised, when everyone left for lunch that the afternoon panels were gonna be as spectacular as the ones in the morning. So, you're on. - Thank you. I wanna start actually by taking a moment of privilege to say something about the center because I think that we can stand here quite proudly after the morning session as being a fascinating introduction into the world of litigation finance, at least for those of us who are not in that world. This is a very unusual academic enterprise. This was set up as essentially a joint venture of plaintiffs and defense firms who decided to put up a significant amount of money with a five-year commitment and it has two unusual features in terms of academic enterprises of this sort. First, we are not naming anything after anyone. So, this is not the you-pick school of laws. Actually, for a certain price that is available. If you need it, we can talk about it. (audience laughs) Here is our fourth co-director who just walked in, Troy McKenzie, who just got fired from the Department of Justice. Is that why you're here? - [Troy] I'm playing hooky. - Playing hooky, so Troy is one of the founding co-directors. So, there's no honors given to anybody in particular for the significant contributions we have received. The other thing that's completely unusual about this is that more than half of our board of directors and the people who sustain this enterprise had no prior institutional affiliation with NYU. So, these are folks who gave of their time and their money and they come to our board meetings and they sustain our activities despite the fact that this was not their institution. This is simply a commitment that there needed to be a place where we could have discussions like the one we've been having and we will continue to be having. So, this is a great achievement for us as an institution and we're very proud and very happy for the work of Peter and Linda and for the support that we've had in this enterprise. So, let me introduce this panel. My first exposure to the world of entrepreneurial financing, of litigation as a distinct area of legal enterprise took place about five, six years ago, the first time I was lecturing in Australia. And I kept being introduced to this concept of litigation finance that was increasingly taking hold there and playing a very significant role in shaping the kinds of cases that were viable under the Australian system, where there are not contingency fees, there are uplifts, but there is fee-shifting so that somebody had to immunize the lead plaintiff, for example, in a securities class action. And the world of litigation finance had taken hold there. And now all of the sudden, you had financiers coming in and essentially acquiring massive control rights in the litigation and turning the original lawyers who brought the case into hourly employees. And it shifted all the conceptions of risk, all the conceptions of how we want lawyers to be running cases, and this was quite unlike anything I had seen. And one of the unfortunate problems of getting older is that whenever you see something that's new, you react. You say, well, that's bad. Right? Because that's not what I'm used to. And that was my reaction. Well, this is just wrong. This is not the way we do it. And then it made me think that there are three functions that we assign to lawyers in the United States and basically concentrate in the bar. metadata.title: The Private Equity Shift: Turning Your Law Firm From a Founder-Led Practice to a Scalable Asset
metadata.author: Jon and Marc
metadata.shortDescription:
A group of private equity and legal transactions experts joins the show to discuss the influx of outside institutional capital into the plaintiff law ecosystem. Boris Ziser, Benji Grossman, Josh Porte, Tom Lenfestey, and Juan Acevedo break down how law firms are evaluated, structured, and scaled for potential exit.

The conversation covers the difference between Management Services Organizations (MSOs) and Alternative Business Structures (ABSs), detailing why investors prefer service models over regulated law entities. The panel also shares why personal injury practices offer more predictable cash flows for private equity compared to mass torts dockets.

Furthermore, the discussion addresses the emotional and operational challenges founders face when trying to sell their practices. True firm value requires moving away from a founder-centric model toward institutionalized systems, cloud-based case management, and white-label branding. Without these adjustments, transition risk lowers firm valuations.

Finally, the panel addresses the future of the legal marketplace. Artificial intelligence and private equity backing are accelerating a massive consolidation. This changes how trial lawyers operate, as rising case acquisition costs make it harder for traditional independent firms to compete.

39:00 - AI Disruption and the Future of Capitalized Firms

metadata.title: How mass torts are won, from hormone therapy to Roundup | Tobi Millrood
metadata.author: Drop In, A Parambil Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Tobi Millrood has spent more than 25 years in pharmaceutical, medical device, and complex injury litigation. He was the first lawyer in the country to file a hormone therapy lawsuit and helped lead that litigation for a decade. He later served as president of the American Association for Justice, and today chairs the Mass Tort Department at Kline & Specter. 

In this conversation, Tobi and Sara get into how mass tort cases actually work — why proving causation requires both the broad science linking a product to a type of harm and the specific proof that it harmed this person — what it takes to prepare a trial team for a case that can take months to get ready for, how jury psychology shapes which narratives land and which don't, and where he sees the system heading next, including how AI tools are starting to help consumers evaluate whether a law firm is actually equipped to take their case to trial.

This is the second episode of Drop In, a podcast from Parambil, the AI platform built for complex litigation. Each episode features conversations with the attorneys, experts, and innovators shaping the biggest cases in the country. Follow now so you don't miss what's next.

metadata.title: The Hidden Process That Delays Every Mass Tort Payout
metadata.author: Jon and Marc
metadata.shortDescription:
A mass tort settlement hits the news and clients start asking about payouts, but most law firms do not have a clear answer.

This week’s Jon & Marc podcast hosts Gary Goldberg, who brings a perspective that most law firms never see. As Executive Vice President of Mass Torts at Archer, he operates on the back end of settlement administration, lien resolution, and fund distribution. His role requires coordination between law firms, courts, and third parties to move cases from settlement to payment.

A settlement headline creates immediate expectations from clients, even though the agreement is often not finalized. The time between announcement and payout is filled with legal, administrative, and financial steps that most claimants do not understand.

Allocation models must be finalized, claimant data must be validated, and settlement matrices must be applied across thousands of cases. At the same time, lien resolution begins across Medicare, Medicaid, private insurers, and other third parties. 

Probate issues, bankruptcies, and missing documentation can further delay individual payouts. These layers create a process that can take months before any money is distributed and even longer before final payments are completed.

Law firms that do not understand this process often struggle with client communication, which leads to frustration, negative reviews, and internal operational strain. 

Watch the full episode the learn how the firms that perform best in mass torts are disciplined in data management, proactive in communication, and aligned with partners who understand how cases are proven and processed through the full lifecycle.

#MassTorts #PersonalInjuryLawyer #LegalMarketing #LawFirmGrowth #CaseAcquisition #PlaintiffAttorney #LegalTechnology #MassTortLaw #JonandMarc

About The Jon & Marc Podcast

The Jon & Marc Podcast is for lawyers who care about growth and the bottom line. Jon and Marc interview leaders in plaintiff law to break down how major cases are built, how firms scale, and how strategy plays out behind the scenes. If you want to understand how the biggest players in the space think and operate, you’re in the right place.
New episodes every week.

Chapters
00:00 - Intro
00:32 - Meet Gary Goldberg and Archer’s role in mass torts
01:50 - Why client expectations become a major issue
02:36 - Why mass tort timelines are difficult to predict
04:49 - How claimants misunderstand verdict headlines
06:24 - Archer’s role as a neutral administrator
09:10 - The three types of mass tort settlements
11:42 - What happens after a global settlement is reached
12:08 - Why settlement announcements are not final
13:57 - How settlement matrices determine payouts
14:00 - Why lien resolution slows everything down
16:16 - The scale problem with thousands of claimants
18:22 - Fraud, vetting, and data verification in mass torts
19:53 - Realistic payout timelines for claimants
22:40 - How law firms can speed up the process
24:52 - The reputation risk of mishandling mass tort clients
27:27 - Why claimants feel disconnected from firms
30:11 - The shift toward new types of mass tort cases
34:55 - Final thoughts on improving payout speed

metadata.title: Leading the Way in Mass Tort Litigation Management

metadata.shortDescription:
Uncover the secrets of managing mass tort litigation with Bernadette Catalana, Partner at MG+M The Law Firm.

With a focus on toxic exposure cases and Child Victims’ Act claims Bernadette is an authority in mass tort litigation. As National Coordinating Counsel for a Fortune 100 client, she leads strategic defense efforts across the US. Recognized as a Super Lawyer for six years, Bernadette also mentors young lawyers, nurturing their growth. 
Discover her strategies for efficiently managing high-volume cases and adapting to legal marketing trends. Tune in now!

Key Takeaways:
00:00 - Introduction 
1:00 - Journey as a mass tort litigation superlawyer
3:14 - The critical challenges in managing mass tort litigation 
6:11 - Implementing a robust case management system using tools
9:15- Continuing to evolve as technology evolves
15:27 - How to intentionally attract business
18:53 - What it means to market and to build a brand 
22:05 - Final thoughts: the power of authenticity
