Pull back the curtain, share more about how you look at a project, how you look at a tort and really just kind of what your thought process is so other people can learn how to underwrite and evaluate an investment they might make in the future. So, when you're looking at things, there's a lot of different topics, but let's just break it down one by one. The first one I'm thinking about, and let me know what your thoughts are, is the legal viability. You know, how do you look at the legal viability of a project? >> I I think right off the top, you made a great point. Each of these mass tors are different, right? We're going to have different defendants. We're going to have different products. We're going to have different injuries. So each one does need to be examined on a case-bycase basis, but the first thing we look at anytime a potential new mass comes across our desk is is this case going to be viable? So if you're in a traditional PI practice and you're familiar with car accident or slip and fall cases, you got to look at can we win this case, right? Is this case going to get kicked out early on on a motion to dismiss? So some of the things that we're going to be looking at is going to be the different causes of actions that we're going to bring and whether under the law that we're going to be able to win on that. We also look at right the injuries that that are caused by the plif. Um we're also going to be looking at um whether there could be potential statute of limitation issues. Could there be potential statute of repose issues? Um other issues that we need to look at is could there be uh an arbitration agreement that's going to govern this claim. So really the first step is when we take a 30,000 foot view is to say okay can we proceed with this case and can we ultimately get past that initial hurdle and beat back that initial argument whether it's there's an arbitration provision or this case is preempted. And so before we even get into the evidence in the case um and whether we can win on that, that's the first thing everybody needs to evaluate. And those five points are what I kind of look at right off the top before I think it's time to get involved and invest and try to help these clients. >> And there's a lot of nuances to that, right? So, like a lot of times it's usually best to ask ask someone like you, you know, what happens if the statute is different in different states? What happens if uh it's a 510k or you know what what if there's a preeemption conversation happening? A lot of times you guys can figure out ways to uh to navigate that within the legal space. And so someone might say, "Hey, look, there's a discovery rule or 510K stay away or 510K we can get into this." So is it better to kind of ask you in those situations if someone's on the fence about whether or not a claimant might qualify? >> Yeah, definitely. We're around to kind of answer questions on those, but th those are two huge issues. And um those are those are big things in the mass tour world, right? the discovery rule that that applies in more than 40 states have some form of the discovery rule where it's you weren't uh the statute doesn't begin to run from the date you were injured. It's when you knew or should have known you were injured. So in these cases, if there's fraudulent conduct on the part of the defendant where they're concealing this wrongful act, somebody could be injured. They could be diagnosed with ovarian cancer or non-hodkkins lymphoma but they have no knowledge. Um other cases are are harder like you're talking about the preeemption right that makes the drug cases harder than a than a traditional product case and then the approval process that it goes through with the FDA uh and the type of device and classification is some of them automatically are kicked out. So just dealing with these type of cases over the years, those are definitely um some things you have to look at in each case and each case is going to be different. But the majority of the cases I think we can get by on some sort of discovery rule absent a recall that makes it a little bit more challenging. But those are two factors you need to look at in every case. Um we do that every time. So if you guys have questions evaluating that, you know, reach out to myself or Michael. But we're happy to point you in the right direction. >> Yeah. And then one more one more question on that that I get a lot that I actually got right before this podcast was, you know, I'm not licensed to practice in the state that the MDL is consolidated into. Does that prohibit me from participating? >> Yeah, good question. We we we see that a lot. So MDL's that stands for multi-dist litigation. So it's in federal court. Typically, you're admitted to practice in a specific federal court. Um but usually when there's MDLs formed and consolidate it uh the judge usually waves that requirement that you would have had been omitted in that specific court. So that then allows you to do the direct filing filing the complaints. If you have to do some sort of motion, you're allowed to do that. So that's not an automatic disqualification. Uh sometimes you have to take a course on the local rules in that specific court but not a hurdle people need to really be worried about at all in terms of the MDLs. >> Love that. Thank you so much man. Uh it kind of goes right into the next part of the process which is you know the science right? I mean that this is this is a difficult part because a lot of lawyers they didn't they didn't go to med school they didn't study biology they didn't study you know human physiology and different effects so how do you distill this down into a very easy to understand process like what is you what is your approach when you look at a project to go okay I I like this science I don't like this science like what are you looking for >> yeah so each one of these cases is going to come down to the experts it's mass tors is really means battle of the experts. So, cuz we're involving uh claims that involve products, we're going to need to put forward our experts to pretty much say how these products were defective. Um, we'll talk about failure to warn in our claims as well. But you really need strong experts in these cases and the majority of the cases are going to go through a Dolbert examination. So after you get past that legal viability and you say, "Hey, we can win on statute of limitations and preeemption, the next thing we need to win on is going to be the Dolber ruling. Is our expert going to be permitted to testify in front of the jury?" So you're going to need to look at what was the reason and the triggering event in the litigation. So was there some sort of recall? Um, if there's an FDA recall, that usually signals there's a serious problem and and those cases seem to be stronger. But if it's just a a study that came out, for me personally, maybe one study wouldn't be enough for me to bet the firm and get involved in a case. Typically when we see a study, we see um a couple studies follow that in in the years following and then throughout the life cycle of the case uh more studies come out or there'll even be summaries of cohorts of different studies that summarize all the different ones. So for me typically one study usually isn't enough for me to end up spending a significant amount of time and resources in a case. But you'll usually hear, "Hey, we're waiting on this next study to come out." Another thing that in terms of science can help is when you see the the label change, right? So, we could have the FDA recall. A lot of these are products. They have a blackbox warning. When that changes or the label gets updated, that's another strong indication that the science is going to be on our side. But when you're just relying on these, you know, studies, my rule of thumb is one usually isn't enough. But you'll see some excitement when a new study comes out. Typically, I wait for that second or third one to come out to really validate it. And what's important is to look at that study yourself. Get a copy of it and read it and see how many people were involved in that study. Was it under 100? That's going to be really tough to rely on that. But when you get the number of patients that were studied, 10,000, a couple thousand plus, that makes it stronger evidence. So that's a huge issue and the balance of the case always hangs on whether or not our experts going to be able to come in. So it's going to be uh a little bit risky, a little bit stressful until we get past that Dalbert ruling because the defendants bring them in every single case. >> That's interesting. I mean, the Dobert ruling, it's also called Daware from some areas of the United States. Uh, we Let's dive into that in one second. I actually wanted to mention to somebody for fun in case people wanted to participate before I mention it, but one of the biggest first blackbox warnings was actually cigarettes. That was that was one of the most massive changes in our in our legal sphere. So, I'm actually going to take it back for a moment because you mentioned a few different really key pieces in a litigation, right? The Dobert uh you mentioned uh some different processes throughout a litigation. So, maybe you can walk us through just for a moment of what are different phases like what's an emerging litigation? At what point does it become more of a litigation stage and at what point is it more of a settlement stage? like where does live in that process and maybe just for a moment like what is dobert what is that causation kind of conversation that correlation conversation? >> Yeah. So so Dolbert is just basically the legal standard you have to satisfy uh in order to get the expert admitted to be able to testify at trial. And so what happens is the judge they they serve as the gatekeeper. And what they do is they evaluate the opinion of the expert and one of the factors they look at is is this scientific or uh specific knowledge outside the usual scope of what the juror has and then they look at you know what was the methodology and the reasoning that the expert uh utilized in reaching their opinion. The judge isn't supposed to make the ruling based upon the opinion of the expert, but more so whether or not a similar expert presented with a similar question would evaluate and look at a case in the same way. So, what studies did they use? Did they look at all 50 studies or did they cherrypick two or three studies? What evidence did they use? What specific research or testing did they do on their own? Did they look at a very small cohort of patients and limit all of their opinion to that or is it really looking at the totality of the evidence presented through the case and the studies through the depositions the hot documents to reach the opinion? So the judge does an evaluation on each expert and each opinion and there there's always a lot of briefing involved with that and then there's hearings because in mass torchs we typically have a couple experts on each issues and so we'll have a Dalbert hearing that will expand two or three days and then usually we get a ruling from the judge 60 or 90 days but a Dolbert uh argument that usually comes towards the end of a case life cycle. So I would say that's about 2/3 to 3/4 of the way done. And once we get past that Dolbert hearing, that means that we're headed to trial, right? And so the judge says we have the scientific support to show that generally speaking, this product can cause this injury we're claiming. Generally speaking, the judge has ruled that Roundup uh could cause, you know, non-hodkkins lymphoma based upon our expert testimony and opinion. Whether you can prove that in a case- specific causation, so did this plif a use Roundup and get cancer, that's the next step. But this Dolbert ruling would apply to all of the cases in the MDL and it comes usually far down that. And once we win the Dolbert, a lot of excitement builds in the case. It seems like we're going to get towards trial and hopefully a settlement. >> So now you mentioned those trials. Are these the bellweather trials? And maybe like just take a moment and just walk us through, you know, what is what is the process of a bellweather trial? Like is is it the end all beall? Is it a good indication of where a a horizon is going to go? you know, maybe just take a moment on what those trials look like and what they're really what their purpose is. >> Yeah, a bellweather trial is in essence a test case. So, in mass tors there could be thousands or tens of thousands of cases and it's impossible for the parties and the court to utilize resources to have every single case worked up for a trial ready case. So instead what we do is we go through this bellweather process where the idea is to take representative cases of the entire inventory which has the facts, the science and the issue that applies to every case. Get those cases worked up like you did in a oneoff trial case and then get before the trial judge. Get in front of the jury, have the jury speak, and then they'll give their opinion on the value of the case, which facts they believed, which ones they didn't, and you get a feel for how strong the cases are. But how the process usually works is towards the beginning of the case, maybe 3 to 6 months in, you agree upon a bellweather process. And what we've seen now is there'll be some cases selected by the defendants that they think are representative of the inventory, which maybe the plaintiffs believe are a little bit weaker cases. And then the plaintiffs will pick a group of cases as well that they think are representative, which I'm sure the defendants say the same thing that we're cherry-picking the stronger cases. And then a lot of times now we have the judges coming in and they're selecting random cases. So neither side gets the opportunity and then those cases get worked up like you would and we'll do fact specific discovery. We'll do depositions of the plaintiffs of their spouses, of the treating physicians, and then we even move on to the expert case specific causation in each one of those cases. And along those stages, we're kind of chopping the inventory down from initial batch of 50 to 30 to 10 trial ready cases. And then it's kind of flip of a coin. Which case goes first for trial? And then the idea is you get a verdict. If that doesn't lead to a larger settlement, the next case is worked up and ready for the second Bellweather trial. >> So that's very important, right? So this is this is a situation that if you're just getting involved in mass tors, this is kind of why you want either a mentor or someone with you in the process because if you have someone uh a person that's hired you for representation or they're trying to hire you for representation, criteria and intake are so important at that level because if you take on a case and you file that case and it was not really a it's it's it's not really a strong matter that could potentially be picked out by the defense. And while you had all good intentions and there might still be reasons you want to do that, uh if it's not a good case and it's not a strong science and everything's not together, you could potentially have this trial go up there to the bellweather as an example of what all of these individual cases look like and all of a sudden you have you have a um you know a poor situation for the pliff bar. And so it's really important to run these these uh these these filed cases by someone like Joe uh you know just so that they can go hey look this kind of this kind of fits the mold for what we're looking for in the right kind of criteria and what a good example case looks like. Um maybe go into plan numerosity for a moment. I know that's a it's kind of an interesting term and it's an area that you know in marketing is really important because it's really how many people are impacted right so in these mass tors they're consolidated under 1407 right the JPML is consolidating them because they're like hey there's a lot of cases that while brought as individual cases they all kind of fit a similar pattern a similar injury profile they have unique stories and so they're all going to be represented differently but they have a unique injury profile. So, how important is it to have or what are the impacts uh of having a large amount of people who were potentially uh impacted? It's called an adverse event a lot of times in this in this industry and you know developed the cancer or had a broken medical device or whatever the signature injury is. How important is it to have a a large volume or what what does what does it mean when people have when a lot of people have that injury versus not a lot to you? >> Yeah. So it's a really important factor and like you mentioned one of the factors that the JPML the judicial panel multi-dist litigation considers when whether or not they're going to form and consolidate these cases into an MDL is numerosity. Usually before the panel we need to see more than 25 cases to get an MDL formed. Um typically 25 cases I wouldn't consider that a mass tort. But when I'm looking at these cases is uh you really want to see the the numerity. So you want to get a feel for what's the total number of potential plaintiffs that are out there, right? So how many people were um implanted with this medical device? You can pull that data and get that. How many people were prescribed this medication? You can get that information. Um how many people are diagnosed with a certain type of cancer each year? You can get that information and then from there you need to see right how many of these potential plaintiffs were exposed to this product and had the the negative kind of impact. But a huge factor and what you really need to remember is even the people with the injury and even the people with the potential claims, 100% of them don't come forward. I've typically seen that the number is maybe down to single digits, only 8 to 10% of the people that do have viable claims end up coming forward. So, if you want to get to uh, you know, a mass tort that's going to have 10,000 plus people, you're going to need a 100,000 people that have this injury caused by the product. So, if you're dealing with a product that was only prescribed for a short window or a product that was only implanted in a small number of people, it it's probably from my side, you know, not a case that's going to have that numerosity in there to to get, you know, a lot of excitement and a case to really invest your time and resources uh to best serve your firm and also your clients. >> Yeah. Yeah. and and and from a marketing perspective, right? And this is a lot of these factors that we're going to be talking about, you know, really kind of culminate into what a what an acquisition of a of a of a viable claimant might look like. And so when someone has when when you're looking at a project and they don't have a lot of individuals who are harmed, it's going to be very difficult to acquire those people because you have to raise awareness. A lot of your marketing campaigns are raising awareness as Joe was saying and so you have a situation where if only 8 to 10% of people are actually going to move forward on average right you you can have more or less in different situations then you really should factor that into whether or not uh you wanted to get into that uh that that tort. Now before we go back into the stage of litigation, I you know two more factors really curious about one of them is the actual defendant right so how do you look at a defendant at a potential defendant you know uh we have to we have to go to them and a lot of times you can't make change right you can't get a a warning on a label you can't get a product removed unless you have a financial impact negatively to that defendant And that's also going to be the way you get your claimants paid. So, how do you look at a defendant uh in that aspect? >> Yeah, that's a a key point, right? Is the the viability of this defendant, right? Is this a defendant that potentially could be facing hundreds of millions or billions of dollars of liabilities and are they going to be able to really survive this? So mass torch really evolved over the last couple years, even the last decade I would say. And a lot of these cases now have become bet the company cases like these companies are facing potential extinction due to the threat of the injuries that were caused by their defective and dangerous products. It's not because we're doing anything wrong. It's they put this dangerous product out there and now they're being held to a point. So, we definitely look at, you know, the market share, the market cap of these different defendants. We look at other litigations they're involved in. We look at um whether or not we have the proper defendant based here in the US or if they're going to be really a foreignbased defendant. So, we have the HEG convention and we can work with that. But really trying to hold that parent company accountable if all of their assets are are held abroad. That's going to make it much more challenging. And then we also look at it. What's the history of this defendant in terms of defending these mass tour cases? We we've come across unfortunately some of the same players time and time again. So we know their playbook. Are they going to be fighting us tooth and nail and extending and dragging out this case for a decade plus or are we going to have some reasonable attorneys on the other side? One big factor that goes into that is going to be bringing about finality of the litigation. So, from the defendant's perspective, if they're still selling the product, if it's still on the market, if it's one of their biggest sellers, that's going to be a lot bigger fight and a lot longer fight because they're still making money off of that product. Whereas, if the product's been withdrawn from the market or recalled, we might have a little bit of a sense that the defendant could be a little bit more reasonable because they're still not depending on it for resources. So, we also look at, you know, where are the defendants home, right? What what state are they in? What type of laws are going to be um applied potentially to these different claims? Are they in a really consumerfriendly state or are they going to be in a really um business uh friendly state? Those are all factors that you have to look at with the defendants. And even if you satisfy some of the earlier factors that we're looking at, right? Even if you have the legal viability, you have the science on your side, uh if you look at the defendant itself and it's not going to be standing and it's not going to be able to withstand this litigation, it might not be the right one to get involved with. >> So, you just touched on a really important part and I'm so glad you did. The venue. So, how is a venue, if you want to talk to me about that actually, how is a venue selected? And then how important is it to you? Where the venue is, who the judges are, what about the venue is important. >> The the venue is huge, right? So, the venue is going to allow us to have different judges and depending upon the state, depending upon the court, uh that's going to shape the rulings. Of course, we can right appeal them up and go to higher court, but that's more time, that's more expenses, that's delaying justice for the client. So, the venue where the court is is going to be huge. So, typically in the JPML, when we file the petition for consolidation, we recommend and suggest a court where we want the case to be sent to. And then the defendants, they usually oppose that and are suggesting another court. So, um maybe some states that have less favorable laws potentially to plaintiffs like New York. Um that's maybe where the defendants want to go. And you'll see a lot of times um good consumer law states that I would say potentially California. We'll we'll try to get the MDLs out there. Um so having the right venue is huge. And then also in addition to the the federal level, the MDLs, we also have state court levels. So there there's an option to have these litigations in state court. Obviously over history, everybody knows that federal court is more favorable and friendly to the defendants, to the corporations, to the ones with the money. So when you go into state court, they can try to re uh remove the case up to federal court. if if they're able to do that, they will. But sometimes we're able to get the cases in some state courts across the country that do these consolidated actions like New Jersey or Philadelphia or California or Missouri. Um, but most of the time the mass tors are venued in federal court and then it's just going to come down to that judge. So that's a huge issue. Um, you want to consider that. You won't know that right up front when the litigation's getting started, but as time goes on, you you'll see who the judge is and get a sense for some of the rulings. And we even see the same judges time and time again. So, we we know from experience what issues, you know, maybe we'll be successful on or some other points we're really going to have to dig deep into the discovery to survive. >> Amazing. Amazing. So, we have a situation right now, right? So you you you went over legal viability, science, the plaintiff numerosity, the venue, the defendant, and just as importantly, you went over the stage of litigation. Now, here is here is the uh the money at the money question, right? When you're looking at when you are going to actually get involved, do you have a preference or are you weighing all of these kind of equally? Like are you getting in early assuming the science is going to be there based on what you've evaluated? Are you getting in kind of later stage after dobert or are you getting in late stage when the bell weathers are already happening and right before some sort of potential global resolution or is that not the right way of thinking about it? Is it is it kind of fluid? >> That that is the right way to think about it. So it it really comes down to your own risk tolerance. Um it's it's like a a stock price, right? In the beginning that the stock it's going to be cheaper, right? But then when it's been around for a year, it's going to go up in price. It's going to go up once we survive that initial motion to dismiss. Then once we get into the discovery and we learn all these crazy facts or how they knew about this problem or issue for years or decades, then the case builds stronger and and it's going to be more likely that you get a successful outcome for your client. And then the further along you go um through Dolbert to trial is is when the cases are going to get more expensive to acquire. So a lot of mass tour firms like myself, we're the ones that are really getting in at the onset, right? When you hear about the recall, when you hear about that initial study coming out, sometimes we even have consumers call us, right? Like sometimes we learn about uh complaints from these clients directly even before we're investigating a certain case. Um, and dependent upon that and the other factors we talk about, a lot of firms do get involved real early and there's an opportunity to service a lot of clients. You can um have a bigger impact that way, but some firms might be less uh tolerant to that risk because a lot could go wrong up front and a lot less could go wrong when you're two or three years into the case and it's really already built up. 100% 100%. And so I'm really excited about this next kind of step to what you and I have cooking for something. It's it's going to be a conversation where people can kind of come in with you on an investment that you're really excited about. If you can tease I'm not sure if you're willing to tease on this, you know, podcast or not. You what are what are just, you know, your top one or two projects right now? Not to put down any other tort that's out there, but what are you really looking at in the next, you know, one to two months? >> Yeah. So, I I think what we're trying to do here is really just help as many people as possible. So, the more we're able to share our knowledge and our experience, um it will allow more law firms to get involved, which ultimately helps more clients get justice. And that's really what we're about. But right now there there's a lot of projects going on. Typically my firm's involved with you know 8 to 12 cases at a time. But right now two of the cases I I think that have a lot of excitement a lot of momentum building are the social media addiction cases. We have a trial going on the first trial out in California right now. It's the trial of the year. Everybody's talking about it. Whether you're in the legal community or not. This is a huge issue for everybody to really help our children and make a difference. And then the other case that I really like and I'm excited about right now is this hair relaxer, the chemical hair relaxer causing these certain type of cancers. So those that case is really mature along. We we already have more than 10,000 cases which is a a big number but there's more people out there as these products has been on the market for you know decades. So, those are two cases that I'm really excited about. You know, happy to share a little bit more with the people about what I've seen, what we've learned over the years, and they're not super risky. Um, I didn't just get an FDA alert about them today. They're more mature. So, getting in towards that tail end a little bit of the litigation. >> It's amazing. It's amazing. And so the end of this month uh we're going to have a webinar where we jump into those two tors and deep dive. But you don't have to wait till end of the month. Uh there's actually going to be a conversation if you're down for it next week where we can actually, you know, use some of this methodology and you can tell us why these are these are projects that you're really interested in. Um mostly because we can help a whole lot of people, right? And it's an area where you feel very confident that all the different factors of underwriting are aligned and it's going to be a a a place where a firm can be successful. and working through you, you can remove some of that barrier of entry and that, you know, mystical uh scariness that comes with jumping into a mass torp because you can actually help educate someone and if they so desire, they could actually co-consel with you and work with you and join in with you on these projects. >> Yeah, there there's a lot of opportunity for people to get involved. We we know there's a lot of reasons why people are hesitant, but I I think this is going to be helpful us just sharing a lot of what we learned over the years and then we'll ultimately be able to better serve the clients and the more people we have in the fight here, the better it's going to be for everybody. >> That's amazing. And I'm I'm so excited about next week for doing that conversation. I'm very excited about the end of the month. How do people find you in the meantime, Joe? Uh, I think a lot of people follow me on LinkedIn. So, if you're active on there, give me a follow, send me a connection. Would love to connect with you. Or they could just reach out to me at Rosen injury lawyers. Um, or you'll see me on the circuit tour hanging out with Michael. >> What is your what is your hashtag that you like to use again? >> Oh, Joe does law. >> Joe doesLaw. So, if you type in Joe doeslaw, if you can't spell Fantini, which is pretty easy to spell, but if you can't, type in Joe doesLaw write into LinkedIn and you'll see his beautiful face. And if you wanted to follow me as well, it's masstorr Michael. And we will love to see you on the circuit. And we look forward to seeing each other and all of you join us on a podcast next week and hopefully also on that webinar. That webinar is going to be stock full of information that is going to be a deep dive and you'll really be able to understand the the scope and the horizon and why this is something that uh we believe in you know together so enthusiastically and so genuinely is because we think we can actually help a lot of people and that's you know a way of being better together. any uh any closing parting thoughts before we before we we we head off and sign off? >> Yeah, thank thanks for having me. I I know it was a lot, but uh in this series, I know we'll continue to break down these in in more details, but uh reach out to us if you guys have any questions or need any information. >> Sounds good. Sounds good. Well, thank everybody. Thank you everybody for watching. Thank you Joe for joining and we'll see you next time. Love you guys.

metadata.title: Ep 295 - How One Mass Tort Firm Uses Supio, the AI Platform for PI Lawyers
metadata.author: LawNext
metadata.shortDescription:
Supio, an AI-driven platform developed specifically for personal injury lawyers, has been generating a lot of buzz. On the heels of reporting record growth last year and raising $25 million in Series A funding in October, last month it raised another $60 million in a Series B round. But what do the lawyers who use the platform think of it? On today’s LawNext, we hear from one of those lawyers, as well as from the company’s cofounder and CEO.
Our guests today are:

Tyler Schneider, managing partner of the personal injury law firm TorHoerman Law. Schneider was an early adopter of Supio. He and his firm used it to help obtain a $495 million verdict against Abbott Labs in a case involving allegations that cow’s milk-based infant formula caused intestinal inflammation in premature babies.

Jerry Zhou, the CEO of Supio who cofounded it in 2021 together with his childhood friend and coworker Kyle Lam after having held product management and engineering roles at Microsoft and Avalara. 

In their conversation with host Bob Ambrogi, Zhou and Schneider talk about the development of Supio, its real-world impact on plaintiffs’ lawyers, and their wish lists for further development of the product. They also share their thoughts on how AI is likely to reshape PI practice more broadly.

The dark side of personal injury law rarely gets talked about publicly, until now.

In this episode, K'Lee Terrazas sits down with Jimmy Goff, second-generation personal injury attorney and founder of Goff Law in Dallas–Fort Worth, TX. Jimmy exposes the hidden dangers PI lawyers face when it comes to shady marketing, illegal client solicitation, barratry, and unethical lead generation practices that put firms at risk.

From his early career in insurance defense to building his own PI firm, Jimmy shares why tort reform is gaining ground, how lack of enforcement fuels misconduct, and what ethical firms can do to protect their reputation while still scaling profitably.

What You’ll Learn:

Why DA’s rarely prosecute barratry, even though it’s a felony
How shady lead gen companies can put your license in jeopardy
The real risks of pay-per-lead marketing for law firms
How to audit your marketing for compliance and integrity
Why storytelling can reshape public perception of PI lawyers
Low-cost marketing strategies that outperform big ad spends
How to build a trusted referral network without ads

Marketing Debate You Can’t Miss:
Jimmy and K'Lee break down the false promises of “secret sauce” lead generation vs. the power of transparent, ROI-driven marketing systems you own. You’ll also hear real examples of story-driven branding that earns trust and separates ethical firms from ambulance chasers.

Practical Takeaways for Law Firms:

Strengthen your inner-circle referral network
Create video content that humanizes your brand
Turn courtroom moments into powerful marketing assets
Use storytelling and PR to flip the “ambulance chaser” narrative

If you’re a PI lawyer, law firm owner, or legal marketer, this episode delivers an inside look at legal ethics, brand strategy, and marketing with integrity.

About Jimmy Goff:
Recognized by Best Lawyers: Ones to Watch and Super Lawyers Rising Stars, Jimmy Goff focuses on wrongful death, product liability, and complex injury cases. His mission: fight for clients while challenging unethical practices in the legal industry.

This video is for educational purposes only. It is not legal, financial, or professional advice. Always consult with a qualified professional before making business decisions. No guarantees are made regarding results.

metadata.title: How Filevine, MyCase and Smokeball Won Small Law Firms | Ep 4
metadata.author: Sagar Pratap Singh
metadata.shortDescription:
A small law firm can go live on new software on Friday and be back on spreadsheets by Monday. That Monday is why selling to small firms is so hard, and why Filevine, MyCase and Smokeball are worth studying: each won this buyer with a different move.

In Episode 4 of Who Brings The Business (WBTB), Sagar Pratap Singh breaks down how three practice management companies won small and mid-sized law firms. Filevine went deep in personal injury and litigation before going wide. MyCase built around the client relationship and later joined AffiniPay, the company behind LawPay, where firms already took payments. Smokeball sold lawyers their own time back with automatic time capture. The episode closes with three questions every firm owner should ask before switching platforms, and what anyone selling to small businesses can borrow from all three.

Welcome to The Legal Intake Experts podcast! For more than a decade, Answering Legal has helped growing law firms ensure they never miss a chance to connect with new leads. Now, we’re pulling back the curtain to share our best strategies for strengthening your intake process and turning more callers into clients.

In our second episode, hosts Nick Werker and Tony Prieto dive into the essentials of building a strong legal intake process. They stress the importance of having a well-structured intake script and strategizing intake calls to turn leads into clients. 

Nick and Tony also discuss the value of using a CRM, effective client communication, and the benefits of employing a third-party answering service. With practical tips and insights, this episode provides a comprehensive guide for law firms looking to improve their client intake process and ensure they never miss a chance to connect with new leads.

metadata.title: David Perla on Litigation Finance, Law Firm Investment, and the Future of Legal Talent
metadata.author: The Future Is Bright Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
When permanent capital, AI disruption, and a rapidly fracturing talent market collide inside the legal industry, the old rules for how law firms grow, get funded, and build their next generation of lawyers stop making sense.

David Perla, Vice Chair of Burford Capital, joins hosts Chris Batz and Howard Rosenberg to break down why permanent capital is a fundamentally different proposition than traditional private equity for boutiques and founder-controlled firms ready to grow, and why the AmLaw 100 is unlikely to move anytime soon.

The more urgent conversation is about what neither capital nor strategy can fully solve. Law firm leaders are making multi-year associate class decisions without any reliable sense of what their workforce looks like in twelve months. Startups that needed fifty people eighteen months ago now run on seven or eight. The associate pipeline, in-house departments, recruiting timelines: all of it is under pressure that is accelerating faster than most leaders want to admit.

Perla's advice is deceptively simple. Get curious. Ask hard questions of people who think differently. The firms that navigate this moment well are the ones willing to challenge assumptions before the market forces the issue.

Episode Breakdown:
00:00 Introduction: David Perla, Vice Chair of Burford Capital
06:05 Building Pangea3 and Pioneering Legal Outsourcing
12:51 How Burford Capital Invests in the Legal Industry
23:44 Where Private Capital Is Heading in Law Firm Investment
29:51 AI, Legal Talent, and the Associate Pipeline Crisis
39:23 Legal Tech Valuations and the Coming Shakeout
46:06 Advice for Law Firm Leaders Navigating Disruption


Listen and learn from Chris Batz and Howard Rosenberg’s bi-weekly podcast, The Future is Bright.

Enjoy a front-row seat as Chris and Howard speak with thought-provoking C-Suite executives and leaders from corporations, both public and private, professional service firms, and of course, the legal industry from around the United States.

Podcast production and show notes provided by HiveCast.fm

the internet and technology could do

to paraphrase what a friend said to me

throughout college I just sort of had

so now.

videos.full_text: Greetings listeners, when law firms meet capital markets and AI hits legal talent, not all money or strategy looks the same. In this episode, Burford Capital Vice Chair David Perla joins Howard and I to unpack how litigation finance, private equity, and permanent capital are reshaping law firms, talent, and the future of the industry. Enjoy. Welcome everyone to The Future Is Bright podcast. My name is Chris Bats and joined by my co-host Howard Rosenberg. Howard and I are at the center of law firm talent and strategic growth here in New York City. Howard is a partner and the head of talent intelligence and acquisitions at Berkeleys and Bunnell, and I advise and facilitate law firm M&A and PE investments at Columbus Street. And today, we have a very exciting guest, David Perla, Vice Chair of Burford Capital. David, welcome to the podcast. >> Thanks so much, Chris. Great to be here. >> Uh David, if you would do me a favor and provide my audience just a quick overview of your role right now at uh Burford. >> Absolutely. So, I'm currently Vice Chair of Burford Capital. My remit is fairly broad and and fairly diverse. It includes uh public policy, communications, public relations. It It overlaps with marketing, so all of our public-facing functions. And I also have an active role working with our development office, which is what we term all of our non-core litigation finance investments. So, um that includes legal tech investments, direct and in funds. That includes law firm equity, and that includes investments in managed service organizations. >> Excellent. So, David, just out of the gate, I just happened to notice you cut your teeth on big law. Was it Katten that you started with? >> Yes, at the at what was then Rosenman & Colin and then merged into into Katten Muchin. So, I spent nearly 5 years as an M&A lawyer in the 90s. >> It's you amazing. And but it seems like you quickly went in-house and took on various roles. What what got your interest to do more of the business side? >> So I had a what looks to be a fairly typical career in in hindsight, which is nearly 5 years as a corporate lawyer in the 90s. In my mind it was one of the greatest times to be a a young lawyer. It was the the sort of the dawn of internet 1.0 really happened in '94 '95, so I started in 1994. And by the late 90s, by the time I I was facing the decision do I want to stay and make partner, there was just so much excitement around what the internet and technology could do that to paraphrase what a friend said to me was if I'd been alive during the Renaissance, I I'd like to think I would have at least tried painting. And that's what it felt like and I had the opportunity to go in-house at at the parent company of monster.com, which is a very fast-growing job board and and resume board at the time. They were looking for someone who understood the internet and technology, but also understood M&A, so it was it was really a perfect fit. It was exactly what I wanted to do and exactly what they needed and I ended up spending 5 and 1/2 years there as a as a result. >> And David, if I start at the beginning, why did you want to go to law school and become a lawyer before the the the Caplin and the and the track that you that you that you've got through? >> Yeah, we have to go to the wayback machine, Howard. >> Yeah, I know. >> So I I was one of those kids who if you'd asked me when I was young what I want to be, I would have said a lawyer and I had no idea why or what that meant. So for for me it was always a path. I it was a reasonably good student and throughout college I just sort of had the expectation I would go and again was very fortunate and I went to a law school that number one is very interdisciplinary at the time and more so now. And also for the most part sends their graduates into large law firms and so I followed a well-trodden path. I I veered from that well-trodden path 10 years into my career by founding a company, but at the time I sort of always expected I would go to law school. The main difference, you know, Howard would be if you'd asked me when I was young, I would have said, "Oh, well, yeah, I'll be a courtroom lawyer." It was in law school I discovered I really liked corporate and finance and and the math side of law. >> And so you were part of Pangea. Talk us a little bit about that journey being at Pangea and then also selling to Thomson Reuters. >> Sure. So in many respects, I am a creature of um what people will call luck. We call it the intersection of hard work and opportunity. Um I I spent 10 years practicing, nearly five at the law firm and and over five at Monster. And somewhere kind of nine years in, so a year before I left, I sat down with my my then best friend from law school, Sanjay Kamlani. And we he had gone in-house at a client of his that was a startup outsourcing company in India. I was in-house and we had been exposed to entrepreneurs and we had seen the best of what entrepreneurship brings and both had caught the bug in some respect. But weren't sure what the idea was, but but we were we were both sure we wanted to start businesses by sometime in 2003. Uh and we also were exposed to people who to be frank were very encouraging. A lot of people were were saying to both of us in separate conversations, "Y- you have what it takes to start a business." which I think a lot of lawyers reflexively think they don't. They think there's some magic um or some training you need to be an entrepreneur. That's changed, but at the time, 20 years ago, certainly lawyers didn't think that way. And um we sat down and started spitballing ideas and and ultimately came up with the idea that what we really knew how to do was law, technology, and recruiting based on on kind of what we had done for the last 10 years. We had a incredible network and expertise in India, primarily through Sanjay, but I'd also done a lot of business there and I'd been there already at that point. And we came up with the business plan and and then it took about eight months and we we quit our jobs. Um but it really was I would say exposure to entrepreneurs in the while buying my case, while buying companies, in Sanjay's case, working for two guys who had quit, you know, prestigious investment banks to start a company. >> And what was that investment process like in the early days? Because you kind of were pioneering a business that never really kind of went through this process before, right? >> It's such a It's such a fun question for me, Howard, because um no one had really done it in legal and um the inv- investment environment looked different. There was no such thing as a SAFE in 2004. No one had ever The concept hadn't been invented on the West Coast yet. So, everyone was doing sort of traditional seed round preferred equity investments. Um At the time, I knew how to do those. I had I had represented a lot of startups in in the course of my practice i- in the law firm. So, it'd been 5 years, but I really knew how to do those deals. And we had a reasonably good network. By the time we we left our jobs, each of us had three or four professional colleagues who had committed to invest and and enough friends and family that we felt certain we could invest. But to to really answer the question, what we learned along the way was none of that really matters. At the end of the day, when you ask someone to take a dollar out of their pocket and give it to you, you're going to learn what's wrong with your business model. And um what ours really depended on, what people really wanted to see, because we were an outsourcing business, was who who was on our team, who had committed to join the company. And so, we really started the company in earnest in August of '04, and it was only 6 weeks later we got on a plane to India to go recruit. That that was really what it all depended on, and once we proved to people we had the team, it really wasn't hard to convince um clients to to at least try us, and it wasn't hard to convince people to invest in us, understanding that, you know, statistically, likely to fail. Most most startups do. So, we didn't hide that fact. Um and, you know, we had to negotiate. We found a lead investor, but that part I knew how to do. Um I And I want to sort of maybe address a question you didn't ask, but I think it's a valuable one. I think today's environment, in some respects, is not healthy for entrepreneurs. Um the valuations have gotten too high, and they they force the entrepreneurs to once they get through their seed round to try and either not raise more money because they're trying to keep the they they don't want to do a down round, or to try and get revenue growth rates or ARR growth rates that aren't that they're not ready for. And I I don't think it's a good dynamic. I tell a lot of entrepreneurs, it's okay if your valuation is a little lower, take the pressure off yourself. I I appreciate you don't want to be diluted, but it's too much pressure to raise money. You know, I see startups at you know, cap you know, they're capped at let's say 25 or 30 million dollars, which they think becomes their valuation, and it's not sustainable for the bulk of companies. >> Well, let's let's let's stay on the arc of your career at the moment because that So So Pangea 3 sold out to Thomson, and then um you wound up at Bloomberg. So, what happened there? Did you kind of Did they find you? You found them? What was the the motivating reason to kind of join Bloomberg? >> So, they found me. I spent 2 years at Thomson Reuters, very happily. We We sold our business. We understood it was their business after we sold it. We We had a happy post-exit relationship. We remained happily friends with many people at Thomson Reuters. Um and I By the way, I attribute that for both of you guys to to us being transactional lawyers as we we know how to get along with people, but we also understood when someone buys your company, it's theirs. It's not yours. It's not your child. It's a company, and they're going to largely do things you disagree with. So, we knew that. We knew that intellectually and emotionally. Um and then we were done. And And I was thought I would spend the rest of my career doing startup things, and my phone rang in January of 2014. So, it was a year after I left Thomson Reuters. It was a recruiter uh asking about Bloomberg Law. We had known about the product cuz the the work to to build the database was actually done in India by a competitor's a competitor of ours. So, we knew the product. And we just started chatting, and over the course of a five-month process, um I I became convinced one I could do the job, but also there was an experience set that I didn't have. You know, I was 44 years old at the time, and the the part of my experience that I I had never done was I had never run a large unit at a large company. I sold Pangea 3000 Reuters, but that's very different than coming in and and having 420 odd people reporting at a company like Bloomberg, and I'd never really worked at a place like Bloomberg, which, you know, if you if you grow up in New York, you know, it's it's practically a household name. So, for me it was really too good to pass up, even though I'd always thought I'd stay on the entrepreneurial side. >> Well, the the that really next big move is where you are today, um being that you're at Burford. Um I'd love to hear that story. Getting to Burford and your track, um I mean, you were there about a about a year and a half before COVID happened. But, yeah, I'm just curious about that journey. >> So, Burford may be the perfect fit, which explains why I'm why I'm going on eight years here and and and I'm vice chair. I started out as a managing director, became the co-chief operating officer in January of 2020, and we did a reorg to break down all the geographic barriers right before COVID. So, a lot of things sort of worked out, but uh Burford was was looking for a a role that I would describe as um highly unique, almost idiosyncratic. That was a function of Burford having bought um a private fund called GK C back in 2016, and the three founders, one of whom is now back, Travis Lickliter is now back at Burford. But the three founders had brought particular skill sets and then at the end of 17 they left and Burford recognized that it wanted to replicate some of those skill sets and went out to market to find them. And um I met Chris Bogart uh who's a a fascinating person and you know, kind of a remarkable founder public company CEO. Um we sat down on a couple of occasions. I met a bunch of the team and it was really something he said to me that convinced me to to come work back at what was then a a UK listed public company. Now we're listed in New York and in London. Um I was sort of happily doing stuff with Sanjay again. I was doing entrepreneurial. I had I was making money. It wasn't I was not an unhappy person in my life and he at the end of the second meeting he said, "Oh, come on David." He goes, "You're bored. I can see it right now." He goes, "You you need to be knee deep five days a week, sleeves rolled up building something and breaking things." I got in the car home and I called my wife and I said, "You know, he's kind of right." He kind of he just picked up on you know, to the extent I was happy it was not going to last very long just sort of being out in the market and here was this cool opportunity. It was a platform wanted a you know, wanted to continue what was a very fast growth trajectory uh populated by the smartest people in the legal business and and legal smart, but Burford is really really smart. metadata.title: Is a Lawsuit a Financial Asset? Inside Litigation Finance
metadata.author: TALKSONLAW
metadata.shortDescription:
What if a lawsuit is a financial asset? Chris Bogart — co-founder and CEO of Burford Capital, the world's largest litigation finance firm — joins New Law Order to explain how legal claims get underwritten, priced, and financed, and what that reveals about the structural limits of the traditional law-firm partnership.

In this episode of New Law Order, co-hosts Joel Cohen and Yale Law Professor John Morley talk with Bogart about:
- How litigation finance began (from Cravath to GC of Time Warner)
- Why law firms aren't structured to finance contingency litigation
- Treating legal claims as portfolio assets
- Risk, capital allocation, and institutional money in disputes
- What it means for clients, firms, and access to justice


New Law Order is a podcast and limited series about the coming shake-up in legal services, co-hosted by Joel Cohen and Yale Law Professor John Morley.

Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/new-law-order/id1868796372
Facebook: http://www.facebook.com/talksonlaw
Instagram: http://www.instagram.com/talksonlaw
X/Twitter: http://www.twitter.com/talksonlaw

And so the company then turned around and uses that capital in its business in a more efficient way and investors are pleased with that net outcome. >> Okay, I got it. So that was the case in which you weren't financing legal fees, you were financing recoveries really. You were financing a company's balance sheet, not unlike a traditional corporate lender. Yeah. >> That's right. Except that, you know, just look at those two words that you used though, balance sheet and lender. Um the balance sheet part, remember that affirmative litigation doesn't show up on a corporate balance sheet. So, it doesn't even show up in the notes. Defensive litigation does, but but affirmative litigation doesn't, even if it's going really well. A company can't take it onto their balance sheet and book value against it. So, it's invisible on the balance sheet. >> Yeah, I was going to say it's a hidden asset. >> It's a hidden asset, and we're not the lender because our capital is non-recourse, and so we're not adding to the company's leverage. Um we're putting capital, we're putting invisible capital against the invisible asset. And either the case will win, in which case we'll share the proceeds, or the case will lose, in which case we lose our capital and the company has no obligation. >> Hm. But, in the meantime, the company gets more cash. >> Yes. >> So, Chris, in a sense, are you are you getting a discount on these assets because they're hidden? Is it the fact that accounting's structure has made this decision that's creating a lot of value for you? >> I think there's something to that, but I don't see that changing in the world of accounting. And so, you could say the same thing about lots of other, you know, corporate vehicles to maximize balance sheet flexibility, like leasing. You know, before there was leasing, you know, the only way to buy a big piece of capital equipment was with cash. And now you can lease it, and that has a very different balance sheet implication. And leasing companies made money because that was desirable. So, I'm effectively doing the same thing. I'm effectively doing leasing for litigation. >> Hm. Hm. >> [snorts] >> A little bit of analogy. Let's talk about AI for a minute. Everybody's talking about AI. We talk a lot about AI. I'll I'll let Joel I'll let Joel jump in here. >> No, no, please, John. I'm I'm just fascinated what what Chris is is seeing in in his industry. I mean, we didn't talk about how how you find top experts, but I know that that's been, you know, one of the [clears throat] secret sauces, I suppose, of Burford is is bringing in people who, you know, can can analyze cases better than most. I'm wondering, are you seeing value already with AI in this space? Is it opening up new fields for you? I'm I'm curious your thoughts. >> So, we're seeing AI have an impact, and I I'll use AI sort of writ large. I'll I'll I'll use AI to encompass complex technology. Um with machine learning. We're seeing AI in a couple of of interesting ways. Um the first, and and right now, possibly the most important, is at the law firm level, in fact, because the ability what what's happened over the last 20 years or so is an explosion of data in the hands of clients. Right? So, if you go back, you know, when I started practicing law, just to date myself, you know, we were still living in largely a paper-based world. And so, most of the stuff flowed through people's offices in paper. They threw out most of it at the end of the day. And so, as a result, their footprint was fairly narrow. It was just the things that they had elected to put in the filing cabinets outside their door, um that that gave rise to litigation discovery. And so, you had a world where young lawyers could page through the documents and figure out what was responsive and what wasn't. That's all gone today. Now, you've got these enormous pools of data because of retention obligations. And so, they're unmanageable by humans. And so, you had a an interim period there where the data pools were very large, and the technology able to assess the data pools was not as robust as it should have been. Um and that is changing now. And so you're getting much better ability to analyze those pools of data from people. And that's doing two things. It's making it easier to assess litigation risk. And it's also showing up more potential litigation claims. Um because now you can use sophisticated technology to start mapping behavior. You know, when when people conspire to fix fix prices, they don't tend to do it nakedly, right? It's not like Joel and John say going for, you know, email each other and say, "Hey, my profits are kind of low this year. Why don't we agree not to compete in in Chicago so that I can raise my prices." You know, you don't see those documents very often. >> Sure, John, send me over the contract. >> [laughter] >> But instead, what you see is that Joel and John's calendars disclose that they met for coffee at the industry conference. And lo and behold, a few days later, you know, Chicago pricing started to climb. And and you see that repeated then when they went to the next industry conference and figured out that worked well for them. And now they're going to do the same thing in LA. >> [snorts] >> So So there's all sorts of uses of technology at the law firm discovery level that I think are very helpful um and that have a second order impact on our business because we get better quality analysis than we used to. Then you go to our business and the question is can we can we make increasing use of technology to bring in data and make our investment decisions even better? And that's what we've been investing in at Burford for the last 7 years. We started investing in our quantitative resources and our technology resources in 2018. And we've now built that to be really a coequal part of our investment process sitting beside the skilled experienced litigators that we have. And that looks to all sorts of things. It looks to settlement dynamics, it looks to, you know, predictability factors in courts, but it also does some other things that are relevant to investing capital, which is a time-based undertaking. And it looks at things, you know, pretty basic things like, you know, how long is this judge going to take to get through this case? What do we know about the predilections of this judge and how he or she manages the docket? Um so, there are lots of things going on at sometimes at a fairly basic level and sometimes at quite a sophisticated level. We use AI technologies, for example, to to screen for new potential cases. So, it's a We've got a wide range of technological applications and, you know, as a as a former technologist, I think that's only going to continue to be better and more value-enhancing. >> How do you see AI changing the business models of law firms? You've already talked about the use in litigation discovery and mastering comprehension of the fact. Do you Do you think the prediction will come true that associates become less useful than they were before? >> Well, I think that the job becomes different. Um and that has been occurring anyway with technology. You know, the the job of the associate when I was an associate in 1992 is certainly different than than the pre-AI associate in 2020. Um and so, the skill set is different um and I think that will continue to evolve. So, I'm not sure that we, you know, there are all these, you know, horse door, oh, there will be no associates. I don't think that's true. Um I I do think that it removes a degree of the drudgery of the jobs. Um both for law firm associates and look at investment banking associates. You know, you used to spend hours and hours and hours at night pulling concepts. Um now you can do that with the pressing button. Um does that mean that you might need fewer associates? It might mean that. Um it might well mean that and therefore it might also mean um the need for a change in the the pyramid um billing structure of some of the big law firms. Um but I don't think that we're talking about eliminating the practice of law and transforming it to to machines anytime soon. >> I suspect it may mean that firms will be a little more willing to take on alternate fee structures. Uh especially as you know as they're they're seeing efficiencies raised um interfering with their billable hour and maybe understanding uh better the value of cases or the value of transactions or the value of disputes. >> I think that's very possible. The The other thing that I think is very very significant um especially on the litigation side is that technology has enabled the creation of the litigation boutique in a way that wasn't the case before. So if you think about big case litigation 20 years ago, it was really only done by the big law firms because you needed the army of people, you needed all the resources that those firms had. And now >> We'll bury you in paper. >> Exactly. Now look at Now look at how many boutiques there are. And so part of the reason is it avoids conflicts and so on but part of it is because you can stand up a dozen people and practice law at a very high level because of the advances in technology in a way that you absolutely could not have done before. And that's exciting for me on a number of reasons. It's exciting because it dislocates the market Joel as you were as you were describing and it lets all sorts of different models bloom. But it's also exciting for me as Burford because those boutiques generally speaking need to be financed. And so those are creating more opportunities for us as people want to leave the often the corporate funded comfort of big law firms and strike out on their own. >> Chris, before we let you go, what are you excited about in the next, you know, 10 years, 5 years? >> I'm super excited with the opportunity here. Um and and the reason for that is going right back to where we started. You've got these two pools of users. You've got law firms and you've got corporates. And you know, I talk to lots of people on both sides of that aisle. I never go and talk to a group of CFOs or CEOs and have even a single one of them say to me, "Oh, I'm perfectly happy. I'm perfectly happy with what we spend on legal stuff. I have no complaints, no issues. I'm fine for that to just carry on without any change." Every single one of them doesn't like it. Every single one of them would like something different. And then over here at law firms, you have an industry that has changed some amount in the last 25 years, but is still pretty darn recognizable if you go back 25 years in time. So, you've got a big, profitable, but relatively change-resistant business over here. But all of them know who we are and know what we offer and know what we can do to help them. And so, being able to continue to put those two sides together with us in the middle is to me an enormously exciting thing to do, especially as we get to do it ever more around the world and in really big, interesting complicated pieces of litigation. So, it's just for me, it's a combination of a really interesting business dynamic and just a whole bunch of intellectual candy um that goes along with it. >> Given that our audience for this is going to be mostly lawyers, another big winner is the legal industry in general. You're financing a lot of lawyers' day-to-day jobs. >> We are. We're probably, if you look at the numbers, we're probably the largest single buyer of legal services in the world today. Um and that's a fun place to be. Lets me talk to lots of smart people. >> Chris Bogart is the founder and CEO of Burford Capital. Chris, it's been a real pleasure. >> Thanks, Chris. >> Great being with [music] you. Thanks, guys. >> John, what do you think of the conversation with Chris? >> Uh, I really enjoyed it. I learned so much and I'm really appreciated his willingness to join us. >> I know, I got to say, it made me think, should I own Burford stock? >> I wish I had bought Burford stock 15 years ago as well. >> I know. >> And look, I find the thesis compelling that there's still a long a lot of room for growth in this industry. >> I do think we will be seeing more innovation in this space and I wonder to what extent AI will make it more affordable to do financing to even smaller cases, cases that aren't lucrative enough lucrative enough for Chris at this point. >> Yeah, I guess if a lot of what makes lending to small cases difficult is the expense of the underwriting analysis, one might hope that AI tools would simplify that underwriting analysis and standardize it to unlock financing for smaller cases. >> Or the discovery, maybe it'll make discovery cheaper so that we'll see. We'll see about this. >> Yeah, I mean, in a way this gets to the heart of the debate about AI's effect on the legal profession. Will it shrink the legal profession by reducing the amount of services that are required or will it grow it or keep it the same by by expanding the by meeting more of the currently unmet need. There's so much legal work that doesn't get done right now due to cost. >> Most of it. >> Yeah, most of it. Yeah. >> I mean, no dispute that I've had has gone to litigation, knock on wood. >> God willing. >> But, part of it is because I don't want to have to fork up the capital and I don't have Chris Bogart on speed dial ready to loan me an amount that's beneath their interest level. >> Yeah. Yeah, that's right. You really would have to um to reach below the highest dollar value litigation. You really would need kind of a different underwriting model. >> What did you think of his argument against the argument that litigation finance is a negative or against public policy? >> In my mind, there's no question that it results in more litigation. That's kind of the point. Obviously, many of those lawsuits would be brought. But, surely if if litigation financing is truly adding value, then we would have to believe that there are more lawsuits brought and perhaps they're litigated for longer than they wouldn't than they would be otherwise. However, I find completely compelling his argument that it's only financing meritorious cases. I mean, if his success rate really is as high as he says it is, then he's not financing vexatious litigation. It just doesn't make sense for him. >> Yeah, it seems like the vexatious litigation is not going to come from outside capital. It's going to come from, you know, an extremely rich plaintiff who is willing to take the loss. >> Yeah, I mean, I I think we've all seen that. There are people who litigate out of spite. And the nice thing about a litigation funder is that it's completely impersonal and cold-hearted about it, which on the one hand makes them kind of scary and on the other hand makes them uh less scary. >> Objective. [laughter] >> Yeah, that's right. That's right. >> I love talking to to you about this cuz I could just see whenever he was discussing kind of the structural imperfections or the peccadillos of the law industry, I I just see your excitement. >> that's >> I mean, generational conflict is a topic that fascinates me. I'm writing a book about it. The basic issue is that unlike in conventional public companies where the equity lasts forever, in law firms, the equity interests only last as long as a partner's tenure with a firm. When you retire, your partnership interest is gone. And that creates all sorts of difficult challenges in law firms. One of them is the inability to finance activities over the long firm. In an ordinary public company, if you do something today that will generate profits in the future, the stock price increases immediately today in anticipation of that. So, you can reap the value of it even if you're going to sell tomorrow. You can't really do that in a law firm, and I feel like litigation financing is is one way, not the only way, but one way to cope with that problem, and for that reason, I find it very exciting. >> I was a little surprised to hear that they've taken equity positions, obviously not in the US, but in law firms. Um yeah, what did you think about that? It seems to me related to their core business, but if they see so much upside in cases, are they buying Yeah, it was kind of surprising me that they would buy the whole uh buy the whole cow instead of the milk. >> Yeah, you know, with every provider of capital, there's always needs to be a fit between the provider's expertise in assessing information and the business of the company. You know, like hedge funds have particular domains of expertise, private equity funds have particular domains of expertise, and even if there are opportunities out there, if they lie beyond that domain of expertise, often the investors will avoid it because they feel like we can't really evaluate it. And for a litigation funder, really so much of the value of the business is tied up in the expertise of evaluating cases. So, it does feel like a little bit of a um a risk or a stretch for a litigation funder to finance not a set of cases, but a whole law firm, which might include um you know, things beyond the immediate portfolio. He did say that it was a litigation only law firm. So, it meant that he didn't have to evaluate risk. Also, it was a law firm and not another kind of business. And one can imagine that if this if the portfolio of cases was large enough relative to the size of the firm, there might not be that much of a difference between financing cases and financing the firm. You know, let me just riff on this for a moment, Joel, and say um we talked with Chris a lot about uh equity stakes in law firms, whether there might come a day when it's legally allowed outside of Utah and Arizona. To me, as a kind of corporate lawyer, the line between equity and debt is thin and porous. And you can construct a nominally There's no interest There's no problem with extending debt to law firms. But you can construct the terms of a debt interest in such a way that it begins to look a lot like equity. And so, one wonders if one of the workarounds for the current legal prohibitions on investments that produce equity stakes in law firms is just to offer debt interests that functionally look like equity. >> Yeah, we spoke with John Quinn for this series as well, and there we have a mega litigation law firm. You could imagine you would you know, a company like Burford coming in and saying, "Hey look, we'll buy, you know, a tranche of the upside of your patent litigation cases." >> That's right. And if you buy a tranche of the upside of 100% of Quinn Emanuel's cases, then you've just made an equity investment. Yeah, like I mean, it gets it gets very close. Or you could say, "We're taking an interest rate that varies with your profitability," which is functionally like profitability, right? >> The other side of the investing in law firms um point that I think we're were making was maybe it's just uh getting a bigger slice of the upside. You know, if you're able to you imagine a world where where there weren't these constraints on capital investing in lawsuits, maybe Burford would want to buy the entire case and run the entire case with its own, you know, chosen experts. And maybe that's what they'll be able to do with these you know, boutique law firms that they're taking equity positions in. >> Yeah, well, you know, we didn't ask Chris we should have asked him whether this equity interest was paired with any degree of control or oversight. Also, one of the long-running controversies in litigation financing is the degree of control over the litigation >> Right. >> that the that the funders have. Um but I agree. I mean if New York and Florida and other big states lift their restrictions on investor ownership of law firms, it's a very quick transition from for Burford Capital and others in its industry from financing lawsuits to running lawsuits. That that that's that's how it that's how it happens. >> be a logical next step. >> Yeah, yeah, it's one of the many ways in which the transition would happen. And in any event, it already establishes proof of concept for how these things could work. >> I found it fascinating and I hope that our listeners did. And if there are comments or questions, you know, we've been asking this I hope it's not redundant for our regular listeners, but we'll provide uh an email in the show notes in case you have suggestions or ideas on how to make the series better. >> Yes, thanks very much. We always uh welcome your comments and thoughts. >> That didn't sound genuine, John. It seemed like you really don't welcome them. >> [laughter] >> But he does. He does. I know he does. Thanks for watching and John, thanks for the time. >> Thank you. >> Mhm.

metadata.title: Mass Tort Power Rankings: The "Rocket Docket" Surges & A Game-Changing $27M Precedent
metadata.author: Jon and Marc
metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome back to Tort Talk! With the summer season kicking off, the mass tort landscape is moving faster than ever. In this episode, co-host Marc Rioux sits down with mass tort powerhouse Joseph Fantini of Rosen Injury Lawyers to break down our highly anticipated Monthly Mass Tort Power Rankings. While Jon Robinson is away on paternity leave catching up on some much-needed sleep, the guys jump straight into the dockets that are generating the most leverage, the fastest trial dates, and the biggest settlements for plaintiffs.

We dive into a comprehensive review of the active dockets shaping law firm case acquisition strategies across the country. Joe provides a masterclass on how the NEC litigation successfully broke through defense barriers to survive a crucial motion to dismiss, paving the way for upcoming trials. We also check in on the massive volume behind the pre-COVID Bair Hugger docket and how parallel state court actions like the JCCP in California are keeping litigations like Video Game Addiction moving forward even without an active MDL.

Corporate defense maneuvers take center stage as we break down how certain tech litigations are fighting high-stakes battles over minor-consent arbitration clauses. For firms looking to optimize their immediate marketing spend, Joe highlights tactical intake adjustments, including the essential dual-front screening parameters required for the expanding Weight Loss Drug gastrointestinal and vision loss dockets, and updates from the recent face-to-face Uber sex abuse mediations.

Finally, we analyze the structural darlings of the current landscape: the historic velocity of the Depo Provera rocket docket, the massive 12,000+ file volume pushing Hair Relaxer toward its fall deadlines, a shocking $27 million settlement that has completely shaken up the tech-defense landscape, and the crucial appellate arguments that could completely revive the Tylenol docket overnight.

Tune in to get the raw docket updates you need to confidently direct your firm's capital.

0:50 - #10

18:37 - #1

#MassTorts #powerrankings #lawfirms  #HairRelaxerLawsuit #depoprovera  #weightlossdrugs  #OzempicLawsuit #legalmarketing  #CaseAcquisition #torttalk  #RosenInjuryLawyers #MDLUpdates #personalinjurylawyers 

About The Jon & Marc Podcast.

The Jon & Marc Podcast is for lawyers who care about growth and the bottom line. Jon and Marc interview leaders in plaintiff law to break down how major cases are built, how firms scale, and how strategy plays out behind the scenes. If you want to understand how the biggest players in the space think and operate, you’re in the right place. New episodes every week.

Welcome back to another episode of the Law, AI & Money podcast, hosted by Rocco Strangio. Today, Rocco is joined by Cara Wall, an attorney and partner at the Law Firm of Zoll & Kranz. After graduating from the University of Michigan Law School in 2012, Cara joined Zoll & Kranz to work in their mass tort department. Cara has extensive experience as a mass tort attorney and has since worked on numerous mass tort cases ranging from DePuy ASR to her Executive Committee appointment in the Exactech MDL. In today’s conversation, Rocco and Cara discuss the evolution of mass torts, the role of AI for attorneys, and the need to be tech forward in the ever changing legal space.
